domain.title: Foundations
domain.tag: machine model · Python & C · data structures · discrete math · calculus · toolchain
domain.why: Right now a computer is a box that does what you tap on it. By the end of this domain it stops being magic. You'll know exactly what happens between you pressing a key and a letter appearing on screen, what a variable actually is inside the machine, and why a program can crash. This is the one domain almost nothing else in Whetstone can skip: memory before pointers, pointers before data structures, loops before recursion. Go slowly here. Everything later assumes you can do this in your sleep, and it's supposed to feel almost too easy — that's how you know it actually stuck.

sections.note: Everything later assumes this picture. Build it once, properly.

L0.body:
1 switch = 1 bit (0 or 1) -> 2 states
1 byte = 8 bits -> 2**8 = 256 distinct patterns (0..255)
1 KiB = 1024 bytes   1 MiB = 1024 KiB   1 GiB = 1024 MiB
CPU register width = 'word' (typically 64 bits = 8 bytes on modern machines)
Memory is an ordered street of numbered byte mailboxes (addresses 0, 1, 2...)
L0.cloze: 1 byte = {{c1::8}} bits, which encodes {{c2::256}} distinct values.

concepts.L1: A bit is one binary digit—a single physical switch holding 0 or 1. A byte is a bundle of 8 bits and is the fundamental unit of computer memory: every byte has its own distinct numerical address. A word is the natural chunk of data a CPU processes at one time (usually 64 bits / 8 bytes on modern computers).
concepts.L2: A common trap is thinking a bit has its own memory address. Memory is addressed byte-by-byte like houses on a street, not bit-by-bit. Another miss is treating 'word' as text: in computer architecture, a word is simply the CPU's register width (how many bits it computes in one cycle).
concepts.L3: Each bit you add doubles the number of possible combinations: 1 bit gives 2 states (0, 1); 2 bits give 4 (00, 01, 10, 11); 8 bits give 256 patterns (2**8). The largest unsigned value in 8 bits is 255 because counting starts at 0 (2**n - 1). Because hardware addresses only whole bytes, reaching an individual bit inside an array requires loading its byte, then using a shift and a bitwise mask. Historically, computer architectures evolved from 8-bit to 16-bit, 32-bit, and 64-bit register widths, which is why technical manuals and programming ABIs preserve legacy word sizes for compatibility.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many distinct values can be represented in {n} bits?
L4.explanation: Each bit doubles the number of patterns, so n bits give 2**n. Note this is the count of patterns, not the largest value - the largest unsigned value is 2**n - 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many bytes are in {k} KiB?
L4.explanation: KiB is the binary kilo: exactly 1024 bytes. kB with a lowercase k means 1000 bytes in SI usage; disk vendors use the SI form, operating systems usually report the binary one, which is why a '1 TB' drive shows as ~931 GiB.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the largest unsigned integer that fits in {n} bits?
L4.explanation: n bits give $2^{n}$ patterns, but one of them is zero, so the largest unsigned value is $2^{n} - 1$: all ones. Off-by-one here is the classic error - 8 bits hold 256 values, the biggest of which is 255. Adding 1 to the all-ones pattern carries out of the top bit and wraps to 0, which is the seed of 'Fixed-width integers wrap'.

int.bit_length() is the number of bits needed to write the value without leading zeros. Every draw is of the form $2^{k} - 1$, an all-ones pattern that needs k bits; adding 1 gives $2^{k}$, a single 1 followed by k zeros, which needs k + 1 bits. So 255 needs 8 bits and 256 needs 9. Python ints are unbounded, so nothing wraps - the count just grows.

L4.prompt_tpl: A drive is sold as {tb} TB, where the vendor's T is the SI prefix, 10^12. An operating system that reports in binary units shows the same capacity in GiB. About how many GiB does it show? Answer with the number of GiB.
L4.explanation: Nothing is missing from the drive. $10^{12}$ bytes divided by $2^{30}$ bytes per GiB is 931.3, because $2^{30} = 1073741824$ is 7.4% more than $10^{9}$, and the gap compounds with every prefix step: 2.4% at kilo, 4.9% at mega, 7.4% at giga, 10% at tera. Vendors use SI because it prints a bigger number; the OS uses binary because memory sizes are powers of two.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must store {n} boolean flags. As an array of bool, one byte each, that is {n} bytes. Packed one flag per bit into a bitset, how many bytes are needed?
L4.explanation: Eight flags fit in each byte, and a partial byte still costs a whole byte, so the count is $\lceil n/8 \rceil$, not $n/8$. The trap draw is 4097: 4096 flags fill exactly 512 bytes and the single extra flag forces a 513th. The saving is 8x in space; the price is a shift and mask on every access, because a bit has no address of its own.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Win32 header declares a struct field as DWORD. Your program is built for 64-bit Windows. How wide is that field?
L4.answer: 32 bits: DWORD is two 16-bit 8086 words, frozen for compatibility
L4.explanation: In the Windows API, WORD is 16 bits and DWORD is 32 bits on every Windows platform, because the names were fixed when the 8086's word was 16 bits and binary file formats depend on them never changing. Types that follow the pointer width have their own names: DWORD_PTR, SIZE_T, INT_PTR. This is the concrete case behind 'ask whose word'.
options: 32 bits: DWORD is two 16-bit 8086 words, frozen for compatibility
64 bits: it doubles with the register width
The same as a pointer: 64 bits on x64, 32 bits on 32-bit Windows

L4.prompt_tpl: A bit array is stored in memory as consecutive bytes starting at byte index 0, with bit 0 of each byte being its least significant bit. Which byte index holds bit number {b} of the array, and which single-byte mask, written as a decimal number, selects that bit? Answer with the byte index.
L4.answer: byte $\lfloor b / 8 \rfloor$, mask $2^{b \bmod 8}$: 13 -> byte 1, mask 32; 37 -> byte 4, mask 32; 100 -> byte 12, mask 16; 1023 -> byte 127, mask 128; 4100 -> byte 512, mask 16
L4.explanation: Because only bytes have addresses, a bit is located by division with remainder: byte index $\lfloor b/8 \rfloor$ (in C, b >> 3) and bit position $b \bmod 8$ (b & 7), whose mask is 1 shifted left that many places. Reading the flag is then (bytes[b >> 3] >> (b & 7)) & 1. Setting it is bytes[b >> 3] |= 1 << (b & 7). Every bitmap - free-block maps, permission bits, Bloom filters - is this one computation.

CHAR_BIT is the number of bits in a byte as C sees it - 8 on every mainstream platform, and the C standard only guarantees at least 8. sizeof counts bytes, so multiplying by CHAR_BIT gives bits. Under LP64 (x86-64 Linux) short is 2 bytes, int 4, long and pointers 8 - the register width. The same code prints '8 32' for long under 64-bit Windows (LLP64), which is why 'word' must be pinned to a document, not a feeling. See 'Types, sizes and sizeof'.

prereqs: literacy:Text is bytes: UTF-8 in one concept
numeracy:Powers, roots, and the index laws
literacy:What a computer is made of

L0.cloze: 0x{{c1::FF}} == 255 == 0b11111111, and one hex digit is exactly {{c2::4}} bits.

concepts.L1: Base-2 and base-16 are positional notations for the same integers decimal denotes. Hex is used because 16 = 2**4, so one hex digit is exactly four bits and a byte is exactly two hex digits, with no arithmetic needed to convert.
concepts.L2: Hex is not 'how computers store numbers'. Memory holds bits; decimal, hex and binary are three renderings of the same bits. Separately, a leading 0 in C means octal: 0755 is 493, not 755. Permission and version constants are where this bites.
concepts.L3: In base b, digit d at position i contributes d * b**i. So 0x1F = 1*16 + 15 = 31. Because 16 is a power of 2, each hex digit maps onto a fixed 4-bit group and no carry ever crosses the group boundary: 0xB -> 1011, 0x1F -> 0001 1111. Grouping bits in fours from the right converts binary to hex by inspection. Decimal conversion needs repeated division because 10 is not a power of 2 - that asymmetry is the entire reason hex exists rather than decimal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Convert 0x{h} to decimal.
L4.explanation: Weight each digit by 16**position from the right. 0x2A = 2*16 + 10 = 42. Sanity check: any two-hex-digit value is 0..255, so an answer outside that range is wrong before you check the arithmetic.

L4.prompt_tpl: Write the byte 0b{b} in hexadecimal.
L4.explanation: Split into two nibbles and convert each: 1100 = C, 1010 = A, so 0xCA. No carries cross the nibble boundary because 16 is 2**4.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the largest unsigned value that can be written with exactly {n} hexadecimal digits? Answer in decimal.
L4.explanation: n hex digits are 4n bits, so they enumerate $16^{n} = 2^{4n}$ patterns, from 0 up to $16^{n} - 1$. Two digits give 255 (one byte); eight digits give $2^{32} - 1$ (a full 32-bit register). All-F in every digit is the maximum, exactly as all-9 is the decimal maximum.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python 3 executes the statement print(0x{h}) - what number is printed?
L4.explanation: After 0x every digit is a hex digit even when they all happen to look decimal: 0x255 is 2*256 + 5*16 + 5 = 597, not 255. Weight each digit by a power of 16 from the right. Python prints an int in decimal whatever notation the literal used, because the notation never survives parsing - the object is just the integer.

L4.prompt_tpl: Convert the binary number 0b{b} to decimal.
L4.explanation: Bit i from the right has weight $2^{i}$: 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Two shortcuts worth owning: a run of k ones is $2^{k} - 1$ (11111 = 31, 1111111 = 127), and a single one followed by k zeros is $2^{k}$ (100000 = 32). Alternating 1010101 is 64 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 85 = 0x55.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux, a C program compiled with gcc declares int x = 0{o}; and later executes printf("%d\n", x); - what number is printed?
L4.answer: The constant is octal: 0755=493, 0644=420, 0100=64, 017=15, 0777=511 (verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux).
L4.explanation: A leading 0 on a C integer constant makes it octal (C17 6.4.4.1): 0755 = 7*64 + 5*8 + 5 = 493, and %d prints that value in decimal. This is why permission constants carry the leading zero on purpose, and why a zero-padded 'decimal' such as 0100 silently becomes 64. The platform is irrelevant here; the base of a constant is fixed by the language grammar, not the machine.

L4.prompt_tpl: Programmers print {thing} in hexadecimal rather than decimal. Which reason is the real one?
L4.answer: One hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is always two digits and hex-to-binary conversion is digit-by-digit with no arithmetic
L4.explanation: Memory holds bits; hex, decimal and binary are three renderings of the same bits, and no rendering 'occupies' memory differently. The processor computes on bits, not on any base. Hex wins purely because $16 = 2^{4}$: digit boundaries coincide with 4-bit group boundaries, so a dump can be read bit by bit by eye. Decimal cannot do that because 10 is not a power of 2.
options: One hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is always two digits and hex-to-binary conversion is digit-by-digit with no arithmetic
Hexadecimal values occupy less memory than decimal values
The processor performs its arithmetic in hexadecimal

L4.prompt_tpl: How many hexadecimal digits does 2^{n} have when written without leading zeros?
L4.explanation: $2^{n}$ is a single 1 bit at position n. Bits 0 to n span floor(n/4) + 1 nibbles, and each nibble is one hex digit. The trap is n = 31 versus 32: $2^{31}$ = 0x80000000 still fits in 8 digits, while $2^{32}$ needs a ninth. When n is a multiple of 4 the result is a 1 followed by n/4 zeros, e.g. $2^{20}$ = 0x100000.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python 3 executes the statement print(0{o}) - what happens? Answer with the printed number, or with the exception class name if it does not run.
L4.answer: SyntaxError
L4.explanation: Python 3 forbids leading zeros on a non-zero decimal literal precisely to kill the C octal trap: 0755 is a SyntaxError ('leading zeros in decimal integer literals are not permitted'), neither 755 nor 493. Octal must be spelled 0o755 (which is 493), just as binary is 0b and hex is 0x. Python 2 accepted 0755 as octal, which is why the rule was made explicit.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive why grouping binary digits in blocks of {m} from the right converts binary to base 2^{m} by inspection, with no arithmetic crossing a block boundary. Then name the familiar base that m = {m} gives, and say why base 10 has no such shortcut.
L4.answer: The bit at position $mk + j$ with $0 \le j < m$ has weight $2^{mk + j} = (2^{m})^{k} \cdot 2^{j}$. Summing a block, the k-th block of m bits contributes $g_{k} \cdot (2^{m})^{k}$ with $0 \le g_{k} \le 2^{m} - 1$, which is exactly a base-$2^{m}$ digit in position k. No carry crosses a block because $g_{k} < 2^{m}$. m = 3 gives octal, m = 4 gives hexadecimal. Base 10 has no shortcut because no integer m satisfies $2^{m} = 10$.
L4.explanation: The whole argument is the index law $2^{mk + j} = (2^{m})^{k} 2^{j}$. It fails for base 10 because no m makes $2^{m} = 10$, so a decimal digit does not own a fixed set of bits and conversion needs repeated division. Octal (m = 3) suited the 12-, 18- and 36-bit words of early machines; hex (m = 4) suits 8-bit bytes because 8 is a multiple of 4 and not of 3, so a byte is always exactly two digits.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C program on Linux calls chmod(path, {d}) intending the usual permission bits that ls-style octal writes as {d}. The file's permissions come out wrong. What mode did the file actually receive? Give it as an octal number without a prefix, in the style of chmod 1777.
L4.answer: The decimal number re-read in octal: 644 -> 1204, 755 -> 1363, 600 -> 1130, 664 -> 1230.
L4.explanation: mode_t is just a number; chmod never sees how you spelled it. Decimal 644 = 512 + 128 + 4 = $1 \cdot 8^{3} + 2 \cdot 8^{2} + 0 \cdot 8 + 4$, i.e. octal 1204: sticky bit set, owner write-only, group nothing, others read (ls shows --w----r-T). The fix is 0644 in C, 0o644 in Python, or the S_IRUSR family of symbolic constants. The bug is invisible until the mode is read back in octal - see File permissions.

L0.cloze: In 8-bit two's complement the range is -{{c1::128}} .. {{c2::127}}, and -x == ~x + {{c3::1}}.

concepts.L1: The standard signed-integer encoding. The top bit carries weight -2**(n-1) instead of +2**(n-1); every other bit keeps its positive weight. For n bits the range is -2**(n-1) .. 2**(n-1) - 1.
concepts.L2: There is one more negative value than positive, so -INT_MIN is not representable: negating it in the same width returns INT_MIN unchanged. In C, -INT_MIN and abs(INT_MIN) are undefined behaviour, not a wrap - and that asymmetry has produced real CVEs in length checks.
concepts.L3: Weights: bit $n-1$ counts $-2^{n-1}$, every other bit $i$ counts $+2^{i}$, so for $n = 8$: 0b10000000 = -128 and 0b11111111 = -128 + 127 = -1. The pattern for a negative $v$ is the unsigned number $v + 2^{n}$, i.e. every value is stored as its residue mod $2^{n}$. The payoff: $\mathrm{pattern}(a) + \mathrm{pattern}(b) \equiv a + b \pmod{2^{n}}$, so an unsigned adder that drops the carry-out already yields the correct signed bits - only the reading differs, never the circuit. Negation: $x + \sim x$ sets every bit, and all-ones is $2^{n} - 1$, which reads as $-1$; hence $\sim x = -1 - x$ and $\sim x + 1 = -x$. The single exception is $x = -2^{n-1}$: $\sim x + 1 = 2^{n-1} - 1 + 1 = 2^{n-1}$, which does not fit and wraps back to $x$. That gap is what 'Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C' turns into a language rule, and that 'Fixed-width integers wrap' shows in unsigned form.

L4.prompt_tpl: In {n}-bit two's complement, what value does the pattern with only the most significant bit set represent?
L4.explanation: The MSB's weight is -2**(n-1) and all other bits are 0, so the value is exactly that weight. This is also the most negative representable value.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give the 8-bit two's complement encoding of -{k} in hexadecimal.
L4.answer: 0x100 - k as two hex digits: -1=0xFF, -2=0xFE, -5=0xFB, -10=0xF6, -100=0x9C
L4.explanation: The encoding of a negative value v is v + 2**8 = 256 + v. For -100 that is 156 = 0x9C. Equivalently, invert the bits of 100 (0x64 -> 0x9B) and add 1 -> 0x9C.

L4.prompt_tpl: An 8-bit register holds the bit pattern whose unsigned reading is {u}. Read the same eight bits as a two's complement int8_t. What value is that?
L4.explanation: The top bit weighs $-128$ instead of $+128$, a difference of exactly 256. So a pattern whose unsigned reading is 128 or more is its unsigned reading minus 256: 200 - 256 = -56. Patterns below 128 have the top bit clear and read the same either way, which is the draw 127. Signed and unsigned share every bit; only the weight of one bit changes.

Python ints are unbounded, but bitwise operators treat a negative int as an infinite two's complement string of leading 1s. Masking with 0xFF keeps the low 8 bits, which is the 8-bit encoding of $-k$: $256 - k$, e.g. 256 - 100 = 156. Masking with 0xFFFF gives the 16-bit encoding $65536 - k$, whose hex shows the sign-extended 0xff.. prefix. For k=200, $-200$ does not fit in an int8_t, so the 8-bit mask gives 56, the residue of -200 mod 256.

L4.answer: Undefined behaviour: 2^31 is not representable in int, so the program has no defined meaning, even though the x86-64 NEG instruction would leave the bits unchanged
L4.explanation: C 6.5p5: if an exceptional condition occurs during the evaluation of an expression (the result is not representable), the behaviour is undefined. C23 does fix the representation as two's complement, but it did not make signed overflow wrap; only unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo $2^{n}$. On x86-64 with gcc -O0 you will observe INT_MIN, because NEG wraps, but an optimiser is entitled to assume the overflow never happens and delete the check you wrote around it. abs(INT_MIN) is UB for the same reason.
options: Undefined behaviour: 2^31 is not representable in int, so the program has no defined meaning, even though the x86-64 NEG instruction would leave the bits unchanged
y == INT_MIN, guaranteed: two's complement negation wraps, and C23 mandates two's complement
y == INT_MAX: signed negation saturates at the representable limit

L4.prompt_tpl: An 8-bit adder adds the two's complement bytes for {a} and {b} and discards the carry out. Reading the result byte as int8_t, what value comes out?
L4.explanation: The adder computes the sum of the two patterns mod 256 and knows nothing about signs. When the true sum lies in $[-128, 127]$ that residue is the true sum. When it does not, the residue is the true sum $\pm 256$: 127 + 1 = 128 becomes -128, 100 + 50 = 150 becomes -106, -100 - 50 = -150 becomes 106. Overflow happens exactly when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign; operands of opposite sign can never overflow.

L4.prompt_tpl: An int8_t holds the byte whose unsigned reading is {u}, so it is a negative number. It is assigned to an int16_t, which widens it by sign extension. What is the unsigned reading of the resulting 16-bit pattern?
L4.explanation: Widening must preserve the value, not the leading zeros. The 8-bit pattern encodes $u - 256$; the 16-bit pattern for the same value is $u - 256 + 65536 = u + 65280$, which is the original byte with eight 1s in front. Copying the sign bit upward is what makes that work: the new bits 8..15 contribute $2^{8} + \dots + 2^{14} - 2^{15} = -256$, while bit 7 changes weight from $-128$ to $+128$, a change of $+256$; the two cancel exactly. Zero-extending instead would turn -1 (0xFF) into 255.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that in {n}-bit two's complement, ~x + 1 equals -x for every value x except one. Identify the exceptional x and state what ~x + 1 gives for it.
L4.answer: For every bit position exactly one of x and ~x has a 1, so $x + \sim x$ is the all-ones pattern, whose value is $2^{n} - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod{2^{n}}$. Hence $\sim x \equiv -1 - x$ and $\sim x + 1 \equiv -x \pmod{2^{n}}$, and whenever $-x$ is representable the congruence is an equality. The exception is $x = -2^{n-1}$ (n=8: -128; n=16: -32768; n=32: -2147483648): $\sim x = 2^{n-1} - 1$, and adding 1 gives $2^{n-1}$, which exceeds the maximum $2^{n-1} - 1$ and wraps to $-2^{n-1}$, i.e. back to x.
L4.explanation: The proof rests on one observation: $x + \sim x$ = all ones = $-1$, because the two patterns are bit-complements. Everything else is arithmetic mod $2^{n}$. The identity only fails where the target value does not exist: the range holds $2^{n-1}$ negatives but only $2^{n-1} - 1$ positives, so $-(-2^{n-1})$ has no pattern and the wraparound returns the input. That single value is why -INT_MIN and abs(INT_MIN) are undefined behaviour in C.

L4.answer: h == INT_MIN: abs(INT_MIN) is undefined behaviour, and on x86-64 it typically returns INT_MIN, so bucket is a negative index and the table reads or writes out of bounds
L4.explanation: There is one more negative int than positive, so abs() cannot return a valid result for INT_MIN; the C standard makes it undefined (7.22.6.1) and the machine wraps it to INT_MIN. Then INT_MIN mod n is negative or zero in C, because % takes the sign of the dividend, so the index can go negative on 1 hash in $2^{32}$ - rare enough to pass tests, common enough to be hit in production. Fix: index with the unsigned reinterpretation, (unsigned) h % n, which is always in range.
options: h == INT_MIN: abs(INT_MIN) is undefined behaviour, and on x86-64 it typically returns INT_MIN, so bucket is a negative index and the table reads or writes out of bounds
Any negative h: abs() is only defined for non-negative arguments, so every negative hash must be masked before the call
Nothing breaks: abs() always returns a non-negative int, so the modulo is always in range

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 the signed 32-bit division instruction idiv raises a divide-error exception (delivered on Linux as SIGFPE) for exactly one pair of operands with a non-zero divisor. Which pair, and why does the two's complement range make it unavoidable?
L4.answer: INT_MIN / -1, i.e. -2147483648 / -1. The true quotient is $+2^{31} = 2147483648$, but the largest int is $2^{31} - 1$, so no result pattern exists. idiv detects that the quotient does not fit and raises #DE, the same fault as division by zero. In C the expression INT_MIN / -1 is undefined behaviour (6.5.5), and INT_MIN % -1 is undefined too, although the mathematical remainder would be 0, because it is computed by the same instruction.
L4.explanation: Two's complement has $2^{n-1}$ negative values and $2^{n-1} - 1$ positive ones, so the single value $-2^{n-1}$ has no negation; dividing it by -1 asks for exactly that negation. The hardware cannot wrap here the way NEG does, because idiv must also produce a remainder, so Intel specified a fault. This is the only case where a C integer division with non-zero divisor can crash the process, and it is why 'Integer division truncates - but toward what?' matters for range as well as sign.

concepts.t: Memory as one addressed array of bytes

L0.body:
addr        bytes
0x1000      48 65 6c 6c 6f 00      <- "Hello\0"
0x1006      2a 00 00 00            <- int32 42 (little-endian)
0x100a      ...
L0.cloze: A process sees memory as a flat array indexed by {{c1::address}}; each element is one {{c2::byte}}.

concepts.L1: A running process sees memory as a single flat array of bytes indexed from 0. Every variable, every instruction, every stack frame is a contiguous range of that array. Memory itself has no types - only bytes, plus whatever interpretation the code applies.
concepts.L2: That flatness is a fiction the MMU maintains; addresses are virtual, and most of the space is unmapped. Touching an unmapped address faults immediately, which is the friendly case. Touching a mapped address with the wrong type reads plausible garbage silently - far worse.
concepts.L3: Give the machine an address and a width and it returns that many consecutive bytes; nothing else is stored. An int at 0x1006..0x1009 (a compiler would pad it to 0x1008 - see 'Padding and alignment' - but the bytes do not care) means one 4-byte load, and the decision to read those bytes as a two's-complement integer lives only in the load instruction the compiler emitted, never in memory. So a pointer cast such as (unsigned char *)&x changes no bits and costs nothing: it only changes which load the compiler picks next. A value conversion is different: (double)x must produce new bits, since int and double encode numbers differently, so a conversion instruction (cvtsi2sd on x86-64) is emitted. Memory keeps no record of the type, so a wrong-type load cannot be caught by the hardware: the bytes were always valid bytes. Next: 'Endianness' asks in which order those four bytes hold the value.

L4.prompt_tpl: An array of 4-byte ints begins at address 0x{base}. At what address does element {i} start? Answer in hex.
L4.answer: base + 4*i  e.g. 0x1000 with i=3 -> 0x100C; 0x40A0 with i=7 -> 0x40BC
L4.explanation: Element i starts at base + i * sizeof(element). Indexing is address arithmetic, not a lookup - which is why an out-of-range index computes a perfectly valid address and reads whatever lives there.

L4.prompt_tpl: An array of {n} elements, each {w} bytes, begins at byte address {base} (decimal). What is the byte address of the first byte after the end of the array? Answer in decimal.
L4.explanation: The array occupies bytes base .. base + n*w - 1, so the first byte past it is base + n*w. This one-past-the-end address is the only out-of-array address C lets you form; the loop condition p < end depends on it. Element i lives at base + i*w, and i = n lands exactly on this address, which is why a[n] reads whatever is stored next.

L4.answer: 65 + i, the ASCII code of the letter at that index: i=0 -> 65 (A), i=2 -> 67 (C), i=3 -> 68 (D), i=5 -> 70 (F), i=7 -> 72 (H). Verified by running gcc.
L4.explanation: s[i] is one byte of memory holding the value 65 + i; 'A' is 65 in ASCII and the letters are consecutive. Nothing in the byte says 'character'. Printing it with %d shows the integer; %c would show the letter - the format string, not the memory, decides. The byte is promoted to int when passed to printf, which is why %d is the right conversion.

L4.prompt_tpl: Bytes 0x1006..0x1009 hold 2a 00 00 00. A program later reads them as a 32-bit int and gets 42. Where is the fact that they form one int, rather than four separate chars, recorded?
L4.answer: Nowhere in memory: it lives in the load instruction the compiler emitted for that access
L4.explanation: Memory is bytes with addresses and nothing else. The compiler turned the declared type into a 4-byte load; the bytes carry no tag and the page table records only mapping and permissions (read, write, execute), never a type. That is why reading the same bytes through a char pointer works silently and why the hardware cannot detect a type-confusion bug.
options: Nowhere in memory: it lives in the load instruction the compiler emitted for that access
In a type tag the hardware stores beside the four bytes
In the page-table entry for the page that contains them

L4.prompt_tpl: A C string of {n} characters is stored NUL-terminated starting at byte address {a} (decimal). A 4-byte int is placed immediately after it, with no padding. What is the byte address of the int's first byte?
L4.explanation: The string occupies n + 1 bytes: its n characters plus the zero byte that marks the end, so the int starts at a + n + 1, not a + n. This is the layout in the L0 dump: 'Hello' is five letters but six bytes, 0x1000..0x1005, and the int begins at 0x1006. Forgetting the NUL is the off-by-one behind many buffer sizes that are one byte short.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 32-bit int is stored starting at byte address {a} (decimal). What is the address of its last byte?
L4.explanation: Four bytes starting at a occupy a, a+1, a+2, a+3; the address a+4 is the first byte of whatever comes next. Half-open ranges (start inclusive, end exclusive) are the convention precisely so that size = end - start with no plus-or-minus one; the closed range's last byte is start + size - 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program forms an address {k} bytes past the end of a 16-byte buffer and loads 4 bytes from it. The address lies inside a page the process has mapped read-write. At the machine level, what happens on that load?
L4.answer: The load returns the 4 bytes that happen to live there; nothing signals that they belong to another object
L4.explanation: The MMU checks only whether the page is mapped and with what permissions; it knows nothing about buffers, objects or bounds. A mapped address returns its bytes, so an overrun that stays inside mapped memory silently reads or corrupts a neighbour - the dangerous case in L2. Only an unmapped page faults. In C the access is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may also do something else entirely; see 'Undefined behaviour'.
options: The load returns the 4 bytes that happen to live there; nothing signals that they belong to another object
The MMU raises a fault because the address is outside the buffer's bounds
The load returns zero, because bytes outside any object read as zero

L4.prompt_tpl: int grid[{r}][{c}] (4-byte ints) begins at byte address {base} (decimal). C stores 2-D arrays row-major: all of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on. Derive the byte address of grid[{i}][{j}]. Answer with the address in decimal.
L4.explanation: Row i starts i rows in, each row holding c elements of 4 bytes: base + 4*i*c. Element j of that row adds 4*j. The row count r never enters the formula - only the row length c does, which is why a function taking a 2-D array must know c but not r. Walking j fastest touches consecutive bytes; walking i fastest jumps 4c bytes each step, which the cache punishes - see 'The memory hierarchy'.

memcpy moves four bytes and changes none of them; u is the same 32 bits read under a different interpretation. For a power of two $2^{k}$ the fraction bits are all zero and the biased exponent is $127 + k$, sitting above the 23 fraction bits, so the pattern is $(127 + k) \cdot 2^{23}$: 1.0f is 0x3f800000. The value 1 and the value 1065353216 are the same bytes; only the instruction that reads them differs. See 'IEEE 754 binary64'.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C, the pointer cast (unsigned char *)&x compiles to no instruction at all, while the value cast (double)x on an int x compiles to a real conversion instruction. Explain both facts in terms of where a type lives, then say what this implies about detecting a type-confusion bug at run time.
L4.answer: A type is a compile-time decision about how to interpret bytes, recorded only in the instructions the compiler emits. A pointer cast changes that future decision (which width and kind of load) but not the address, so it needs no instruction. (double)x asks for a different value representation - two's complement and IEEE 754 encode the same number as different bits - so new bits must be computed (cvtsi2sd on x86-64). Because the bytes carry no type, a load through the wrong type is indistinguishable from a correct one at run time; the hardware cannot detect it, and catching it needs the compiler or an added instrumentation layer (sanitisers), or a language that stores tags with its values.
L4.explanation: The distinction is reinterpretation versus conversion. A pointer cast reinterprets: same address, same bytes, different load emitted later. An arithmetic cast converts: the representations differ, so bits must change. Both facts follow from memory being untyped bytes; and the same fact means a type-confusion read is silent - the bytes were always valid bytes. Python avoids this by storing a type pointer in every object header, which is the price of 'Names are bound to objects'.

L0.cloze: On a little-endian machine, 0x12345678 is stored with byte 0x{{c1::78}} at the lowest address.

concepts.L1: Endianness is the order in which the bytes of a multi-byte scalar are laid out in increasing addresses. Little-endian puts the least significant byte first; big-endian puts the most significant byte first. x86-64 and default ARM are little-endian.
concepts.L2: Endianness never affects arithmetic or bit-shift results - those are defined on values, not on byte layout. It only becomes visible when you reinterpret the bytes: casting a pointer, memcpy into a different type, writing to a file, or sending over a socket.
concepts.L3: Take uint32_t x = 1 at address A. Little-endian puts $x \bmod 256$ at A, $\lfloor x/256 \rfloor \bmod 256$ at A+1, and so on, so *(uint8_t*)&x, *(uint16_t*)&x and x itself all read 1: the address of a value is the address of its low byte whatever the width, and narrowing needs no address arithmetic - why x86 and ARM chose it. Big-endian puts the most significant byte at A, so the same one-byte read gives 0; that is the classic runtime test. Arithmetic never sees any of this, because x >> 8 is defined on the value, so buf[0] = x >> 24, buf[1] = x >> 16, ... is portable serialisation while memcpy(buf, &x, 4) is not. Network protocols fix big-endian 'network byte order'; htonl and ntohl are the identity on a big-endian host and a byte swap on x86. 'Padding and alignment' is the second reason *(uint32_t*)buf is wrong on a byte buffer; 'IEEE 754 binary64' doubles follow the same rule.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a little-endian machine: uint32_t x = 0x{val}; unsigned char *p = (unsigned char*)&x; What is p[0] in hex?
L4.answer: the least significant byte: 0x78, 0xFF, 0xDD
L4.explanation: Little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, and p[0] is the lowest address. Reading p[3] would give the most significant byte instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A uint32_t with the decimal value {v} is stored little-endian starting at address A. What is the byte at address A+{k}? Answer with the byte's value in decimal.
L4.explanation: Little-endian means the byte at offset $k$ is base-256 digit $k$ of the value, counting from the least significant: $\lfloor v / 256^{k} \rfloor \bmod 256$. Write the value in hex, split it into pairs, and read the pairs from the right: 0x12345678 gives 78, 56, 34, 12 at offsets 0, 1, 2, 3. Big-endian would read the pairs from the left instead.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3. What does this print?

import struct
print(struct.pack('<I', {n}).hex(), struct.pack('>I', {n}).hex())
L4.explanation: In struct format strings '<' means little-endian and '>' big-endian; 'I' is a 4-byte unsigned int. The big-endian hex string is just the number's 8-digit hex spelling (4660 = 0x1234 -> 00001234); the little-endian one is the same byte pairs in reverse order (34 12 00 00). Note that '<I' with no prefix is not the same as 'I' alone: the native format '@' also adds alignment padding.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two consecutive bytes in memory, at addresses A and A+1, hold the decimal values {b0} and {b1}. Read as a little-endian uint16_t at address A, what is the value in decimal?
L4.explanation: Little-endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address, so the byte at A weighs 1 and the byte at A+1 weighs 256: value = b0 + 256*b1. Big-endian would weight them the other way round, 256*b0 + b1, which for (52, 18) gives 13330 (0x3412) instead of 4660 (0x1234).

L4.prompt_tpl: C, uint32_t x = 0x12345678; uint32_t y = x >> 8; the program prints y with the format %08x. What is printed on a little-endian x86-64 machine, and what on a big-endian machine?
L4.answer: 00123456 on both: shifts act on the value, and endianness only describes where the bytes sit in memory
L4.explanation: The C standard defines >> on the value of the operand: $x / 2^{8}$ for an unsigned x. The CPU loads the four bytes into a register in whichever order the machine uses and the register then holds the value 0x12345678 on both; the shift happens there. Byte order can only be observed by addressing individual bytes of the object - a char pointer, memcpy, a union, I/O - never by arithmetic, which is the whole content of L2.
options: 00123456 on both: shifts act on the value, and endianness only describes where the bytes sit in memory
00123456 on big-endian but 56341200 on little-endian, because the shift moves bytes toward lower addresses
34567800 on little-endian and 00123456 on big-endian, because the least significant byte is at the lowest address

L4.prompt_tpl: An x86-64 program does fwrite(&x, 4, 1, f) where uint32_t x holds the decimal value {v}. The file is copied to a big-endian machine, which does fread(&y, 4, 1, f) into a uint32_t y. What decimal value does y hold?
L4.explanation: fwrite copies the object's bytes in address order, so x86 writes the least significant byte first: x = 1 becomes the file bytes 01 00 00 00. The big-endian reader treats the first byte as most significant and sees 0x01000000 = 16777216. In general the four bytes are reversed. That is why file formats and protocols fix a byte order and why you serialise with shifts or htonl rather than dumping struct memory.

x = 0x12345678 sits in memory as 78 56 34 12. Offset 2 starts at bytes 34 12, and reading those two bytes as a little-endian uint16_t puts 34 in the low position and 12 in the high: 0x1234, the high half of x. The trap is to answer 3412 - the bytes are 'reversed' twice, once when stored and once when read, so the high half comes out with its digits in natural order. Verified with gcc 13 on x86-64.

L4.prompt_tpl: x is a uint32_t at address A on a little-endian machine. Derive from the byte layout why *(uint8_t*)&x, *(uint16_t*)&x and *(uint32_t*)&x yield x mod 2^8, x mod 2^16 and x itself, all from the same address A. Then state what the corresponding narrower reads at A give on a big-endian machine, and say why the little-endian property appealed to hardware designers.
L4.answer: Little-endian stores $\lfloor x / 256^{k} \rfloor \bmod 256$ at A+k. An $n$-byte read at A gathers bytes $0 \dots n-1$ and weights them $256^{0} \dots 256^{n-1}$, which is exactly $x \bmod 256^{n}$: 1, 2 and 4 bytes give $x \bmod 2^{8}$, $x \bmod 2^{16}$ and $x$. On big-endian the byte at A is the most significant, so an $n$-byte read at A gives $\lfloor x / 256^{4-n} \rfloor$, the top $n$ bytes; a uint32_t 1 reads as 0 through a char pointer. The appeal: a value or a pointer can be narrowed without moving the address, and multi-word addition walks upward from A carrying into the next byte, so the low byte is where the hardware starts anyway.
L4.explanation: The proof is base-256 place value: byte $k$ at offset $k$ means the memory order equals the digit order, so any prefix of the bytes is a prefix of the digits, i.e. a residue mod $256^{n}$. Big-endian reverses it, so prefixes are quotients instead. Neither is more natural; big-endian matches how we write numbers and how packets are dumped, little-endian matches how adders and address arithmetic work, which is why Cohen's 1980 'Holy Wars' note could only plead for a convention, not decide one.

L4.answer: len is byte-swapped on x86-64 (a wire length of 1 arrives as 16777216), and the test passed only because both ends made the same mistake; decode with ntohl or with shifts over buf[0..3], which is correct on every host and also avoids the unaligned uint32_t read
L4.explanation: The cast reinterprets the four bytes in host order, so on x86 the wire bytes 00 00 00 01 read as 0x01000000. A loopback peer that wrote its length with the mirror-image memcpy produces bytes the reader happens to decode correctly, so the test proves nothing about the protocol. Portable decode: memcpy into a uint32_t and ntohl, or (buf[0] << 24) | (buf[1] << 16) | (buf[2] << 8) | buf[3], which never depends on host order. The cast has a second, independent defect - a possibly unaligned access, and a strict-aliasing violation - covered under 'Padding and alignment'.
options: len is byte-swapped on x86-64 (a wire length of 1 arrives as 16777216), and the test passed only because both ends made the same mistake; decode with ntohl or with shifts over buf[0..3], which is correct on every host and also avoids the unaligned uint32_t read
The only defect is alignment: buf may not be 4-byte aligned, and declaring it with a 4-byte alignment attribute makes the cast read the right value on every machine
Nothing is wrong: recv delivers the bytes in network order and the cast reads them in that same order, so len is correct on any host

L0.body:
x86-64 general-purpose: rax rbx rcx rdx rsi rdi rbp rsp r8..r15  (16 x 64-bit)
rsp = stack pointer   rip = instruction pointer
mov rax, [rbx]    ; load 8 bytes from the address in rbx into rax
L0.cloze: On x86-64 the stack pointer register is {{c1::rsp}} and the instruction pointer is {{c2::rip}}.

concepts.L1: Registers are the handful of named storage slots inside the CPU that instructions operate on directly. x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers plus vector registers. Access takes well under a nanosecond; there is no address involved.
concepts.L2: Registers are not 'fast memory' - they are not memory at all. They have names, not addresses, so you cannot take a pointer to one. That is why C's `register` keyword could never be combined with `&`, and why a variable the compiler keeps in a register may be invisible to a debugger in an optimised build.
concepts.L3: An instruction names each register operand with a few bits - 4 on x86-64 (3 in ModRM plus one REX bit), 5 on ARM64 and RISC-V - so the count is small and frozen by the ISA encoding. Registers are fast because they sit inside the datapath: no address decode, no translation, no cache lookup, just wires into the ALU; everything a program computes passes through them. On a load/store ISA such as ARM64, `a = b + c` on values in memory is literally load, load, add, store; x86-64 lets `add` take one memory operand, but the core still fetches it into an internal temporary first. Register allocation is the compiler deciding which variables occupy the slots at each point; when live values outnumber the supply it spills one to the stack, and the loop slows down suddenly. Registers are the only state not already in memory, so a context switch must save them - see 'What a process is'.

L4.prompt_tpl: True or false: you can take the address of a value that lives only in a CPU register. Justify in one sentence.
L4.answer: False - registers have names, not memory addresses, so the compiler must first spill the value to memory to give it an address.
L4.explanation: Addresses index the memory array; registers are not part of it. Taking &x forces the compiler to give x a memory home, which is why address-taken locals are harder to keep in registers and can be measurably slower.

L4.prompt_tpl: An instruction set encodes each register operand of an instruction in a {b}-bit field. How many registers can such a field name?
L4.answer: $2^{b}$: 3 bits -> 8 (the original 8086 set); 4 bits -> 16 (x86-64: a 3-bit ModRM field plus one REX-prefix bit); 5 bits -> 32 (ARM64, RISC-V); 6 bits -> 64.
L4.explanation: A b-bit field has $2^{b}$ distinct patterns, one per register, so the register count is fixed by the instruction encoding, not by how much storage a chip could afford. Going from 8 to 16 registers in x86-64 needed a new prefix byte (REX) to carry the extra bit; ARM64 and RISC-V budgeted 5 bits from the start and get 32. This is the whole reason the count is tiny and fixed by the ISA.

L4.prompt_tpl: An ISA has {n} general-purpose registers, each {w} bits wide. How many bytes of general-purpose register storage does one core expose to the programmer?
L4.explanation: Sixteen 64-bit registers are 16 x 8 = 128 bytes: the entire working set an x86-64 instruction can touch without an address is smaller than one page, smaller than a single cache line pair. That is why the compiler's job of deciding what lives there (register allocation) matters, and why everything else must be loaded from memory and stored back. Vector and floating-point registers are separate files and not counted here.

L4.answer: The second line, int *p = &n. C forbids taking the address of an object declared with the register storage class (the operand of unary & may not be a register variable), because such a variable may have no memory location at all. gcc reports 'address of register variable n requested'. Removing the register keyword, or the &, fixes it.
L4.explanation: register is a request to keep n in a CPU register, and a register has a name, not an address, so &n cannot be given a value. The standard makes it a constraint violation rather than letting the compiler silently spill n to memory (C17 6.5.3.2, 6.7.1). Modern compilers ignore the keyword as a hint but still enforce the rule, which is exactly the L2 point: registers are not memory. Verified here with gcc, which rejects the program at compile time.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64, rax holds 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF. The instruction mov eax, 1 executes (eax is the low 32-bit view of rax). What does rax hold afterwards?
L4.answer: 0x0000000000000001 - a 32-bit write is zero-extended into the full 64-bit register
L4.explanation: x86-64 defines that a 32-bit result written to a general-purpose register is zero-extended to 64 bits, while 8-bit and 16-bit writes (al, ax) leave the upper bits untouched (Intel SDM Vol. 1 s3.4.1.1). Verified here with inline assembly: after movl $1 the register reads 0x1; after movw $1 it reads 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF0001. This asymmetry is why compilers zero a register with the 32-bit form and why mixing sub-register widths silently corrupts values.
options: 0x0000000000000001 - a 32-bit write is zero-extended into the full 64-bit register
0xFFFFFFFF00000001 - only the low 32 bits change, the upper half is preserved
It is unspecified: the upper 32 bits may hold either value depending on the CPU

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64, rax holds {init} (decimal), a value whose low 16 bits are all zero. The instruction mov ax, {v} executes, where ax is the low 16-bit view of rax. What does rax hold afterwards, in decimal?
L4.answer: $\mathrm{init} + v$, because a 16-bit write leaves the upper 48 bits alone: 65536 + 300 -> 65836; 65536 + 1000 -> 66536; 65536 + 5000 -> 70536; 131072 + 300 -> 131372; 131072 + 5000 -> 136072. Verified here with inline assembly on gcc, x86-64 Linux.
L4.explanation: Unlike a 32-bit write, which zero-extends, an 8-bit or 16-bit write to a general-purpose register modifies only those low bits and preserves the rest (Intel SDM Vol. 1 s3.4.1.1). Since init has a zero low half-word, the result is simply init + v. A learner who answers v alone has applied the 32-bit rule to a 16-bit write; a learner who answers init has forgotten the write happened. The partial-write rule is a common source of stale-bits bugs in hand-written assembly.

L4.prompt_tpl: A register read completes within one clock cycle. A core runs at {f} GHz and one main-memory (DRAM) access takes about {t} ns. Roughly how many register reads, one per cycle, fit in the time of one memory access?
L4.answer: $f \cdot t$ (GHz times ns cancels to a count): 3 GHz, 100 ns -> 300; 2 GHz, 80 ns -> 160; 4 GHz, 100 ns -> 400; 4 GHz, 80 ns -> 320.
L4.explanation: At f GHz a cycle is 1/f ns, so t ns holds f*t cycles: two to four hundred register reads per DRAM access. This is the quantitative content of 'well under a nanosecond' in L1, and the reason a spill (a store plus a later load) costs far more than the add it was making room for. The exact figures vary by machine; the ratio, hundreds to one, is what to remember. See 'The memory hierarchy'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A compiler has {r} registers free for allocation. At the busiest point of a loop body, {n} values are live at the same time. What is the minimum number of those values that must be spilled to the stack at that point? (Answer 0 if none.)
L4.answer: $\max(0, n - r)$: 12 live, 14 free -> 0; 20 live, 14 free -> 6; 20 live, 15 free -> 5; 40 live, 31 free -> 9; 40 live, 14 free -> 26.
L4.explanation: Each live value needs a slot; if n exceeds r the excess n - r must live in memory at that moment, and if n does not exceed r nothing must be spilled - the answer is zero, not negative. The numbers are realistic: x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers, but rsp is reserved and rbp often is, leaving about 14; ARM64 has 31 minus the stack pointer, frame pointer and link register. Spills are why a loop with too many live variables slows down suddenly, as L3 says.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design question. A fixed-width {w}-bit instruction word must hold an {o}-bit opcode and three equal-size register fields (one destination, two sources) and nothing else. Derive the largest number of registers such an ISA can have. Answer with the number of registers.
L4.answer: $2^{\lfloor (w - o)/3 \rfloor}$: 32-bit word, 8-bit opcode -> 24 bits left, 8 per field -> 256 registers; 11-bit opcode -> 7 per field -> 128; 14-bit -> 6 per field -> 64; 17-bit -> 5 per field -> 32; 20-bit -> 4 per field -> 16.
L4.explanation: The w - o bits left after the opcode are split three ways; each field of k bits names $2^{k}$ registers, and a fraction of a bit is useless, hence the floor. This is the trade an ISA designer makes: more registers means wider fields, which means fewer opcode bits or wider instructions. RISC-V spends 7 opcode bits plus 10 function bits and gets exactly 5-bit fields, so 32 registers; x86-64 escaped its 3-bit fields only by adding a prefix byte. See 'What an ISA is'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A process is preempted by a timer interrupt in the middle of a computation whose intermediate values are all in registers, and another process runs for 10 ms. Where must those register values go, who moves them, and why can the memory system (caches, virtual memory) not preserve them by itself?
L4.answer: They must be copied into memory - the trap hardware pushes some onto the kernel stack, and the OS's context-switch code stores the rest into the process's saved-context structure - and copied back by the OS before the process resumes. The memory system cannot do it because registers are not memory: they have names, not addresses, so no cache, page or write-back mechanism ever sees them. Only explicit store instructions executed by the kernel can capture them, and the next process will overwrite every one of the 16.
L4.explanation: Registers are the only program state that is not already in the addressed byte array, so they are exactly the state a context switch must save and restore by hand (OSTEP ch. 6, Limited Direct Execution). Everything else - heap, stack, code - stays where it is in the process's address space. This is also why a switch has a fixed cost proportional to the register-file size, and why the same values are invisible to a debugger until they are spilled. See 'What a process is'.

L4.prompt_tpl: You build a correct C program with gcc -O2 -g, stop in gdb inside its inner loop, and print i answers <optimized out>. The same program built with -O0 -g shows i's value at the same line. Explain what happened to i, in terms of where values live, and name one way to see the loop's counter in the -O2 build without rebuilding.
L4.answer: At -O2 the compiler kept i in a register (or transformed it away, e.g. into a pointer that steps through the array), so at that line there is no memory location holding i and the debug information cannot point at one; at -O0 every local is stored to its stack slot after each statement, so gdb can read it from memory. To see it anyway: disassemble the loop, find which register the loop uses, and read it with info registers or `p $rcx` (or whichever register), or set a breakpoint where the value is stored to memory.
L4.explanation: A debugger reads variables through addresses; a value that lives only in a register has none, and the DWARF location list may say so for a whole range of instructions. The program is not wrong - the compiler simply never wrote i to memory. Reading the register directly is the honest answer; the alternatives (-Og, volatile, a temporary) all change the build. This is the L2 claim made concrete, and it recurs in 'Debugging with a debugger'.

L0.body:
loop forever:
    instr = memory[rip]      # fetch
    op, operands = decode(instr)
    rip += size(instr)       # advance BEFORE executing
    execute(op, operands)    # may overwrite rip (a jump)
L0.cloze: The CPU reads the next instruction from the address in {{c1::rip}}, then advances it by the instruction's {{c2::size}}.

concepts.L1: The CPU's only loop: read the instruction bytes at the instruction pointer, decode them into an operation and operands, advance the pointer, execute. A jump is nothing more than an instruction that writes a new value into the instruction pointer.
concepts.L2: Instructions and data live in the same memory and are the same bytes - the CPU distinguishes them only by which register points at them. That is why buffer overflows can execute attacker data, and why W^X and NX bits exist as a mitigation rather than being inherent to the design.
concepts.L3: Trace x = x + 1 with x at 0x2000: fetch mov rax,[0x2000], rip advances, execute -> rax = mem[0x2000]; fetch add rax,1, execute -> rax += 1; fetch mov [0x2000],rax, execute -> mem[0x2000] = rax. rip moves only by the size decode reported (1 to 15 bytes on x86-64) or by a jump. Advancing before execute is why lea rax,[rip] yields the next instruction's address and why call pushes exactly that value as the return address. A conditional branch writes rip = target only if a condition on the flags holds (je: ZF = 1; jne: ZF = 0; jl: SF differs from OF); otherwise the fall-through instruction is fetched. Real CPUs pipeline and speculate across dozens of these, but the ISA's contract is this loop: results must be as if instructions ran one at a time, in order. 'The classic five-stage pipeline' and 'Speculative execution and its security cost' show what that promise costs and where it leaks.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a function call must save a return address somewhere, given only the fetch-decode-execute loop.
L4.answer: Because a call overwrites rip with the callee's address, the value rip would have had must be stored (on the stack) so that ret can restore it.
L4.explanation: The CPU has exactly one instruction pointer. Jumping into a function destroys the information about where to resume, so the caller's next address has to be saved before the jump - which is precisely what the call instruction pushes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Three consecutive instructions, none of them a jump, sit back to back in memory starting at byte address {a} (decimal); their encoded lengths are {n1}, {n2} and {n3} bytes. After the third has been fetched and decoded, and before it executes, what value does the instruction pointer hold? Answer in decimal.
L4.explanation: Each trip round the loop adds the size decode reported to rip before execute runs, so after three fetches rip has moved past all three instructions and points at the fourth. Nothing in the loop ever moves rip by anything other than an instruction's size or an explicit jump, which is why instruction sizes, not counts, are what the pointer tracks; on x86-64 those sizes vary from 1 to 15 bytes.

L4.answer: $2 + 2\lceil \mathrm{lim}/k \rceil$: one fetch for set, two fetches (add, jl) per loop trip, one for halt. k=3, lim=10 -> 10; k=4, lim=10 -> 8; k=5, lim=12 -> 8; k=3, lim=20 -> 16; k=5, lim=20 -> 10. Verified by running Python 3.
L4.explanation: Every instruction that executes was fetched exactly once, jumps included: the jl is fetched each time round, whether or not it jumps. acc climbs by k per trip and the jl keeps jumping back while acc < lim, so the add runs ceil(lim/k) times and the jl the same number; add the set at the start and the halt at the end. Note pc = pc + 1 happens before execute, and the jl simply overwrites that advanced value.

L4.prompt_tpl: In terms of the fetch-decode-execute loop, what is a jump instruction?
L4.answer: An ordinary instruction whose execute step writes a new value into the instruction pointer
L4.explanation: A jump goes through fetch, decode and execute like anything else; the only thing special is what execute does, which is to store the target into rip so the next fetch reads from there. Memory does not deliver instructions, it answers loads at whatever address the CPU presents, and decode is never skipped: the CPU must decode the jump to learn that it is one and where it goes.
options: An ordinary instruction whose execute step writes a new value into the instruction pointer
A fetch that skips the decode step and reads the target instruction directly
A request to the memory system to start delivering instructions from a different address

L4.prompt_tpl: Suppose the loop were reordered so that rip += size(instr) ran AFTER execute instead of before it. A {s}-byte jump instruction at address {a} (decimal) executes and writes {t} into rip. Under the reordered loop, from which address is the next instruction fetched? Answer in decimal.
L4.answer: $t + s$: the advance is applied to the value the jump just wrote, so the fetch misses the target by the jump's own size. s=2, t=4000 -> 4002; s=5, t=5000 -> 5005; s=2, t=9000 -> 9002; s=5, t=4000 -> 4005.
L4.explanation: With advance-after-execute the increment lands on whatever execute left in rip, so a jump to t fetches from t + s, s bytes into the target instruction, and decode reads garbage. Advancing first means execute sees rip already pointing at the fall-through instruction and can overwrite it cleanly; that ordering is also what makes call push the correct return address and lea rax,[rip] give the next instruction's address.

L4.answer: $7 + n$: n=0 -> 7; n=1 -> 8; n=3 -> 10; n=5 -> 12; n=8 -> 15. Verified by running gcc 13 on x86-64 Linux at -O0 and -O2.
L4.explanation: While the first lea executes, rip has already been advanced past it, so a is the address of the first nop (or of the second lea when n = 0). The second lea likewise reads the address of whatever follows it. The distance between those two points is the 7 bytes of the second lea plus the n nops. If rip still pointed at the executing instruction, the answer would be 7 + n as well but measured from the first lea; the value a itself is what the ordering changes, and call, ret and every RIP-relative operand depend on it.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3. The program and the data it modifies share one list; poke writes an instruction tuple into a memory cell.

mem = [("set", 1), ("poke", {addr}, ("add", {k})), ("add", 10), ("add", 10), ("halt",)]
acc = 0
pc = 0
while True:
    instr = mem[pc]
    pc = pc + 1
    if instr[0] == "set":
        acc = instr[1]
    elif instr[0] == "add":
        acc = acc + instr[1]
    elif instr[0] == "poke":
        mem[instr[1]] = instr[2]
    elif instr[0] == "halt":
        break
print(acc)

What number is printed?
L4.answer: addr = 1: 21 for every k - the poke overwrites its own cell, but that instruction was already fetched and decoded, so both add 10s still run (1 + 10 + 10). addr = 2 or 3: 11 + k, because one add 10 is replaced by add k before it is fetched: k=2 -> 13; k=5 -> 16; k=7 -> 18. Verified by running Python 3.
L4.explanation: Instructions are data in the same memory: poke is an ordinary store, and the loop fetches whatever bytes are at pc when it gets there. A cell rewritten before its fetch runs the new instruction; a cell rewritten after its fetch has no effect on the copy already in flight. Real CPUs make this murkier because they fetch far ahead: x86 promises to notice such stores anyway, while ARM requires explicit cache maintenance before the new instruction is seen. This is the L2 fact that lets a buffer overflow execute data.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C program copies attacker-controlled input into a stack buffer without a length check, and the copy runs past the buffer into the saved return address. Using only the fetch-decode-execute loop and the fact that instructions and data share one memory, explain (a) how the attacker's bytes come to be executed, and (b) exactly which step of the loop the NX bit interferes with, and why that makes NX a mitigation rather than a fix.
L4.answer: (a) ret pops the saved return address into rip. The attacker overwrote it, so the next fetch reads from an address of their choosing, for example inside the buffer they filled; the CPU fetches those bytes and decodes them as instructions because nothing in memory marks them as data. (b) NX is a per-page bit the fetch step checks: fetching from a page marked non-executable faults instead of decoding. It does nothing to the overwrite of rip itself, so the attacker can still point rip at code that is already executable (return-oriented programming), which is why NX closes one target class and leaves the underlying bug.
L4.explanation: The loop has one instruction pointer and fetches from wherever it points; ret is just an instruction whose execute step loads rip from the stack. Because bytes carry no type, the fetch that follows treats the attacker's data as code. NX adds a check to that fetch, not to the write of rip, so it converts 'run my bytes' into a fault while 'run your bytes in my order' survives. See 'Stack buffer overflow' and 'Return-oriented programming' in the security domain.

L0.body:
$ gcc -c hello.c        # C source -> x86-64 machine code
$ objdump -d hello.o    # machine code -> assembly mnemonics
$ uname -m              # x86_64 | aarch64 | riscv64
L0.cloze: The {{c1::ISA}} defines the instructions, registers and memory model a program may rely on; the microarchitecture is how one chip implements it.

concepts.L1: An instruction set architecture is the specification a CPU promises to honour: which instructions exist, what registers exist, how memory behaves. x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V are ISAs. It is the boundary between software and hardware.
concepts.L2: ISA and microarchitecture are routinely conflated. Zen 5 and Golden Cove are microarchitectures implementing one x86-64 ISA - the same binary runs on both. Performance is a microarchitecture property; correctness is an ISA property. Spectre leaked microarchitecture through a contract that only spoke of correctness.
concepts.L3: An ISA is a document, not a chip. It fixes the architectural state (registers, program counter, flags, memory as addressed bytes), the encoding of every instruction, what each one does to that state, what happens on an exception, and how loads and stores may be ordered (x86-64 promises total store order; ARM64 promises less). Caches, pipelines and branch predictors are microarchitecture, visible only through timing. The rule that lets implementations diverge is 'as if sequential': whatever a core does internally, the architectural state at every instruction boundary must match what the fetch-decode-execute loop would produce. That is why gcc's default x86-64 output runs on a 2008 Core 2 and a 2026 server part, and why an ARM Mac needs Rosetta. The contract is versioned by extensions (SSE4, AVX-512): a chip lacking one traps with SIGILL. See 'The ISA as a contract' and 'Spectre'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary compiled for x86-64 fails to run on an ARM64 machine. Is this an ISA problem or a microarchitecture problem? Justify.
L4.answer: ISA - the instruction encodings themselves are undefined for an ARM64 decoder. Microarchitecture differences never prevent a binary from running, only change how fast it runs.
L4.explanation: Same-ISA chips differ in speed; different-ISA chips differ in meaning. This distinction is the reason emulation layers translate instructions rather than just adjusting performance.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of the following is fixed by the ISA, so that every chip implementing it must agree, rather than by one chip's microarchitecture?
L4.answer: The number and width of the general-purpose registers a program may name
L4.explanation: Registers are architectural state: an instruction names one with a few bits of its encoding, so the count is part of the contract (16 x 64-bit on x86-64, 31 on ARM64, 32 on RISC-V). Cache geometry and retire width are microarchitecture - a Zen 5 and a Golden Cove differ in both and run the same binary. Dive into Systems 5.9 gives exactly this split: the ISA is the instructions, their encodings, the registers and their effects; the microarchitecture is the circuitry that implements it.
options: The number and width of the general-purpose registers a program may name
The size and associativity of the level-1 data cache
How many instructions the core can retire in one clock cycle

L4.prompt_tpl: ARM64 and the RISC-V base ISA fix every instruction at 32 bits; RISC-V's compressed extension uses 16-bit ones. A code section holds {n} bytes consisting entirely of {w}-bit instructions. How many instructions does it contain?
L4.explanation: A fixed-width encoding is an ISA property: each instruction is $w/8$ bytes, so the count is bytes divided by $w/8$, i.e. $8n/w$. This is what makes decoding trivial on ARM64 and RISC-V (the decoder knows where every instruction starts) and impossible to do this way on x86-64, whose instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long - an x86-64 code section of 4096 bytes could hold anywhere from 273 to 4096 instructions, and only a decoder walking the bytes can say which.

L4.prompt_tpl: On an x86-64 Linux machine, what exactly does the shell command uname -m print? (Python's platform.machine() returns the same string.)
L4.explanation: uname -m prints the machine's ISA name as the kernel spells it: x86_64 here (verified by running it), aarch64 on 64-bit ARM, riscv64 on RISC-V. It names the contract, not the chip: an Intel i7 and an AMD Ryzen print the same string because they implement the same ISA, and it is the first thing to check when a downloaded binary refuses to run - a binary is compiled for exactly one of these names.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program is compiled on a Zen 4 workstation with gcc -O2 -march=native, which lets gcc emit AVX-512 instructions. The binary is copied to a 2014 Haswell server, which is also x86-64 but has no AVX-512. What happens the first time an AVX-512 instruction is reached, and why does 'same ISA' not save it?
L4.answer: It is killed with SIGILL (Illegal instruction): extensions are part of the ISA contract, and the binary was compiled against a larger contract than Haswell implements
L4.explanation: The x86-64 name covers a baseline plus optional extensions, and -march=native compiles against everything the build machine has. An opcode the decoder does not implement raises the invalid-opcode exception (#UD), which Linux delivers as SIGILL; the kernel does not emulate vector extensions. 'Correctness is an ISA property' still holds - the binary and the chip simply disagree about which ISA. The same trap hits binaries built for Alder Lake's early AVX-512 P-cores when run on later units where Intel fused it off.
options: It runs, but more slowly, because microarchitecture differences only affect speed
It is killed with SIGILL (Illegal instruction): extensions are part of the ISA contract, and the binary was compiled against a larger contract than Haswell implements
The kernel traps the instruction and emulates it transparently, so the program completes with identical output

L4.prompt_tpl: One x86-64 binary executes {n} billion instructions on any chip that implements the ISA, because the instruction stream is fixed by the ISA and the compiler. Chip A sustains {ia} instructions per cycle at {fa} GHz. How many seconds does the run take on chip A? Answer with the number of seconds.
L4.answer: $t = n / (\mathrm{IPC} \cdot f)$ with $n$ in billions and $f$ in GHz (the $10^{9}$ factors cancel): 10 billion at 1.5 IPC, 2 GHz -> 3.33 s; 30 billion at 3 IPC, 4 GHz -> 2.5 s; 60 billion at 1.5 IPC, 4 GHz -> 10 s; 60 billion at 3 IPC, 2 GHz -> 10 s.
L4.explanation: Cycles = instructions / IPC and time = cycles / frequency, so $t = n/(\mathrm{IPC} \cdot f)$. The instruction count is the ISA-side quantity - same binary, same $n$ everywhere; IPC and clock are what the microarchitecture decides, which is the L2 claim in numbers: two chips implementing one ISA can differ by a factor of four here while producing identical results. This is the iron law of processor performance, and it returns in 'CPU microarchitecture'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Python script written on an x86-64 laptop runs unchanged on a Raspberry Pi (ARM64), yet the CPython interpreter binary from the laptop will not run on the Pi. Where exactly does the ISA boundary sit in that stack, and why does the script not care which side of it it is on?
L4.answer: The boundary sits between the CPython binary and the CPU: python3 is machine code compiled for one ISA and must be rebuilt per ISA. The script is never machine code - it is data that CPython reads, compiles to its own bytecode and interprets, so the only contract it sees is Python's language semantics, which CPython promises to honour identically on every ISA. Only when the script calls native code (a C extension, ctypes) does it touch the ISA again.
L4.explanation: An ISA is a contract between machine code and hardware; an interpreter is a program that offers a different contract (the language) to what it runs, paying for the portability with speed. Every layer in the stack has this shape, and the trick of putting a software contract above a hardware one is exactly what Rosetta, the JVM and CPython share. See 'Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments'.

L4.prompt_tpl: An out-of-order core executes instructions in a different order from the program and even starts executing instructions on a branch path that turns out not to be taken. Starting from the fetch-decode-execute contract, state the single guarantee that makes this a legal implementation of the ISA, and then explain why Spectre was possible without that guarantee ever being broken.
L4.answer: The guarantee: at every instruction boundary the architectural state - registers, program counter, memory contents, flags - must equal what the sequential fetch-decode-execute loop would have produced; the core reorders internally but retires results in program order and discards anything from a mispredicted path before it becomes architectural. Spectre: the cache is not architectural state, so the ISA says nothing about it. Discarded speculative loads still leave lines in the cache, and timing a later access reads that footprint. The contract was kept to the letter; it simply never promised to hide the microarchitecture.
L4.explanation: The 'as-if sequential' rule is what an ISA actually promises and it constrains only architectural state. Everything else - cache contents, branch-predictor state, power, timing - is a side channel the contract is silent about, which is why Spectre is a class of bugs rather than one bug and why fixing it means either changing the microarchitecture or extending the contract (leakage contracts). See 'Out-of-order execution: the Tomasulo idea' and 'Spectre'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rosetta 2 runs x86-64 binaries on Apple's ARM64 cores by translating them. List what a translator must reproduce exactly because it is ISA-level, list what it may ignore because it is microarchitecture-level, and explain why Apple built a switchable x86-style total-store-order memory mode into the cores instead of leaving memory ordering to the translator.
L4.answer: Must reproduce: the effect of every instruction on architectural state - the 16 general-purpose and the SIMD registers, the flags, memory as little-endian bytes, the program counter - plus exceptions and signals and the memory-ordering guarantees x86-64 makes (stores become visible in program order). May ignore: caches, pipeline depth, out-of-order execution, branch prediction, all timing. The ordering point is the expensive one: ARM64's weaker model would force the translator to fence almost every load and store to stay correct, so Apple made the hardware itself obey TSO for translated processes (a per-process control-register bit), which keeps the contract cheaply.
L4.explanation: Emulation is the clearest demonstration of where the ISA boundary lies: everything the contract names must be reproduced, everything it does not can be dropped. Most of x86-64 is cheap to translate one instruction at a time; the memory model is not, because it constrains the ordering of many instructions at once. Measured on the M1, hardware TSO costs about 9% versus the native model - far less than software fencing. See 'Memory consistency at the hardware level'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design question. A fixed-width {w}-bit instruction word must hold a {o}-bit opcode, a {f}-bit function field and two {r}-bit register fields (a destination and one source); every remaining bit is a two's-complement immediate. Derive the largest positive immediate such an instruction can carry. (RISC-V's I-type uses 7, 3 and 5.) Answer with the largest positive immediate.
L4.answer: Immediate width $k = w - o - f - 2r$, largest positive value $2^{k-1} - 1$: 32-bit word, 7-bit opcode, 3-bit function, 5-bit registers (RISC-V I-type) -> $k = 12$ -> 2047; 6, 3, 5 -> $k = 13$ -> 4095; 7, 3, 4 -> $k = 14$ -> 8191; 6, 3, 4 -> $k = 15$ -> 16383.
L4.explanation: The encoding budget is part of the contract, and it is a zero-sum split of $w$ bits: after opcode, function and register fields, $k = w - o - f - 2r$ bits remain, and a $k$-bit two's-complement field spans $-2^{k-1}$ to $2^{k-1} - 1$. This is why RISC-V addi accepts only -2048 to 2047 and loading a 32-bit constant needs two instructions (lui then addi), and why x86-64 tolerates variable-length encodings: a 32-bit immediate simply does not fit in a fixed 32-bit word. See 'The RISC-V instruction formats' and 'Two's complement'.
