L0.body:
register   ~0.3 ns      (< 1 KiB)
L1 cache   ~1 ns         (~32-64 KiB)
L2 cache   ~4 ns         (~1 MiB)
L3 cache   ~15 ns        (tens of MiB)
DRAM       ~80 ns        (GiB)
NVMe SSD   ~100 us       (TB)
L0.cloze: An L1 hit costs about {{c1::1}} ns; a DRAM access costs roughly {{c2::80}} ns - about two orders of magnitude more.

concepts.L1: Storage is a pyramid: small and fast at the top, large and slow at the bottom. Caches sit between registers and DRAM and hold recently used lines, transparently. A cache line - 64 bytes on x86-64 - is the unit of transfer, not the byte.
concepts.L2: Caches make sequential access fast, not small data fast. Reading one byte pulls the whole 64-byte line, so a linked-list walk touching 8 bytes per node wastes 7/8 of every transfer while an array gets 8 useful elements per miss. That, not instruction count, is the 10x.
concepts.L3: Caches work because programs have locality: the bytes just touched, and their neighbours, are the likeliest next requests, so a small SRAM answers most accesses. Average cost is $t_{hit} + m \cdot t_{miss}$ with $m$ the miss rate: a 1 ns hit and an 80 ns miss average 9 ns at 90% hits. Trace summing 10 million int32, measured here. Sequential: the prefetcher streams lines ahead at DRAM bandwidth: about 5 ms. Shuffled index array, sum += a[idx[i]]: every element misses but the loads are independent, so the core keeps 10-12 misses in flight and pays about 10 ns each: about 100 ms. Shuffled linked list: each address depends on the previous load, nothing overlaps, each element pays full latency: about 1.15 s. Same O(n) and instructions, 200x apart; the last two differ only in dependence - L2's linked-list penalty. Next: 'Bandwidth versus latency: Little's law for memory' (arch).

L4.prompt_tpl: How many 4-byte ints fit in one 64-byte cache line, and how many cache lines does a contiguous array of {n} ints occupy, assuming the array starts on a cache-line boundary? Answer with the number of cache lines.
L4.answer: 16 ints per line; lines = ceil(n/16) -> 1, 63, 62500
L4.explanation: 64 / 4 = 16 ints per line, so an aligned array of n ints spans ceil(n/16) lines: 16 -> 1, 1000 -> 63, 1000000 -> 62500. The count matters because it is the number of line fetches a full sequential scan costs; contiguity amortises one miss over 16 elements. Drop the alignment assumption and the array can straddle one extra line.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cache hit costs {h} ns. A miss costs that same {h} ns check plus a further {m} ns to fetch the line from DRAM. The hit rate is {p} percent. What is the average time per access, in ns?
L4.explanation: Every access pays the hit check; only the missing fraction pays the DRAM penalty, so the average is hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty. Notice the leverage: going from 99% to 90% hits with a 1 ns hit and 80 ns miss moves the average from 1.8 ns to 9 ns, a 5x slowdown from a 9-point change. That is why hit rate, not hit latency, is the number a programmer can actually fight for.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linked-list node occupies {b} bytes, and every node of the list lands on a different 64-byte cache line. What fraction of each line the walk fetches is actually used? Answer as a decimal.
L4.explanation: The line is the unit of transfer, so a node that uses b bytes still costs a 64-byte fetch and the other 64 - b bytes are dead bandwidth. An array of 8-byte elements uses every byte of every line it fetches (fraction 1.0); an 8-byte-per-node list uses one eighth, which is the 7/8 waste in L2. Halving node size doubles the useful fraction without changing a single instruction.

L4.prompt_tpl: int a[1024] holds 4-byte ints and starts on a 64-byte cache-line boundary. The program reads a[0], which misses and brings its line into L1. Nothing is evicted before the next read. Which of these reads is guaranteed to hit in L1?
L4.explanation: a[0] to a[15] are bytes 0 to 63 of the array: one line, all fetched together, so a[15] is a hit. a[16] begins at byte 64, the first byte of the next line; a hardware prefetcher may well have fetched it, but nothing guarantees that. a[1000] is at byte 4000, line 62. The rule: index times element size, divided by 64, tells you which line; same line means a hit.

L4.prompt_tpl: An array of {n} 4-byte ints starts {off} bytes past the beginning of a 64-byte cache line rather than on the boundary. How many cache lines does the array span?
L4.answer: $\lceil (\mathrm{off} + 4n) / 64 \rceil$: n=16, off=4 -> 2 (1 if aligned); n=100, off=32 -> 7; n=100, off=60 -> 8 (7 if aligned); n=1000, off=4 -> 63; n=1000, off=60 -> 64 (63 if aligned).
L4.explanation: The array occupies bytes off to off + 4n - 1 of a run of lines, so it spans ceil((off + 4n)/64) of them. A 64-byte array that is not aligned always straddles two lines and costs two fetches instead of one; for a long array the alignment adds at most one line, which is why alignment matters most for small hot objects. glibc's malloc guarantees only 16-byte alignment on x86-64; aligned_alloc(64, size) or alignas(64) is how you ask for the boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop reads every {s}-th element of a line-aligned array of {n} 4-byte ints: indices 0, {s}, 2*{s} and so on. How many distinct 64-byte cache lines does the loop touch?
L4.answer: While the byte stride 4s is at most 64, every line of the array is touched: $\lceil 4n/64 \rceil$. Beyond that, each access is its own line: $\lceil n/s \rceil$. n=1024: s=2 -> 64; s=16 -> 64; s=32 -> 32; s=64 -> 16. n=4096: 256, 256, 128, 64.
L4.explanation: Stride 2 does half the reads of stride 1 but fetches exactly the same lines, so its memory traffic is unchanged and its time barely moves: the instruction count halved and nothing else did. The cliff sits at a stride of one line, 16 ints; up to there the line count is fixed by the array size, past it every element is its own fetch and only the prefetcher's stride detection keeps the loop from paying full latency. This is the stride experiment in the 'Gallery of Processor Cache Effects' resource.

L4.prompt_tpl: A shuffled linked list of 10 million nodes is walked in 1.1 s. Profiling shows about 10 instructions per node, nearly all of the time spent waiting on loads. A rewrite cuts it to 5 instructions per node without changing the node layout or the order of the nodes. What is the best prediction for the new time?
L4.answer: About 1.1 s: the walk is bound by one dependent DRAM miss per node, and the instructions were already hidden under that latency
L4.explanation: Each node costs a DRAM latency of roughly 100 ns that the next node's address depends on; the 10 instructions run inside that wait, so removing 5 of them removes work that cost no time. The prefetcher cannot help because the next address is unknown until the load returns. To make the walk faster you must change what memory is touched: smaller nodes, nodes allocated in traversal order, or an array. See 'Array versus linked list: the real trade'.
options: About 1.1 s: the walk is bound by one dependent DRAM miss per node, and the instructions were already hidden under that latency
About 0.55 s: half the instructions, half the time
About 0.1 s: fewer instructions per node let the prefetcher keep up with the walk

L4.prompt_tpl: You sum {n} million int32 values by reading them in a shuffled order through a precomputed index array, so every read is a DRAM miss of {lat} ns but no read depends on another. The core can keep {k} misses in flight at once (k = 1 is the same workload as a pointer chase). Derive the time for the whole sum, in ms.
L4.answer: Little's law: with $k$ misses outstanding one completes every $\mathrm{lat}/k$ ns, so $t = n \cdot 10^{6} \cdot \mathrm{lat} / k$ ns $= n \cdot \mathrm{lat} / k$ ms. n=10, lat=80: k=1 -> 800 ms; k=10 -> 80 ms; k=12 -> 66.67 ms. n=50, lat=100, k=12 -> 416.67 ms.
L4.explanation: Throughput equals outstanding requests divided by latency, so k independent misses in flight cut the per-element cost from lat to lat/k; the total is n million times that. Measured here: 10 million independent random reads took about 100 ms, consistent with k near 10 at 100 ns, while the dependent chase over the same data took 1.15 s, k = 1. k is set by hardware (about 10-12 L1 fill buffers per core), which is why the dependent chain is the worst case. Next: 'Bandwidth versus latency: Little's law for memory' (arch).

L4.prompt_tpl: A program scans {n} records of {S} bytes each, but on every scan it reads only the same {h} hot bytes of each record. You redesign the layout so that the hot fields of all records sit together in one contiguous, line-aligned array (a structure of arrays). How many 64-byte cache lines does one scan fetch after the redesign?
L4.answer: $n h / 64$: 1,000,000 records with 8 hot bytes -> 125,000 lines; 1,000,000 with 16 -> 250,000; 4,000,000 with 8 -> 500,000; 4,000,000 with 16 -> 1,000,000. Before the redesign the scan fetched $nS/64$ lines: 1,000,000 to 8,000,000.
L4.explanation: Before, each record's hot bytes sit inside its own record, so the scan drags all n*S bytes through the cache and discards (S - h)/S of every line. After, the lines hold nothing but hot data, so the traffic falls by the factor S/h, between 4x and 16x on these draws, with the instruction count unchanged. This hot/cold split is why columnar databases and SIMD code both prefer structure-of-arrays layouts. See 'Cache lines and spatial locality' (arch).

L4.answer: The inner loop steps i, so consecutive reads are N*4 = 16 KiB apart: every read is on a different cache line (and a different page), so one column costs 4096 line fetches, and those 4096 lines (256 KiB) are evicted from L1 before the next column could reuse them. Row order would use 16 ints per fetched line. Fix: swap the loops so i is outer and j inner (sum += grid[i * N + j] with j moving fastest), touching consecutive bytes; then 16 elements share each fetch and the prefetcher streams the rows. Measured here: about 150-170 ms column order versus 8 ms row order.
L4.explanation: The program is correct and does the same 16.7 million additions either way; only the order of addresses differs. Row-major storage puts grid[i][j] and grid[i][j+1] in adjacent bytes, so walking j inner fetches a line once and uses all 16 ints in it; walking i inner uses 4 bytes of each 64-byte line and comes back for the other 60 only after 4096 more lines have passed through. Loop interchange is the fix; the general rule is to make the innermost loop walk the innermost (contiguous) dimension.

sections.note: The source of the bugs nobody warns you about.

L0.body:
uint8_t x = 255;
x = x + 1;          /* x is now 0: the stored value is reduced mod 2**8 */
unsigned int u = UINT_MAX;   /* 4294967295, from <limits.h> */
u = u + 1;          /* 0: defined behaviour, no error, no signal */
Python:  2**31 - 1 + 1   # 2147483648: int is unbounded, no wrap
L0.cloze: An unsigned n-bit integer wraps modulo {{c1::2**n}}, so a uint8_t holding 255, incremented and stored, holds {{c2::0}}.

concepts.L1: C's integer types have a fixed bit width, so arithmetic is done modulo 2**n for unsigned types. Results outside the range are not errors and produce no signal - the high bits are simply discarded.
concepts.L2: Python has no fixed-width int, so beginners learn arithmetic that never overflows and then meet C. But NumPy's fixed-width types do wrap: the scalar np.int32(2147483647) + 1 is -2147483648 with only a RuntimeWarning, and the same sum inside an array wraps with no warning at all. The exemption is Python's int, not Python.
concepts.L3: An n-bit register holds a residue class mod $2^{n}$; arithmetic on residues is exact, so 255 + 1 = 256 $\equiv$ 0 (mod 256). The hardware loses nothing: the carry-out lands in a flag (CF on x86-64) that C never exposes. C makes wrap the definition: conversion to an unsigned type reduces the value modulo $2^{n}$ (C17 6.3.1.3), and unsigned arithmetic 'can never overflow' (6.2.5p9). The exploit shape follows. `if (len + 1 > cap) reject;` passes when len is UINT_MAX, because len + 1 is 0, and the allocation that follows is far too small. The fix must avoid the wrapping operation: `if (len >= cap) reject;` compares them with no arithmetic. The tempting `len > cap - 1` only moves the wrap: for cap == 0 it never rejects. Read as two's complement the same bits give the signed value, and there C refuses to define the wrap - see 'Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C'.

L4.prompt_tpl: uint8_t x = {a}; what is x + {b} after assignment back into a uint8_t?
L4.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is exact modulo $2^{8}$, so subtract 256 until the result lands in 0..255. Wrapping is defined behaviour for unsigned types in C and Python's int does not wrap at all - the trap is that C promotes uint8_t to int before adding, then truncates on the store back.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the largest value an unsigned {n}-bit integer can hold? Answer with the number.
L4.explanation: An unsigned $n$-bit integer has $2^{n}$ distinct bit patterns, and the smallest of them is 0, so the largest is $2^{n} - 1$, the all-ones pattern. Adding 1 to it gives $2^{n}$, which needs $n + 1$ bits; the top bit is dropped and the stored value is 0. This one number is the boundary at which every wrap in this concept happens.

L4.prompt_tpl: C: uint8_t x = {a}; x -= {b}; What is x afterwards? Answer with the number.
L4.explanation: Wrap works downwards as well as upwards. The subtraction is done in int after promotion (for example 3 - 5 = -2), and on the store back into uint8_t the value is reduced modulo 256: -2 + 256 = 254. When the true difference is already in 0..255 nothing changes (10 - 5 = 5). A uint8_t can never hold a negative number, so 'x < 0' after unsigned subtraction is always false - the classic bug in a countdown loop with an unsigned counter.

uint16_t holds 0..65535, so 65534 + 3 = 65537 is reduced modulo 65536 on the store and i becomes 1. uint32_t holds 0..4294967295; 0 - 1 is reduced modulo $2^{32}$ to 4294967295, which %u prints as the largest unsigned value. Both are defined behaviour: no error, no warning, no signal. (Verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux.)

Before any arithmetic, C promotes a uint8_t operand to int (integer promotion), so `x + 1` is the int 256 - no wrap has happened yet. The wrap occurs only when a value is converted back to the narrow unsigned type: the cast reduces 256 modulo $2^{8}$ to 0, exactly as a store into a uint8_t variable would. Unsigned wrap is never undefined behaviour; the trap is that it happens at the conversion, not inside the addition. (Verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux.)
options: Undefined behaviour: 255 + 1 does not fit in uint8_t

L4.prompt_tpl: A uint32_t tick counter starts at 0 at boot, increments {hz} times per second and is never reset. Estimate first, then compute: after how many days does it wrap back to 0? Answer with the number of days (decimals allowed).
L4.answer: $2^{32} / (hz \cdot 86400)$ days: 1000 Hz -> 49.71 days (the famous 49.7-day uptime hang in Windows 95/98); 100 Hz -> 497.1 days; 1 Hz -> 49710 days, about 136 years.
L4.explanation: The counter holds $2^{32} = 4294967296$ distinct values, so it returns to 0 after $2^{32}$ ticks. At 1000 ticks per second that is $4294967296 / 1000 = 4294967$ seconds; divided by 86400 seconds per day it is 49.71 days. A millisecond counter feels enormous but wraps in under two months, which is why elapsed-time code must subtract counters in unsigned arithmetic (now - then wraps correctly) rather than compare them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 32-bit platform, so size_t is 32 bits. A file parser reads an element count n from the file, then does p = malloc(n * sizeof(T)); and loops n times writing one element into p. Nothing checks n. With n = {n} and sizeof(T) = {s}, how many bytes does malloc actually receive? Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.explanation: The multiplication is done in size_t, so the product is reduced modulo $2^{32}$: $(2^{30} + 1) \cdot 4 = 2^{32} + 4$, and malloc receives 4 bytes while the loop writes 4 GiB past them. This is the allocation-size overflow behind many real CVEs. The defence is to check the operands before multiplying (reject if n > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(T)) or to use calloc(n, sizeof(T)), which is required to detect the overflow and return NULL.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, int and unsigned int are 32 bits. For unsigned int x, the line `if (x + 1 < x) overflowed();` is a correct detector. Starting from the definition of unsigned arithmetic, explain why it is correct - and why the identical line for a signed int x is not, naming the concept that governs the signed case.
L4.answer: Unsigned arithmetic is defined as reduction modulo 2^32, so x + 1 is always a defined value: it equals x + 1 whenever x < UINT_MAX and equals 0 when x == UINT_MAX. So x + 1 < x is true in exactly the one wrapping case, and the compiler must compute it faithfully. For signed int, x + 1 when x == INT_MAX is undefined behaviour ('Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C'): the standard defines no result, so the compiler may assume x + 1 > x always holds and delete the branch. The signed check must be written without overflowing, e.g. x == INT_MAX or x > INT_MAX - 1.
L4.explanation: The unsigned test works because the standard promises a specific wrapped value (C17 6.2.5p9: a result that cannot be represented is reduced modulo one greater than the largest representable value), so the comparison is over defined numbers. The signed test fails not because signed values do not wrap on x86-64 - they do, in the ADD instruction - but because the language never defined that wrap, and an optimiser is licensed to assume it never occurs. Detecting overflow means checking the operands, never the result.

concepts.t: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C

L0.cloze: In C, {{c1::unsigned}} overflow is defined to wrap; {{c2::signed}} overflow is undefined behaviour.

concepts.L1: The C standard defines unsigned overflow as wrapping modulo 2**n but leaves signed overflow undefined. The compiler may therefore assume it never happens and optimise on that assumption.
concepts.L2: 'Undefined' does not mean 'wraps in practice'. gcc -O2 deletes the check `if (x + 1 < x)` entirely, because signed x + 1 < x is impossible in a program without UB. The test compiles to nothing and the overflow it was guarding against still occurs.
concepts.L3: C17 6.2.5p9: unsigned computation 'can never overflow', it is reduced mod $2^{n}$. 6.5p5: a result not representable in its type is undefined behaviour; int has no modulo clause. The optimiser treats that as a promise: `x + 1 < x` can only be true through UB, so gcc folds it to 0 even at -O0, and `sum = a + b; if (sum < a)` becomes `if (b < 0)` - not deleted, rewritten into a test that never fires on a real overflow. The payoff: with `int i`, `for (i = 0; i <= n; i++)` is assumed to run n + 1 times, so i lives in a 64-bit register; with `unsigned i` and n == UINT_MAX it is legally infinite. Fixes: compare before the operation - `b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b` cannot overflow, INT_MAX - b lies in [0, INT_MAX - 1] - or C23 ckd_add / __builtin_add_overflow; -fwrapv makes it wrap, -fsanitize=undefined reports it. 'Undefined behaviour' extends this licence to pointers and uninitialised reads.

L4.prompt_tpl: C: int sum = a + b; if (sum < a) handle_overflow();  Why can this fail to detect overflow when a and b are signed ints?
L4.answer: Signed overflow is UB, so the compiler may assume a + b did not overflow and rewrite `sum < a` as `b < 0` (gcc 13 -O2 emits a single shift of b's sign bit). The branch now fires for every negative b and never for a real overflow. Check before adding: (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b) || (b < 0 && a < INT_MIN - b), or use C23 ckd_add / __builtin_add_overflow.
L4.explanation: The test relies on the wrapped value existing, but the standard never promised one, and the compiler is allowed to reason from 'no overflow happened' backwards. Do overflow checks by comparing against the limit before the operation - both comparisons stay in range - or use a builtin that the compiler models explicitly. Testing at -O0 proves nothing: gcc folds x + 1 < x to false even there.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, int is 32 bits. According to the C standard, which of these expressions has undefined behaviour?
L4.answer: int x = INT_MAX; x + 1
L4.explanation: 6.5p5: a result not representable in the type of the expression is an exceptional condition, and the behaviour is undefined - INT_MAX + 1 is not an int. 6.2.5p9: unsigned arithmetic 'can never overflow', it is reduced mod $2^{32}$, so u + 1 is 0. The unsigned char case is a trap in the other direction: c is promoted to int before the addition, so c + 1 is simply 256 with no wrap at all; only a store back into c would truncate.
options: int x = INT_MAX; x + 1
unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u + 1
unsigned char c = 255; c + 1

L4.prompt_tpl: C, int is 32 bits, so INT_MAX is 2147483647. int a = {a}; What is the largest int b for which a + b has defined behaviour? Answer with the number.
L4.explanation: a + b is defined exactly when the mathematical sum is representable, i.e. $a + b \leq 2147483647$, so $b \leq 2147483647 - a$. That subtraction is itself safe for $a \geq 0$: it lands in $[0, \mathrm{INT\_MAX}]$. This is the shape of every correct overflow guard - compare against the limit before the operation, never inspect the result afterwards.

L4.answer: 1 if m > k (the true sum exceeds INT_MAX), else 0. Verified on gcc 13: k=0,m=1 -> 1; k=1,m=1 -> 0; k=3,m=2 -> 0; k=3,m=4 -> 1; k=5,m=4 -> 0; k=5,m=10 -> 1.
L4.explanation: __builtin_add_overflow computes the sum in infinite precision, stores the low bits in r, and returns 1 exactly when the stored value differs from the true sum. INT_MAX - k + m fits in an int only when $m \leq k$. This is the portable way to detect overflow: the compiler models the builtin explicitly, so no UB is ever executed. C23 spells the same thing ckd_add(&r, a, b).

L4.prompt_tpl: Which gcc/clang command-line flag makes signed integer overflow defined behaviour that wraps in two's complement, instead of undefined behaviour? Give the flag exactly.
L4.answer: -fwrapv
L4.explanation: -fwrapv tells the compiler to treat signed arithmetic as wrapping mod $2^{n}$ (the Linux kernel and CPython are built with it), which disables optimisations that assume no overflow. Do not confuse it with -ftrapv, which makes overflow trap at run time, or with -fsanitize=undefined (UBSan), which reports each overflow with a message. None of these changes what the C standard says; they change what one compiler does.

L4.answer: Not undefined behaviour: s is promoted to int, 32768 fits in int, and only the store back into short is an implementation-defined conversion (gcc: s becomes -32768)
L4.explanation: The integer promotions (6.3.1.1) turn every operand narrower than int into int before arithmetic, so the addition is 32767 + 1 in int and is representable. Converting the out-of-range int back to short is governed by 6.3.1.3p3: implementation-defined result or an implementation-defined signal, not UB; gcc documents reduction modulo $2^{16}$, so s reads -32768. The UB rule bites only where the result of the expression itself does not fit its type: int, long, long long.
options: Not undefined behaviour: s is promoted to int, 32768 fits in int, and only the store back into short is an implementation-defined conversion (gcc: s becomes -32768)
Undefined behaviour: 32768 is not representable in short, so 6.5p5 applies exactly as it does to INT_MAX + 1
Defined to wrap to -32768 by the standard, because types narrower than int follow the unsigned modulo rule

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc -O2, int is 32 bits. Two ints read at run time hold m == INT_MIN and d == -1, and the program evaluates m / d. What happens?
L4.answer: Undefined behaviour under 6.5.5p6, because the quotient 2^31 is not representable; on x86-64 the IDIV instruction raises a divide error and the process dies with SIGFPE
L4.explanation: 6.5.5p6: if the quotient a/b is representable the result is defined; otherwise the behaviour of both a/b and a%b is undefined. $-2^{31} / -1 = 2^{31}$, one more than INT_MAX. This is the case that -fwrapv does not rescue either: the hardware IDIV cannot produce the value and faults (#DE), which Linux delivers as SIGFPE - 'floating point exception' for an integer instruction. Verified here: the process exits with status 136. Guard the divisor: d == -1 && m == INT_MIN.
options: Undefined behaviour under 6.5.5p6, because the quotient 2^31 is not representable; on x86-64 the IDIV instruction raises a divide error and the process dies with SIGFPE
The result is INT_MIN, defined by the standard: division by -1 is negation and negation of INT_MIN wraps
The result is INT_MAX: the standard saturates a quotient that is out of range

L4.prompt_tpl: Signed ints a and b of arbitrary sign. Derive a check that reports whether a + b would overflow without ever computing a + b, and prove that the comparisons in your check cannot themselves overflow.
L4.answer: Overflow iff (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b) || (b < 0 && a < INT_MIN - b). Positive side: $a + b > \mathrm{INT\_MAX} \iff a > \mathrm{INT\_MAX} - b$, and for $1 \leq b \leq \mathrm{INT\_MAX}$ the quantity $\mathrm{INT\_MAX} - b$ lies in $[0, \mathrm{INT\_MAX} - 1]$, representable. Negative side: $a + b < \mathrm{INT\_MIN} \iff a < \mathrm{INT\_MIN} - b$, and for $\mathrm{INT\_MIN} \leq b \leq -1$ the quantity $\mathrm{INT\_MIN} - b$ lies in $[\mathrm{INT\_MIN} + 1, 0]$, representable. b == 0 can never overflow. Both subtractions move toward zero, which is why they are safe.
L4.explanation: Rearranging the inequality moves b to the side of the limit, and subtracting a same-sign b from the limit always moves the limit toward zero, so the intermediate is in range by construction. The two-sided form matters: the common one-sided check misses a + b with b < 0 underflowing past INT_MIN, which is UB just as much. The compiler can optimise this freely because no step of it depends on a value the standard does not define. C23 ckd_add is this check, written by the implementation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two functions count iterations of a loop whose condition is i <= n, with i starting at 0 and incremented by 1 each pass. In the first, i and n are int; in the second, unsigned. gcc -O2 on x86-64 compiles the int version to straight-line code that returns n + 1 (or 0 when n is negative) with no loop at all, but keeps a real loop in the unsigned version. Which rule of the C standard licenses the first transformation, and which input value makes the two functions genuinely different?
L4.answer: Signed overflow is UB (6.5p5), so the compiler may assume i++ never wraps; then i <= n with i starting at 0 runs exactly n + 1 times (0 if n < 0), a closed form. Unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition (6.2.5p9), so when n == UINT_MAX the condition i <= n is always true, i wraps to 0 and the loop is infinite; the compiler must preserve that, so it cannot replace the loop with n + 1 (which would be 0).
L4.explanation: This is the optimisation the UB rule is sold for: a signed induction variable is provably monotone, so trip counts are closed forms, i can be kept in a 64-bit register without re-sign-extending each pass, and the loop can be vectorised. The unsigned loop has one input on which it never terminates, and that input is a legal program. Verified on gcc 13.3: the int version compiles to a cmovs and a lea, the unsigned version to a compare-and-branch loop.

concepts.t: Integer division truncates - but toward what?

L0.body:
C:       -7 / 2  ->  -3      -7 % 2  ->  -1     /* truncate toward zero */
Python:  -7 // 2 ->  -4      -7 %  2 ->   1      # floor, sign follows divisor
L0.cloze: C truncates toward {{c1::zero}} so -7/2 is -3; Python floors so -7//2 is {{c2::-4}}.

concepts.L1: Integer division discards the fractional part, but the two dominant conventions round differently for negatives. C99 and later truncate toward zero; Python floors toward negative infinity. The remainder is defined to make a == (a/b)*b + a%b hold in each convention.
concepts.L2: The consequence is that C's % can return a negative value, so `hash % nbuckets` may index negatively and corrupt memory. Python's % never does for a positive modulus, which is exactly why Python's modular arithmetic matches the mathematical convention and C's does not.
concepts.L3: Both obey a = q*b + r with |r| < |b|; q has a real degree of freedom whenever a/b is not an integer: round toward zero (truncate) or toward minus infinity (floor), and r then follows. C: -7/2 = -3, so r = -7 - (-3)(2) = -1. Python: -7//2 = -4, so r = -7 - (-4)(2) = 1. Truncation gives r the sign of the dividend, floor the sign of the divisor. C99 chose truncation because x86 idiv truncates, so / is one instruction; Python chose floor so that a % b is periodic in a: the weekday seven days before weekday 1 is (1 - 7) % 7 = 1 in Python but -6 in C. On gcc a negative int shifted right floors (arithmetic shift) while / truncates, so lowering signed x / 4 adds 3 before the shift when x < 0. INT_MIN / -1 overflows: undefined behaviour. For a bucket index write ((h % n) + n) % n, or h & (n - 1) for a power-of-two n and unsigned h; 'Hash table: collisions and probing' relies on it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give the value of {a} % {b} in C and in Python.
L4.explanation: Compute a/b under each rounding rule, then r = a - (a/b)*b. C truncates a/b toward zero, so r takes the sign of a; Python floors a/b, so r takes the sign of b (or is 0). When a and b have the same sign the two agree; when they differ and b does not divide a, the two remainders differ by exactly b.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python 3, both operands are int. What is {a} // {b}? Answer with the integer.
L4.explanation: Python's // is floor division: the largest integer not greater than the exact quotient, so a negative non-integer quotient moves away from zero. -7/2 = -3.5 floors to -4, not -3; 17/-3 = -5.67 floors to -6. Check with the identity a == (a//b)*b + a%b: -7 == (-4)*2 + 1. The same input truncated (C) gives -3.

L4.prompt_tpl: C11, both operands are int, x86-64 Linux, gcc. What is {a} / {b}? Answer with the integer.
L4.explanation: C99 and later define / on integers as the algebraic quotient with any fractional part discarded, i.e. rounded toward zero. -7/2 = -3.5 becomes -3, not -4; 17/-3 = -5.67 becomes -5. The remainder then follows from (a/b)*b + a%b == a, so -7 % 2 is -1. Before C99 the direction for negative operands was implementation-defined; the standard settled on what the hardware does.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3. What does this print?

print(divmod({a}, {b}))
L4.explanation: divmod(a, b) returns the pair (a // b, a % b): quotient floored toward minus infinity, remainder with the sign of b, and a == q*b + r always. divmod(-7, -4): -7/-4 = 1.75 floors to 1, and r = -7 - 1*(-4) = -3, which has the sign of the divisor. divmod(17, -4): 17/-4 = -4.25 floors to -5, r = 17 - (-5)(-4) = -3.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, int h (may be negative, never INT_MIN), int n = 8. Which expression equals the mathematical residue h mod n, in 0..n-1, for every such h, and why?
L4.answer: ((h % n) + n) % n: the inner remainder lies in -(n-1)..n-1, adding n moves it to 1..2n-1, and the outer % folds that into 0..n-1 without changing the residue
L4.explanation: C's h % n has the sign of h, so for h = -7 it is -7, not 1. Adding n gives 1..2n-1, and a second % n brings it into range while preserving the residue class because n is a multiple of n. h % n + n alone is wrong for non-negative h: 7 % 8 + 8 = 15, out of bounds. abs(h) % n is in range but is the wrong residue: abs(-7) % 8 = 7, while -7 mod 8 = 1 (since -7 = -1*8 + 1).
options: ((h % n) + n) % n: the inner remainder lies in -(n-1)..n-1, adding n moves it to 1..2n-1, and the outer % folds that into 0..n-1 without changing the residue
h % n + n: adding n makes the remainder non-negative, and since the remainder is smaller than n the sum is still below n
abs(h) % n: the sign is the only problem, so removing it before the remainder gives the mathematical residue

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3. What does this print?

import math
print(math.fmod({a}, {b}), {a} % {b})
L4.explanation: math.fmod is C's fmod: it truncates, so the result takes the sign of the first argument and is always a float (-1.0). Python's % floors, so the result takes the sign of the second argument and stays an int. They agree whenever the operands share a sign or divide exactly; otherwise they differ by exactly b. The docs recommend fmod for floats precisely because % can lose precision on large float operands of opposite sign.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python 3, ints. Many people assume that a >> k is the same as truncating division by 2^k. What is {a} >> {k}? Answer with the integer.
L4.explanation: Python defines a >> k as a // 2**k, floor division, and an arithmetic shift of a two's-complement value does the same: dropping low bits can only make the value smaller, so -7 >> 1 is -4, not the -3 that truncation gives. Hence a C compiler cannot replace signed x / 2 with x >> 1; it must add 1 first when x is negative. For non-negative values the two agree, which is why the trap survives testing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Let a = {a} and b = {b}. Both C and Python satisfy a = q*b + r, but C truncates q and Python floors it. Derive the general relation between the two remainders, then compute (Python a % b) minus (C a % b). Answer with that difference.
L4.explanation: Subtract the two identities: $r_{py} - r_{C} = b(q_{C} - q_{py})$. Truncation and floor agree unless a/b is a negative non-integer, and then truncation is exactly one larger, so the difference is $b \cdot 1 = b$ (which is negative when b is: 17 % -3 is -1 in Python and 2 in C, difference -3). This is why the two conventions never differ by more than one bucket, and why a port from Python to C that ignores it fails only on negative inputs.

L4.prompt_tpl: x86-64 has a slow idiv, so for int f(int x) returning x / 4, gcc -O2 emits: test the sign of x; if negative add 3; then arithmetic-shift right by 2 (sar). Trace this lowering by hand for x = {x}, remembering that sar floors. Answer with the value the function returns.
L4.explanation: sar computes $\lfloor x / 4 \rfloor$, which for negative x is one too small whenever x is not a multiple of 4. Adding $2^{k} - 1 = 3$ first turns floor into ceiling for those x: $\lfloor (x + 3)/4 \rfloor = \lceil x/4 \rceil$ for integer x, and ceiling is truncation toward zero when x < 0. For multiples of 4 the +3 does not cross a boundary, so nothing changes. This is the fixup 'Two's complement' arithmetic shifts force on every compiler; an unsigned x needs only the shift.

L4.prompt_tpl: C ring buffer of {N} ints, head is an int index in 0..{N}-1 that advances with head = (head + 1) % {N}. To read the most recently written element the author wrote: int prev = (head - 1) % {N}; int last = buf[prev]; The program reads garbage or crashes occasionally. Find the bug, give the value of prev that triggers it, and fix the line.
L4.answer: When head is 0, head - 1 is -1 and C's % truncates, so (-1) % N is -1, not N-1: buf[-1] reads one int before the array. Fix: int prev = (head + N - 1) % N; or if head were unsigned (as size_t) the wrap-around would already give N-1. For N a power of two, (head - 1) & (N - 1) on an unsigned head also works.
L4.explanation: C's remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so a negative dividend gives a negative result and the mathematical wrap-around most people picture never happens. The reliable idiom is to add the modulus before subtracting so the dividend can never go negative: (head + N - 1) % N. It fails only once per lap, which is why it surfaces as an occasional garbage read rather than a deterministic crash.

L0.body:
64 bits =  1 sign | 11 exponent | 52 stored mantissa bits
value = (-1)**s * 1.f * 2**(e - 1023)      (normal numbers)
1.0 -> 0x3FF0000000000000
L0.cloze: A double has {{c1::52}} stored mantissa bits and an exponent bias of {{c2::1023}}.

concepts.L1: The double-precision format: sign bit, 11-bit biased exponent, 52 stored fraction bits with an implicit leading 1. It represents numbers of the form m * 2**e with 53 bits of significand, giving about 15-17 significant decimal digits.
concepts.L2: Floats are not 'approximate'. Every double is an exact binary rational; what is approximate is the mapping from your decimal literal onto the nearest one. 0.1 in source becomes a specific exact value, 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827..., and every subsequent operation is exact rounding on those exact values.
concepts.L3: Decode 0x3FF0000000000000: sign 0, exponent field 0x3FF = 1023, fraction 0, so the value is $(-1)^{0} \times 1.0 \times 2^{1023-1023} = 1.0$. The bias exists because the 11-bit field is stored unsigned: adding 1023 maps the usable exponents $-1022$ to $1023$ onto the codes 1 to 2046, so comparing whole bit patterns as unsigned integers orders non-negative doubles correctly. Both end codes are reserved. Code 0 means zero when the fraction is zero and a subnormal otherwise - implicit leading bit 0, exponent pinned at $-1022$, so values below $2^{-1022}$ decay gradually instead of snapping to zero. Code 2047 means infinity or NaN. Every other code carries a full 53-bit significand at its own scale, so the absolute gap doubles binade by binade: $2^{-52}$ near 1.0, exactly 2 near $10^{16}$ - the spacing that Machine epsilon and relative error is built on.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the largest integer N such that every integer from 0 to N is exactly representable as a binary64 double?
L4.explanation: With 53 significand bits every integer below 2**53 fits exactly. At 2**53 the spacing becomes 2, so 2**53 + 1 is not representable - which is why JSON integer IDs above 2**53 corrupt when parsed into JavaScript numbers.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary64 stores its exponent in an 11-bit field as the true exponent plus a bias of 1023. What unsigned integer sits in that exponent field for the value 2^{k}? Answer with the field value as a decimal integer.
L4.answer: Field = k + 1023. k=0 gives 1023 (0x3FF, the pattern 0x3FF0000000000000 for 1.0); k=10 gives 1033; k=-3 gives 1020; k=52 gives 1075; k=-20 gives 1003. Verified by reading bit 62 down to 52 of struct.pack('>d', 2.0**k).
L4.explanation: The field is unsigned, so a negative true exponent has to be shifted into range: stored = true + 1023. Codes 1 to 2046 cover true exponents -1022 to 1023; codes 0 and 2047 are reserved for zero/subnormals and for infinity/NaN. That is why 1.0 (true exponent 0) encodes as 0x3FF in the exponent field.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux, CPython 3 prints the eight bytes of a double in big-endian order: python3 -c "import struct; print(struct.pack('>d', 1.0).hex())". What exactly is printed?
L4.explanation: Sign 0, exponent field 0x3FF = 1023 (true exponent 0), fraction all zero, so the value is $1.0 \times 2^{0}$. Written out: 0011 1111 1111 0000 ... The leading 1 of the significand is never stored, which is why an all-zero fraction means 1.0 and not 0.0. Big-endian order is forced by '>' so the sign and exponent lead.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux, CPython 3: python3 -c "print(1e16 + 1 == 1e16, 1e16 + 2 == 1e16)". What exactly is printed? Give both words separated by one space.
L4.answer: True False
L4.explanation: 1e16 sits in the binade $[2^{53}, 2^{54})$, where the gap between adjacent doubles is exactly 2. So 1e16 + 1 is halfway between two doubles and round-half-to-even returns 1e16 itself, while 1e16 + 2 is exactly the next double. The number is not too large to be exact - it is the increment that is too small.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary64 has an exponent field of all zero bits and a fraction field that is not all zeros. What does that bit pattern encode?
L4.answer: A subnormal: the implicit leading bit is 0 and the exponent is pinned at -1022, so magnitudes below 2^-1022 stay representable with fewer significant bits
L4.explanation: Exponent code 0 is the low reserved code: fraction zero means $\pm 0$, fraction non-zero means a subnormal, read as $0.f \times 2^{-1022}$ rather than $1.f \times 2^{e}$. It is code 2047 that gives infinity (fraction zero) and NaN (fraction non-zero). There is no true exponent -1023: the bias maps codes 1 to 2046 onto -1022 to 1023.
options: A subnormal: the implicit leading bit is 0 and the exponent is pinned at -1022, so magnitudes below 2^-1022 stay representable with fewer significant bits
A NaN: any reserved exponent code combined with a non-zero fraction means Not a Number
An ordinary normal number with true exponent -1023, the smallest the bias allows

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the largest finite binary64 from the format alone: the largest usable exponent code is 2046 and the largest significand is 2 - 2^-52. Give floor of log10 of that value. Answer with that single integer.
L4.answer: Largest finite double = $(2 - 2^{-52}) \times 2^{2046-1023} = (2 - 2^{-52}) \times 2^{1023} \approx 1.7976931348623157 \times 10^{308}$. Since $2 - 2^{-52}$ is just under 2, $\log_{10}$ of it is just under $1024 \log_{10} 2 = 308.2547$, so the floor is 308.
L4.explanation: Code 2047 is reserved for infinity and NaN, so the top usable code is 2046, i.e. true exponent 1023. The significand runs up to $2 - 2^{-52}$, one ulp below 2, so the maximum is a hair under $2^{1024}$ and $\log_{10} 2^{1024} = 1024 \times 0.30103 = 308.25$. Anything larger overflows to infinity, which is what DBL_MAX in C names.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must order doubles on hardware with no floating-point compare, so you read each 64-bit pattern as an unsigned 64-bit integer and compare those integers. State exactly which inputs this orders correctly, which it gets wrong and why, and name the two choices in the binary64 layout that make it work at all.
L4.answer: It is correct for two non-negative doubles: the sign bit is 0, the exponent field is above the fraction and is stored biased-unsigned, so the bit pattern read as an unsigned integer increases exactly as the value does. It breaks in three ways. (1) Negative doubles are sign-magnitude, not two's complement: a larger magnitude gives a larger unsigned pattern, so negatives come out reversed and all of them compare above every positive; the fix is to flip all bits of a negative pattern (or XOR positives with 0x8000000000000000) before comparing. (2) -0.0 = 0x8000...0 and +0.0 = 0x0 compare unequal although the values are equal. (3) NaN patterns sort as if they were huge numbers instead of being unordered. The two enabling choices: the exponent is stored as an unsigned biased field rather than two's complement, and it is placed above the fraction in the layout.
L4.explanation: This is why the format puts sign, then biased exponent, then fraction, in that order: ordering positives becomes plain integer comparison, which is what memcmp-style key encodings and sortable database keys exploit. The failures are exactly the three things the format treats specially - the sign bit (see Two's complement, which doubles do not use), signed zero, and NaN (see inf, NaN and negative zero, and Comparing floats correctly).

L0.cloze: 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to {{c1::0.30000000000000004}}, because 0.1 has no exact representation in base {{c2::2}}.

concepts.L1: 0.1 is a repeating fraction in binary, exactly as 1/3 is in decimal. The literal becomes the nearest double, slightly above 0.1; so does 0.2; their exactly-rounded sum is a different double from the one nearest 0.3.
concepts.L2: The rounding errors do not merely fail to cancel - they cannot be reasoned about by 'they are tiny'. 0.1 + 0.7 gives 0.7999999999999999, which is below the true value, while 0.1 + 0.2 lands above. Direction depends on the specific bit patterns, so no sign-based intuition survives.
concepts.L3: A finite binary fraction is $k/2^{m}$, so it terminates in decimal too. The converse fails: $1/10 = 1/(2 \cdot 5)$ keeps a factor of 5, so no $k/2^{m}$ equals it; its binary expansion 0.0001100110011... repeats forever and must be rounded - not truncated - to 53 significant bits. That gives $3602879701896397/2^{55}$, a hair above $1/10$, and 0.2 rounds to exactly twice that, also high. The twist: their exact sum $10808639105689191/2^{55}$ has an odd numerator, so it sits exactly halfway between the double nearest 0.3, $10808639105689190/2^{55}$, and that double's successor. IEEE 754 roundTiesToEven breaks the tie toward the even significand, which is the successor, so 0.1 + 0.2 lands exactly one ulp above the double the literal 0.3 gives: 0.3000000000000000444089209850062616169452667236328125, printed as 0.30000000000000004. That one-ulp gap is what Comparing floats correctly absorbs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Predict: sum 0.1 ten times in a loop and compare to 1.0. What does Python print for the sum, and is the comparison True?
L4.answer: 0.9999999999999999, and the comparison is False
L4.explanation: Each addition rounds, and the errors accumulate downward here. This is the canonical reason loop counters and money are never floats.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is the decimal literal {v} exactly representable as an IEEE 754 binary64 double? Pick the statement that is true of this value and says why.
L4.answer: Not exact: a factor of 5 survives in the lowest-terms denominator, so the literal rounds to the nearest double
L4.explanation: Every one of these values keeps a factor of 5 downstairs in lowest terms ($0.1 = 1/10$, $0.7 = 7/10$, $2.4 = 12/5$), and every binary64 number is $k/2^{m}$, so none of them can be stored exactly. Widening to binary128 adds bits, never a factor of 5, so the third option is wrong too. The exact decimals are $0.5 = 1/2$, $0.25 = 1/4$, $2.75 = 11/4$.
options: Exactly representable: the value equals k over a power of two, with k fitting in 53 bits
Not exact: a factor of 5 survives in the lowest-terms denominator, so the literal rounds to the nearest double
Not exact in binary64 but exact in binary128, so the discrepancy disappears with long double

L4.prompt_tpl:
CPython 3.11 on x86-64 Linux runs this script:

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3)

Give the three printed lines, separated by commas.
L4.explanation: repr prints the shortest decimal that round-trips, so the sum shows as 0.30000000000000004 while the literal 0.3 shows as 0.3 - two different doubles. Their difference is exactly one ulp at 0.3, $2^{-54} = 5.551115123125783 \times 10^{-17}$, which is what the subtraction prints (that subtraction is itself exact).

L4.prompt_tpl:
CPython 3.11 on x86-64 Linux runs this script:

print(0.1 + 0.2 > 0.3)
print(0.1 + 0.7 > 0.8)
print(0.1 + 0.3 == 0.4)

Give the three booleans, separated by commas.
L4.answer: True, False, True
L4.explanation: No sign intuition survives: 0.1 + 0.2 rounds up past 0.3, 0.1 + 0.7 gives 0.7999999999999999, below 0.8, and 0.1 + 0.3 happens to round to precisely the double that the literal 0.4 names, so equality holds. Each result depends on where the exact sum falls between two doubles, not on any rule about errors accumulating one way.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary64 value equals an odd integer divided by 2^{m}. Written out exactly in decimal, with no rounding, how many digits appear after the decimal point? Answer with the number of digits.
L4.answer: m digits. Since $1/2^{m} = 5^{m}/10^{m}$ and an odd numerator times $5^{m}$ still ends in 5, the last digit is non-zero: m=55 gives 55 digits (the double nearest 0.1 is $3602879701896397/2^{55} = 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625$), m=52 gives 52, m=54 gives 54.
L4.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by $5^{m}$: $k/2^{m} = k \cdot 5^{m}/10^{m}$, so the value is an integer over $10^{m}$ and has at most m fractional digits. With k odd the numerator ends in 5, so the m-th digit is non-zero and the count is exactly m. That is why exact decimal expansions of doubles are long, never infinite.

L4.prompt_tpl: The double nearest 0.1 is 3602879701896397/2^55; the double nearest 0.2 is exactly twice it. Add the two exactly, with no rounding, write the result over 2^55, and compare it with the double nearest 0.3, which is 10808639105689190/2^55. Say which double binary64 must return for 0.1 + 0.2 and name the IEEE 754 rule that decides it.
L4.answer: Exact sum = (3602879701896397 + 7205759403792794)/2^55 = 10808639105689191/2^55. Doubles near 0.3 lie in the binade [0.25, 0.5), so they are even numerators over 2^55 (spacing 2^-54). The exact sum is odd, so it falls exactly midway between 10808639105689190/2^55 (the double 0.3 names) and 10808639105689192/2^55. This is a tie; roundTiesToEven picks the neighbour whose last significand bit is 0, which is the upper one, 0x1.3333333333334p-2 = 0.30000000000000004.
L4.explanation: The result is not 'error crept in': it is forced. The sum of two doubles is computed exactly and then rounded once, and here the exact sum is precisely halfway between two doubles. IEEE 754's default roundTiesToEven resolves the tie to the even significand, the neighbour above, so the answer is one ulp above the double the literal 0.3 gives. Reversing the tie rule would make 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 true.

L4.prompt_tpl: Consider every decimal with exactly {d} digits after the point in the range 0 less than x and x at most 1, that is k/10^{d} for k = 1 up to 10^{d}. How many of them are exactly representable in binary64? Answer with the count.
L4.answer: 2^d of them. k/10^d is exact iff its lowest-terms denominator is a power of two, iff $5^{d}$ divides k, and the multiples of $5^{d}$ up to $10^{d}$ number $10^{d}/5^{d} = 2^{d}$. d=1: 2 (0.5, 1.0); d=2: 4 (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0); d=3: 8; d=4: 16.
L4.explanation: Cancelling $\gcd(k, 10^{d})$ leaves a denominator free of 5 exactly when $5^{d}$ divides k, and every such value is then $j/2^{d}$, which binary64 stores exactly (d is far below 53 bits). So of the 1000 three-decimal prices, only 8 are exact - the reason money is held in integer paise, not in floats.

L0.cloze: Machine epsilon for binary64 is 2**{{c1::-52}}, roughly {{c2::2.2e-16}}.

concepts.L1: Machine epsilon is the gap between 1.0 and the next representable double: 2**-52. It bounds the relative error of a single correctly-rounded operation at eps/2, which is the meaning of '15-17 significant decimal digits'.
concepts.L2: Epsilon is a relative quantity, not an absolute tolerance. Using `abs(a-b) < 1e-9` as a universal float comparison is wrong in both directions: too strict for values near 1e12 (where the spacing already exceeds 1e-4) and far too loose for values near 1e-12.
concepts.L3: Round-to-nearest makes one operation exact to within half a step: $fl(a \star b) = (a \star b)(1+d)$ with $|d| \leq u = \epsilon/2 = 2^{-53}$. The guarantee is relative, so the absolute step scales with magnitude. For $2^{e} \leq x < 2^{e+1}$ the gap between adjacent doubles is exactly $2^{e-52}$: $2.22 \times 10^{-16}$ just above 1.0; $2^{-33} = 1.16 \times 10^{-10}$ near $10^{6}$ (magnitude times $\epsilon$ is only an upper bound, here 1.9 times too big); and exactly 2 near $10^{16}$, which is why 1e16 + 1 == 1e16. The decimal-digit count comes from the 53-bit significand, not from the exponent in epsilon: $\log_{10}(2^{53}) = 15.95$, so 15 digits always survive a decimal round trip (C's DBL_DIG) and 17 are always enough to name a double uniquely (DBL_DECIMAL_DIG). That is the whole basis of Comparing floats correctly: a tolerance has to be relative, scaled by the operands.

L4.prompt_tpl: Roughly how large is the gap between adjacent doubles near the value 1e{k}?
L4.explanation: The relative spacing is not fixed at eps: it slides between $\epsilon/2$ and $\epsilon$ across each binade. Exactly, for $2^{e} \leq x < 2^{e+1}$ the gap is $2^{e-52}$. At $10^{0}$ that is $2^{-52}$; at $10^{6}$, $2^{-33} = 1.16 \times 10^{-10}$; at $10^{16}$, $2^{1} = 2$, which is why 1e16 + 1 == 1e16. Magnitude times eps is an upper bound, up to twice too large.

L4.prompt_tpl: An IEEE 754 binary format carries {p} bits of significand precision in total, counting the implicit leading 1. What is its machine epsilon, the gap between 1.0 and the next representable value above 1.0? Give a decimal number.
L4.explanation: In the binade from 1.0 up to 2.0 the representable numbers are $1 + j \cdot 2^{-(p-1)}$ for integer $j$, so the step above 1.0 is $2^{-(p-1)} = 2^{1-p}$. The exponent is $p-1$, not $p$: one of the $p$ bits of precision is the implicit leading 1, so only $p-1$ fraction bits are actually stored.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary floating-point format carries {p} bits of significand. How many significant decimal digits is that worth? Compute log base 10 of 2 raised to the power {p}, to two decimal places.
L4.explanation: Each bit of significand is worth $\log_{10} 2 = 0.30103$ decimal digits, so $53 \times 0.30103 = 15.95$ digits for binary64. That is where the phrase '15 to 17 significant digits' comes from: C guarantees 15 digits survive a decimal round trip (DBL_DIG) and that 17 always pin a double down (DBL_DECIMAL_DIG). The driver is the significand width, not the exponent in epsilon.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3 (CPython on x86-64 Linux, where a float is IEEE 754 binary64). What does this print?

import sys
eps = sys.float_info.epsilon
x = 1.0 + eps/{d}
print(x == 1.0, 1.0 + eps == 1.0)
L4.answer: True False
L4.explanation: eps is by definition the gap between 1.0 and the next double, so 1.0 + eps is representable and is not 1.0: the second value is False. Half that gap or less rounds back down: $1.0 + 2^{-53}$ is an exact tie, and round-to-nearest-even picks 1.0 because its last significand bit is 0. So the first value is True. Epsilon is the smallest addend that moves 1.0 at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: A codebase compares doubles with abs(a - b) < 1e-{n}. Estimate the magnitude above which that test becomes equivalent to a == b, because the gap between adjacent doubles already exceeds the tolerance. Estimate with gap is about magnitude times eps, eps = 2 to the power -52.
L4.explanation: Spacing near $x$ is about $x \epsilon$. Setting $x \epsilon = 10^{-n}$ gives $x = 10^{-n} \cdot 2^{52}$. Above that magnitude no two distinct doubles are ever within the tolerance, so the test silently collapses into exact equality. Well below it the opposite failure appears: near $10^{-n}$ itself, enormous numbers of distinct doubles all compare as equal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Summing {n} positive doubles left to right takes one fewer addition than there are terms, and each addition is correctly rounded, contributing a relative error of at most u = eps/2 = 2 to the power -53. To first order the worst-case relative error of the total is the number of additions times u. Compute that bound.
L4.explanation: Each of the $n-1$ roundings scales the running total by $(1+d_i)$ with $|d_i| \leq u$, and $\prod (1+d_i) = 1 + \sum d_i$ to first order, so the bound is $(n-1)u$ for positive terms. It is a worst case, not the typical case: with random signs the error grows like $\sqrt{n}$. This linear growth is why Floating-point addition is not associative bites on long sums, and why pairwise and Kahan summation exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are designing close(a, b) as abs(a - b) less than or equal to rtol times max(abs(a), abs(b)). It must accept any two positive normal doubles that lie in the same power-of-two interval, from 2 to the e up to but not including 2 to the e plus 1, and that are at most {k} representable steps apart. What is the smallest rtol that works for every such interval?
L4.explanation: Inside $[2^{e}, 2^{e+1})$ every step is exactly $2^{e-52}$, so $k$ steps is $k \cdot 2^{e-52}$. The worst case is the bottom of the interval, where $\max(|a|,|b|)$ is only $2^{e}$, giving rtol $= k \cdot 2^{-52} = k \epsilon$; any larger operand needs less. This is the derivation behind Comparing floats correctly: a budget of $k$ ulps is a relative tolerance of $k$ epsilons.

L0.cloze: Because each operation rounds, (a+b)+c can differ from a+({{c1::b+c}}); floating-point addition is not {{c2::associative}}.

concepts.L1: Each operation rounds its exact result to the nearest double, so grouping changes which intermediate values get rounded and therefore the final answer. Addition and multiplication remain commutative but lose associativity and distributivity.
concepts.L2: This is why a compiler may not reorder float arithmetic without -ffast-math, and why a parallel or vectorised reduction gives a different sum than the serial one - not a bug, and not nondeterminism, but a different (often more accurate) evaluation order. The same code on a different thread count can produce a different last bit.
concepts.L3: 1e20 lies in $[2^{66}, 2^{67})$, so consecutive doubles there are $2^{66-52} = 2^{14} = 16384$ apart. Adding 1.0 is far below half that gap, so the sum rounds straight back to 1e20 and the subtraction gives exactly 0. Group it the other way and the two large terms cancel exactly - equal magnitudes subtract with no rounding at all - leaving 1.0. The same loss destroys small terms fed into a big running total: once the accumulator reaches $2^{53}$, adding 1.0 is an exact tie and round-half-to-even hands the accumulator back unchanged. Kahan compensated summation keeps the discarded low part in a second variable and adds it back, holding the error near two rounding units instead of growing with $n$; math.fsum is stronger still - Shewchuk's exact-partials algorithm, which returns the correctly rounded sum. The mirror image of this loss is 'Cancellation when you subtract near-equals'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Predict both results: (1e{k} + 1.0) - 1e{k}  and  (1e{k} - 1e{k}) + 1.0
L4.answer: First: 0.0 (the 1.0 is below the spacing at that magnitude). Second: 1.0.
L4.explanation: Adding a value far smaller than the spacing is a no-op. Cancelling the large terms first keeps the small one - reordering changes the answer, which is exactly non-associativity.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3 on x86-64 Linux (CPython, binary64 doubles). Predict what each line prints:
>>> sum([1e{k}, 1.0, -1e{k}])
>>> sum([1e{k}, -1e{k}, 1.0])
>>> import math; math.fsum([1e{k}, 1.0, -1e{k}])
L4.answer: 0.0, then 1.0, then 1.0 - the same three numbers, three answers. Run on CPython 3 for k = 16, 18 and 20.
L4.explanation: sum() starts at 0 and adds left to right. In the first list the huge term arrives first, so the 1.0 falls below half the spacing at that magnitude and is discarded before the cancellation ever happens. In the second list the two huge terms cancel exactly first, so the 1.0 survives. math.fsum keeps exact partial sums and always returns the correctly rounded total, 1.0.

L4.prompt_tpl: In binary64 let big = 2^{p}. What is the smallest integer m for which big + 2^m is a different double from big? Answer with m.
L4.answer: $m = p - 52$: 1, 8, 14 and 18 for p = 53, 60, 66, 70. At p = 66 that is $2^{14} = 16384$, the spacing just below 1e20.
L4.explanation: The spacing of doubles at $2^{p}$ is one ulp, $2^{p-52}$. Anything strictly smaller than half an ulp rounds away; exactly half an ulp, $2^{p-53}$, is a tie and round-half-to-even keeps $2^{p}$ because its significand is even. So the first addend that moves the value is a full ulp: $m = p - 52$.

L4.prompt_tpl: For binary64 with round-to-nearest, which of these laws still holds exactly for every triple of finite values: commutativity of addition, associativity of addition, or both?
L4.answer: Commutativity only: a + b and b + a round the identical exact sum, but (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) round different intermediate values.
L4.explanation: Each IEEE 754 operation returns the correctly rounded value of the exact result. The exact sum of a and b does not depend on their order, so commutativity survives. Associativity does not: the two groupings form different exact intermediates, each rounded separately, and rounding is not linear. Determinism is real but irrelevant - both orders are deterministic and they disagree.
options: Commutativity only: a + b and b + a round the identical exact sum, but (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) round different intermediate values.
Both: rounding is deterministic, so any regrouping of the same values must give the same double.
Associativity only: the order of the two operands matters, but the grouping cannot.

L4.prompt_tpl: Let small = 2^{m} in binary64. What is the smallest exponent p for which 2^p + small rounds back to exactly 2^p? Answer with p, and remember what round-half-to-even does with an exact tie.
L4.explanation: Half an ulp at $2^{p}$ is $2^{p-53}$. An addend below that rounds away; an addend equal to it is an exact tie, and round-half-to-even picks $2^{p}$ because its significand is all zeros. So the loss begins one exponent earlier than a naive 'must be smaller than half the gap' argument predicts: $p = m + 53$, not $m + 54$.

L4.prompt_tpl: A test asserts that a {t}-thread parallel sum of an array of doubles equals the serial left-to-right sum, and it fails in the last bit. What is the right diagnosis?
L4.answer: Neither sum is wrong: a tree reduction groups the additions differently, and floating-point addition is not associative, so the assertion itself is invalid - compare with a tolerance or with an exactly rounded sum.
L4.explanation: Splitting an array across threads and combining partial sums is a regrouping of the same additions, so a different last bit is expected, not evidence of a race. The tree form is usually the more accurate of the two - its worst-case error grows like $\log_{2} n$ rather than $n$ - so treating serial accumulation as the reference is backwards. Fix the assertion, not the reduction.
options: Neither sum is wrong: a tree reduction groups the additions differently, and floating-point addition is not associative, so the assertion itself is invalid - compare with a tolerance or with an exactly rounded sum.
The parallel sum is racy: threads are updating one accumulator without a lock, which is the only way two sums of the same array can differ.
The serial sum is the reference and the parallel one is wrong: left-to-right accumulation is exact, so any deviation is a defect in the reduction.

L4.prompt_tpl: Worst-case rounding error for a naive left-to-right sum of n positive doubles grows like n - 1 rounding units; for pairwise (tree) summation it grows like log2 of n. For n = {n}, by what factor is the pairwise bound smaller? Answer with the single ratio.
L4.explanation: Each of the n - 1 additions in a serial sum can add one rounding unit to a partial sum that already carries every earlier error, so the bound is linear in n. A balanced tree gives every value a path of $\log_{2} n$ additions instead, so the bound is logarithmic. Same operations, different grouping - which is exactly what non-associativity buys you when you choose the grouping deliberately.

L4.prompt_tpl: Take binary64 values a = 2^60, b = -2^60 and c = 2^{m}. Compute ((a + b) + c) - ((a + c) + b) exactly. Answer with the number.
L4.answer: $2^{m}$: 1.0, 4.0 and 32.0 for m = 0, 2, 5. Left grouping: a + b is exactly 0, so the result is c. Right grouping: a + c rounds back to $2^{60}$, then + b is 0.
L4.explanation: One ulp at $2^{60}$ is $2^{8} = 256$, so any c with $m \leq 7$ is at most half an ulp and vanishes into a. Cancelling the equal-magnitude pair first is exact - no rounding occurs - so c survives untouched. The whole difference between the two groupings is therefore c itself. This is the same effect read from the other side in 'Cancellation when you subtract near-equals'.

>>> 1.0 / 0.0                     # Python: ZeroDivisionError, not inf
>>> float('inf') - float('inf')   ->  nan
>>> float('nan') == float('nan')  ->  False
>>> 0.0 == -0.0                   ->  True
>>> math.copysign(1.0, -0.0)      ->  -1.0     # the sign survived
/* C, x86-64 Linux, gcc:  1.0/0.0 -> inf,  1.0/-0.0 -> -inf */
L0.cloze: NaN is the only value for which x == x is {{c1::False}}, and it is produced by inf - {{c2::inf}}; 0.0 == -0.0 is True, yet math.copysign(1.0, -0.0) is {{c3::-1.0}}.

concepts.L1: IEEE 754 defines three special classes: signed infinities from overflow and division by zero, NaN from indeterminate forms such as inf - inf and 0/0, and a signed zero that distinguishes underflow direction.
concepts.L2: NaN is unordered with everything, so x == x is False and x < y, x > y and x == y are all False at once. A sort comparator written as `a < b` therefore violates trichotomy on NaN and can drive std::sort out of bounds - a real crash, not a wrong ordering.
concepts.L3: All-ones exponent is the escape hatch: mantissa zero means infinity, mantissa non-zero means NaN, sign bit still applies. 0x7FF0000000000000 is +inf, 0xFFF0000000000000 is -inf, and the remaining $2(2^{52}-1)$ patterns are NaNs whose mantissa bits carry a payload. IEEE 754 makes NaN unordered with everything: the predicates $=$, $<$, $>$, $\leq$, $\geq$ are all false, while not-equal is true - which is why x != x detects a NaN and x == x is False. Signed zero is the other half. -0.0 and 0.0 compare equal because comparison is on values, not bit patterns, yet differ in one bit, so 1.0/0.0 is +inf and 1.0/-0.0 is -inf, and math.copysign recovers the sign that == discarded. Underflow from below yields -0.0, recording which side zero was approached from. Unorderedness is what 'Comparing floats correctly' cannot fix: math.isclose(nan, nan) is False, so a NaN-safe check calls math.isnan.

L4.prompt_tpl: Evaluate in Python: x = float('nan'); print(x == x, x != x, x < 1.0, max(1.0, x), max(x, 1.0))
L4.answer: False True False 1.0 nan
L4.explanation: All comparisons with NaN are False, so `!=` is True. max returns the first argument unless a later one compares greater; since nothing compares greater than NaN, max(x, 1.0) keeps nan while max(1.0, x) keeps 1.0 - order-dependent, and a common source of silent NaN leakage.

L4.prompt_tpl: IEEE 754 reserves the all-ones exponent field for the special values. In a binary format with {m} stored mantissa bits, how many distinct bit patterns encode a NaN? Answer with the count of NaN patterns.
L4.explanation: All-ones exponent with a zero mantissa is infinity; all-ones exponent with any of the other $2^{m}-1$ mantissa values is a NaN, and the sign bit doubles every one of those. So binary64 spends 9007199254740990 of its bit patterns on NaN and exactly two on infinity. Those spare mantissa bits are the NaN payload, which is why a NaN can carry diagnostic information.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Evaluate in CPython 3. What does this print?

x = float('inf')
print(x - x, x + x, x * 0.0, 1e308 * 10)
L4.answer: nan inf nan inf
L4.explanation: Overflow saturates to infinity instead of wrapping the way a fixed-width integer does: $10^{309}$ is past the largest finite double, so 1e308 * 10 is inf. But inf - inf and inf * 0.0 are indeterminate forms with no defensible value, so IEEE 754 hands back NaN. Note nothing was imported - the specials are ordinary float values, not a library feature.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which statement about negative zero in IEEE 754 is correct?
L4.answer: -0.0 == 0.0 is True, but the two have different bit patterns, so 1.0 / 0.0 is +inf while 1.0 / -0.0 is -inf.
L4.explanation: IEEE 754 comparison is on values, not on bit patterns, and both zeros have the value zero, so they compare equal. The sign bit is still physically there - 0x8000000000000000 against 0x0000000000000000 - and it survives into division, reciprocals and math.copysign. That is the point of a signed zero: it records the direction an underflow came from.
options: -0.0 == 0.0 is True, but the two have different bit patterns, so 1.0 / 0.0 is +inf while 1.0 / -0.0 is -inf.
-0.0 == 0.0 is False, because IEEE 754 comparison compares the bit patterns of the two operands.
-0.0 is a NaN: a zero has no magnitude, so putting a sign bit on it makes the value invalid.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Evaluate in CPython 3. What does this print?

print(sorted([3.0, float('nan'), 1.0, 2.0]))
L4.explanation: Timsort only ever asks a < b. Every comparison against nan is False, so nan never moves and nothing is ever moved past it: the elements left of it and right of it end up ordered among themselves, but nothing crosses. Nothing raises and nothing warns - the output merely looks plausible. Reject or partition out NaN with math.isnan before sorting.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary floating-point format has 1 sign bit, a {w}-bit exponent field, and {m} stored mantissa bits with an implicit leading 1. Its exponent bias is 2^({w}-1) - 1, and the all-ones exponent field is reserved for infinity and NaN, so the largest usable unbiased exponent is also 2^({w}-1) - 1. Derive the largest finite value this format can represent - the value just below +inf. Answer with that value.
L4.explanation: The largest significand is $1.\underbrace{1\ldots1}_{m}$ in binary, which is $2 - 2^{-m}$. The largest usable unbiased exponent is $2^{w-1}-1$, because the top exponent field is spent on inf and NaN - the format buys its special values with one whole binade. Multiply the two. Anything larger rounds to $+\infty$ instead of wrapping, so float overflow degrades rather than silently corrupting.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux compiled with gcc, a C function clamps a double before it is used as an array index: if x is less than {lo} it is set to {lo}, else if x is greater than {hi} it is set to {hi}, and then x is returned. Trace what the function returns when x is NaN, name the IEEE 754 rule that makes both branches fall through, rewrite the clamp so that NaN maps to {lo}, and say what the original code then does to the array access downstream.
L4.answer: It returns NaN unchanged. Both x < lo and x > hi are false, because a NaN operand makes every comparison predicate false except not-equal, so neither branch fires and the clamp is a silent no-op. Fix it by testing the ACCEPT case rather than the two reject cases: if x is greater than or equal to lo and x is less than or equal to hi, keep x; otherwise set x to lo. That form is false for NaN, so NaN falls into the else and is clamped to lo. Downstream, converting a NaN double to an integer index is undefined behaviour in C (C17 6.3.1.4: the value has no representable integral part); on x86-64 gcc the cvttsd2si instruction yields the integer indefinite value, so (int)nan is -2147483648 and (long)nan is -9223372036854775808 - an out-of-bounds access, not a clamped one.
L4.explanation: This is the trichotomy failure that wrecks a std::sort comparator, in its cheapest disguise. Written as reject-if-out-of-range, a NaN passes every guard; written as accept-if-in-range, a NaN fails every guard and is caught. Prefer positive guards on floating-point input. Connects to Undefined behaviour: an out-of-range double-to-int conversion, NaN included, has no defined result in C.
