L0.body:
int add(int a, int b);        /* prototype: declares, does not define */

void bad(int x)  { x = 99; }        /* caller unaffected */
void good(int *x){ *x = 99; }       /* caller's variable changed */

int v = 1; bad(v);  /* v == 1 */
            good(&v); /* v == 99 */
L0.cloze: C passes every argument by {{c1::value}}; to modify the caller's variable you pass a {{c2::pointer}} to it.

concepts.L1: Every C argument is copied into the callee's frame. To let a function modify a caller's object you copy a pointer to it and dereference. A prototype declares the signature so calls can be type-checked before the definition is seen.
concepts.L2: Passing a pointer is still pass-by-value - the pointer itself is copied. So a function can change *p but cannot change the caller's p; to reallocate a caller's buffer you need int **. This is exactly the same rule as Python's rebinding-versus-mutating distinction, one level lower.
concepts.L3: bad(v) copies the integer into the parameter x (on x86-64 it arrives in rdi, not on the stack); x = 99 writes that copy, which dies with the frame. good(&v) copies the address of v instead; *x = 99 stores through it into main's frame, so the change survives. Each level of caller state you must write needs one more level of indirection: to replace a caller's buffer take char **buf and write char *t = realloc(*buf, n); if (t) *buf = t; - storing the result straight into *buf loses the old block when realloc returns NULL. The prototype also converts arguments: with int add(int, int) visible, add(2.9, 3.7) truncates both as if by assignment and returns 5; with only old-style int add(); the doubles go unconverted and the call is undefined behaviour. An undeclared call was legal in C89 (implicit int); C99 removed it, GCC 14 rejects it by default, and C23 makes int f() mean int f(void).

L4.prompt_tpl: void alloc(int *p, int n) {{ p = malloc(n * sizeof(int)); }}  int *q = NULL; alloc(q, {n}); Why is q still NULL?
L4.answer: p is a copy of q; assigning to p changes only the copy. The function needs int **p and *p = malloc(...), called as alloc(&q, n). The original allocation also leaks.
L4.explanation: To modify a caller's pointer you must pass a pointer to that pointer. This is the standard proof that 'pass a pointer' is not the same as 'pass by reference'.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc.  void inc(int x)  has the single statement  x = x + {k};  and  void incp(int *x)  has the single statement  *x = *x + {k};  In main:  int a = {a}; inc(a); incp(&a); inc(a); printf("%d\n", a);  What number is printed?
L4.answer: {a} + {k}: only the incp call reaches main's a (a=3,k=7: 10; a=5,k=10: 15; a=12,k=20: 32). Both inc calls add {k} to a private copy that is discarded on return.
L4.explanation: inc receives a copy of a; x = x + {k} changes the copy, which dies with inc's frame, so main's a is untouched, twice. incp receives a copy of the address of a; *x = *x + {k} stores through that address into main's variable, so exactly one increment survives: {a} + {k}. Verified with gcc 13 on x86-64. The rule is uniform: every argument is copied, and only a copied address lets the callee reach the caller's storage.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C, main holds  int {v} = 0;  and wants a function f to store a new value into {v} so that {v} has changed after the call returns. Which ONE of these parameter declarations, with the call shown, achieves that?
L4.answer: void f(int *x), called as f(&{v})
L4.explanation: f(int x) receives a copy of the value; assigning to x changes only that copy. f(int *x) called with &{v} receives a copy of the ADDRESS of {v}, and *x = value stores through it into main's variable. f(const int *x) also receives the address, but const on the pointee makes *x = value a constraint violation, so the function can read {v} but the compiler refuses to let it write. Pass-by-value never changes; what you choose is whether the copied thing is a value or an address.
options: void f(int x), called as f({v})
void f(int *x), called as f(&{v})
void f(const int *x), called as f(&{v})

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc.  struct P  has two int members, x and y.  void move(struct P p)  has the single statement  p.x = p.x + {k};  In main:  struct P q; q.x = {a}; q.y = {b}; move(q); printf("%d\n", q.x);  What number is printed?
L4.answer: {a}: the struct is copied whole into p, so p.x = p.x + {k} changes the copy and q.x is still {a} (a=3: 3; a=5: 5; a=12: 12).
L4.explanation: A struct argument is an ordinary value: all of its bytes are copied into the parameter (on x86-64, a struct of two ints even travels in a single register). The callee's p.x is the copy's member; q in main is untouched, so the output is {a}. To change the caller's struct, take struct P *p and write p->x = p->x + {k}, called as move(&q). Passing large structs by value also costs a copy of every byte, which is the practical reason C APIs pass pointers to structs.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. The prototype  int add(int a, int b);  is visible, and the definition returns a + b. main executes  printf("%d\n", add({p}, {q}));  with those two double literals as the arguments. What number is printed?
L4.answer: Each double argument is converted to int as if by assignment, truncating toward zero, so the result is floor({p}) + floor({q}) for these positive values (2.9,3.7: 5; 1.5,4.5: 5; 0.9,9.9: 9; 2.9,9.9: 11).
L4.explanation: C17 6.5.2.2p7: when a prototype is visible, each argument is implicitly converted to the type of its parameter as if by assignment. double to int truncates toward zero, so {p} becomes floor({p}) and {q} becomes floor({q}) before add ever runs; the fractions are gone, not rounded. Verified with gcc 13: add(2.9, 3.7) prints 5. Without a prototype (old-style int add();) the doubles would be passed as doubles to a function reading ints, which is undefined behaviour and prints garbage.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc.  void bump(int a[3])  has the single statement  a[0] = a[0] + {k};  In main:  int v[3]; v[0] = {a}; v[1] = 0; v[2] = 0; bump(v); printf("%d\n", v[0]);  Every argument in C is passed by value. What number is printed?
L4.answer: {a} + {k} (a=3,k=7: 10; a=5,k=10: 15; a=12,k=20: 32). The array is not copied: v decays to a pointer to v[0], that pointer is what is copied, and a[0] = ... stores through it into main's array.
L4.explanation: This looks like an exception to pass-by-value and is not one. An array parameter int a[3] is adjusted to int *a, and the argument v converts to &v[0]; the thing copied is that address. So a[0] = a[0] + {k} is *(a + 0) = ..., a store into main's v. Contrast the struct case, where the whole aggregate is copied and the caller is unaffected: structs are values, arrays are not, and that asymmetry is why a function can fill a caller's buffer but never its caller's struct without a pointer.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc.  struct node  has members  int v;  and  struct node *next;.  The function  void push(struct node *head, int v)  does three things in order: allocates n with malloc(sizeof *n), sets n->v = v and n->next = head, then assigns head = n.  main starts with  struct node *list = NULL;  calls push(list, i) for i from 0 to {n}-1, and prints the length of list by walking next pointers. It prints 0. Explain exactly what happened to the {n} nodes, then give a corrected signature and body and show the corrected call.
L4.answer: head is a copy of list. Each call allocates a node, links it to the current (NULL) head, and then overwrites its own local head - main's list is never written, so it stays NULL and the length is 0. Every one of the {n} nodes is allocated, correctly filled, and immediately orphaned: {n} leaked blocks, each with next == NULL. Fix: void push(struct node **head, int v) with n->next = *head; *head = n; called as push(&list, i). Equivalent fix: return the new head, struct node *push(struct node *head, int v), called as list = push(list, i). Verified: the ** version prints {n}.
L4.explanation: The pointer is passed by value, so the function can write what head points AT (nodes) but not head itself in the caller. The trap is nastier than the plain alloc case because the code that runs is entirely correct locally: nodes exist, are linked, and vanish only because the last assignment lands on a copy. One more level of indirection, struct node **, gives the function the caller's variable. This is the head-insertion bug every first singly linked list has (concept: Singly linked list).

L4.prompt_tpl: Design question, C on x86-64 Linux. A caller owns  char *buf = malloc({n});  and wants a function grow that enlarges buf to {m} bytes, so that after the call the caller's buf points at the bigger block, and that leaves buf and its contents intact if the enlargement fails. Give the signature and body of grow, show the call, and explain (a) why  void grow(char *buf, size_t n)  cannot work even though it receives a real pointer, and (b) why the body must not be  *buf = realloc(*buf, n).
L4.answer: int grow(char **buf, size_t n): char *t = realloc(*buf, n); if (t == NULL) return -1; *buf = t; return 0;  called as  if (grow(&buf, {m}) != 0) handle_error();  (a) With char *buf the parameter is a copy of the caller's pointer: the function could write the {n} bytes it points at, but assigning the new block's address to buf changes only the copy, so the caller keeps the old address. The caller's variable lives in the caller's frame; the only way to write it is to be handed its address, char **, and store through it. (b) realloc returns NULL on failure and leaves the old block allocated and valid. *buf = realloc(*buf, n) overwrites the sole pointer to that block with NULL: the {n} bytes leak and the caller's buf now points nowhere. Store into a temporary, test it, and only then assign through *buf.
L4.explanation: Two independent facts combine. Pass-by-value means one level of indirection per level of caller state you must modify: to change the bytes, char *; to change the caller's pointer to the bytes, char **. And realloc's failure contract (C17 7.22.3.5: on failure the old object is not deallocated) means the returned value must be checked before it replaces the old pointer. The ** signature is the same fix as the alloc and linked-list traps; the temporary is ownership hygiene (concept: malloc, free and ownership).

L0.cloze: Access a member through a pointer with {{c1::->}}, which is shorthand for (*q).{{c2::y}}.

concepts.L1: A struct aggregates named members into one object with a fixed layout. Members are accessed with . on a value and -> through a pointer. Struct assignment copies all members, unlike arrays.
concepts.L2: Struct assignment is a shallow copy: a member that is a pointer is duplicated as an address, so both structs then reference one buffer and both may try to free it. C gives you no way to intercept this - there are no copy constructors - so ownership has to be a documented convention.
concepts.L3: Members are laid out in declaration order at increasing offsets, which is why struct Point's x is at offset 0 and y at 4, and why casting a struct pointer to its first member's type is legal and useful (the basis of the 'inheritance' idiom in C, and of struct sockaddr). Because the layout is fixed and public, a struct maps directly onto a wire format or a hardware register block - though relying on that requires controlling padding explicitly. Passing a large struct by value copies every byte; pass a pointer once the struct exceeds a couple of words.

L4.prompt_tpl: struct S {{ int a; int b; }}; struct S x = {{{a}, {b}}}, y = x; y.a = 0; printf("%d %d", x.a, y.a);
L4.explanation: The line printed is {a} 0. y = x is struct assignment: every member of x is copied into y (C17 6.5.16.1), so y.a = 0 changes y alone and x.a is still {a}. This is exactly what arrays cannot do; a struct is the one aggregate C copies with =. The copy is member-wise and shallow, which only matters once a member is a pointer.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. struct P is declared with two int members, x then y. Inside main:  struct P p; p.x = {a}; p.y = {b}; struct P *q = &p; q->x += {c}; printf("%d %d\n", p.x, (*q).y);  Two numbers are printed. Answer with the first number printed.
L4.answer: {a} + {c}; the line is that number followed by {b} (a=3,c=10: 13 5; a=12,c=4: 16 9; a=20,c=10: 30 9). q points at p itself, so q->x is p.x.
L4.explanation: q = &p makes q the address of p, not a copy of it, so q->x names the same int as p.x and the += lands in p. q->x is defined as (*q).x: dereference the pointer to get the struct, then select the member. The output is {a} plus {c}, then {b}. The only copying construct here would have been  struct P r = p;  which the code never does.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, any conforming compiler. struct P has an int member named {m}. Inside main:  struct P p; struct P *q = &p;  Which ONE of these expressions is a constraint violation, so that the compiler must reject it?
L4.answer: q.{m}
L4.explanation: The . operator requires a struct or union on its left (C17 6.5.2.3p1); q is a pointer, so q.{m} is a constraint violation and gcc reports 'q is a pointer; did you mean to use ->?'. (*q).{m} dereferences first and is what q->{m} abbreviates. (&p)->{m} takes the address of p, then applies ->, which is the same as p.{m}. Rule of thumb: . on a value, -> on a pointer.
options: q.{m}

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. struct P is declared with two int members, x then y. Inside main, p is defined as a struct P with a designated initialiser whose brace pair contains only  .y = {a}  and nothing else; then  printf("%d %d\n", p.x, p.y);  What line is printed? Give it exactly: two integers separated by a space.
L4.explanation: An initialiser with braces that names some members and not others initialises the rest implicitly, the same way an object with static storage duration is initialised: arithmetic members become 0 and pointers become null (C17 6.7.9p21 and p10). So p.x is 0, not garbage, and the line is 0 {a}. Only a struct with no initialiser at all has indeterminate members; the moment you write braces, every member you leave out is zero.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. struct A has exactly one member: int v[8]. Inside main:  struct A x; memset(&x, 0, sizeof x); x.v[{k}] = {a}; struct A y = x; y.v[{k}] = {b}; printf("%d %d\n", x.v[{k}], y.v[{k}]);  Two numbers are printed. Answer with the first number printed.
L4.answer: {a}; the line is {a} {b}. The array inside the struct is copied element by element by y = x, so writing y.v[{k}] leaves x.v[{k}] untouched.
L4.explanation: An array is not assignable and does not copy when passed, but an array that is a member of a struct is part of the struct object and struct assignment copies the whole object, all 32 bytes here. So y has its own v and x.v[{k}] is still {a}. This is the one way to copy an array with = in C, and also why returning a small fixed array from a function is done by wrapping it in a struct. The trap is expecting the two to share storage as two int* would.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc and glibc. struct Buf has two members: char *data and size_t len. make_buf(n) returns a struct Buf whose data is malloc(n) and whose len is n. Code:  struct Buf a = make_buf({n}); struct Buf b = a; strcpy(b.data, "{w}"); free(a.data); free(b.data);  Name every defect and say what happens at run time.
L4.answer: One defect: b = a is a shallow copy. It duplicates the address in a.data, not the {n} bytes it points at, so a.data and b.data are the same pointer. free(a.data) releases the block once; free(b.data) frees it again: undefined behaviour, and glibc detects it and aborts with 'free(): double free detected in tcache 2'. The strcpy is fine on its own ({w} fits in {n} bytes) but it writes through the shared pointer, so after free(a.data) b.data is dangling as well. Fix: give the struct a deep-copy function (malloc a new block, memcpy len bytes) or a documented rule that exactly one copy owns data and only it may free.
L4.explanation: Struct assignment copies members, and a pointer member is just an address, so the copy points at the same buffer. C has no copy constructor to make the copy allocate its own block, and no destructor to free exactly once; the language cannot tell an owning pointer from a borrowed one. Ownership is a convention you write down: who frees, and that assignment does not transfer it. This is the same defect the C++ rule of three exists to prevent.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, any conforming compiler. struct P has two {t} members, x then y. p and r are two struct P values whose members are equal. Why does  if (p == r)  fail to compile?
L4.answer: C defines no == for struct types: a byte-wise comparison would read padding bytes whose values are unspecified, and the standards committee declined to invent a member-wise one
L4.explanation: The == operator's operands must be arithmetic or pointer types (C17 6.5.9p2), so gcc says 'invalid operands to binary =='. The C99 Rationale (6.5.9) records why structure comparison was rejected: a byte-wise memcmp is wrong because padding holes hold unspecified values, and a member-wise rule would have to define comparison for unions and nested arrays. So you write the comparison yourself, member by member. There is no struct-to-pointer decay; only arrays decay.
options: C defines no == for struct types: a byte-wise comparison would read padding bytes whose values are unspecified, and the standards committee declined to invent a member-wise one
A struct value in an expression converts to a pointer to its first member, so == would compare two addresses, which C forbids for non-array objects
It does compile: == on two structs of the same type compares them member by member in declaration order

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, where long is 8 bytes and int is 4. struct T has members in this order: long a; long b; long c; int d;  A callback receives only  int *pd , a pointer to the d member of some struct T, and must recover a pointer to the whole struct. pd holds the address {addr} (decimal). Derive the expression that recovers the struct pointer, using offsetof, and give the resulting address as a decimal integer.
L4.answer: (struct T *)((char *)pd - offsetof(struct T, d)). d sits at offset 24: a, b and c are 8 bytes each and 8-aligned, so no padding precedes d. Address = {addr} - 24 (6295616 gives 6295592; 140737488347160 gives 140737488347136; 4202520 gives 4202496). sizeof(struct T) is 32, since 28 is rounded up to the 8-byte alignment of long.
L4.explanation: Every member lives at a fixed, compile-time offset from the start of its struct: p->d is compiled as a load from p plus 24. Run the rule backwards and a pointer to a member gives a pointer to the struct: cast to char* so the subtraction counts bytes, subtract offsetof, cast back. That is container_of in the Linux kernel, and it is how an intrusive list (a struct list_head embedded in the node) gets from the link back to the node without storing a second pointer. offsetof(struct T, d) is 24 here, verified with gcc 13; never hand-add sizes, because padding can push a member past the sum.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on Linux. bind() is declared as taking  const struct sockaddr *  , yet every program fills a  struct {s}  and passes  (struct sockaddr *)&addr . Both struct types begin with a member of type sa_family_t (the address family). Explain: (1) which rule of the C standard makes a pointer to the whole struct convertible to a pointer to its first member and back, and why the layout rule guarantees it; (2) how bind recovers the real address type at run time; (3) what breaks if a programmer declares a new address struct with the family field second rather than first.
L4.answer: (1) C17 6.7.2.1p15: members have increasing addresses in declaration order, there is no padding at the beginning of a struct, and a pointer to a structure object, suitably converted, points to its initial member and vice versa. So the first member is at offset 0 in every struct that has it first, and the cast changes only the type, not the address. (2) bind reads the family through the generic struct sockaddr pointer (sa_family, at offset 0, the same bytes as sin_family or sin6_family), then casts to struct {s} on that basis and uses the addrlen argument as the real size, since sizeof(struct sockaddr) is only 16 and sockaddr_in6 is 28 bytes. The family field is a tag; the cast is a type-punned dispatch on it. (3) With the family second, offset 0 holds something else (a port or a length); bind reads that as the family, dispatches wrongly or fails with EAFNOSUPPORT, and if it did cast, every member would be read at the wrong offset. The idiom is the whole of C's inheritance: a base struct embedded as the first member, with the child usable wherever the base is expected.
L4.explanation: The standard promises exactly one offset for free: the first member is at 0. Everything else follows from that. Embedding the base struct first makes a pointer to the child also a valid pointer to the base, which is single inheritance without a language feature, and the family field doubles as the run-time type tag that the C++ vtable pointer would carry. The same first-member rule is why (int *)&p reads p.x in this concept's L3, and it is what socket, bind, listen and accept rely on in every networking program you will write.

L0.cloze: Reordering members largest-first shrank the struct from {{c1::12}} to {{c2::8}} bytes with no change in content.

concepts.L1: Each member must sit at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment requirement, and the struct's size is rounded up to the largest member's alignment. The compiler inserts padding bytes to satisfy both rules.
concepts.L2: Padding bytes are uninitialised, so memcmp on two structs with identical member values can report a difference, and writing a struct to a file or socket leaks whatever was in those bytes. Compare member by member; serialise explicitly.
concepts.L3: struct A places c at 0, then i needs a 4-aligned offset so 3 bytes of padding follow, i at 4, d at 8, and the total is rounded from 9 to 12 so that an array of A keeps every i aligned. struct B has the same members in a different order: i at 0, c at 4, d at 5, total 6 rounded to 8. Same data, 33% smaller, purely from declaration order - which is why hot structs are declared in descending size order. Alignment exists because a load crossing a cache-line or word boundary costs extra cycles, and on some ISAs traps outright.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64, what is sizeof(struct {{ {a} x; {b} y; {c} z; }})?
L4.answer: char,double,int -> 24 (c@0, pad to 8, d@8, i@16, pad to 24). char,int,int -> 12. char,double,char -> 24. char,int,char -> 12.
L4.explanation: Place members in declaration order, each at the next offset that is a multiple of its alignment, then round the total up to the largest alignment present. The key assumes the x86-64 System V sizes, where alignment equals size for these types: char 1, int 4, double 8. So char,double,int is c@0, pad to 8, y@8, z@16, total 20 rounded to 24; char,int,char is 0, 4, 8, total 9 rounded to 12. Doing this by hand a few times makes cache-line reasoning automatic later.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. struct S has exactly two members, declared in this order: first char a[{k}]; then a member b whose type T has sizeof(T) == alignof(T) == {s} (short is 2, int is 4, double is 8). What is sizeof(struct S)? Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.answer: a occupies bytes 0..k-1, b starts at the next multiple of s, i.e. ceil(k/s)*s, and occupies s bytes; the total is already a multiple of s, so sizeof = (ceil(k/s) + 1) * s. Worked draws (verified with gcc): k=1, s=4 gives 8; k=5, s=4 gives 12; k=3, s=2 gives 6; k=2, s=8 gives 16; k=5, s=8 gives 16.
L4.explanation: Two rules only: each member starts at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment, and the whole struct is rounded up to the largest alignment present. Here the chars need no alignment, so all the padding sits between a and b; because b ends the struct on a multiple of s there is no trailing padding. If you answered k + s you skipped the alignment step; if you rounded k + s up to s you forgot that b itself must start aligned, not merely the struct end.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. struct S has three members declared in this order: char a; then a member b whose type has sizeof == alignof == {s} (short 2, int 4, double 8, long double 16); then char c. What does offsetof(struct S, c) from stddef.h evaluate to? Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.answer: a is at 0, b must start at the first multiple of s after it, which is s, and b occupies s bytes, so c is at 2s. Worked draws (verified with gcc): s=2 gives 4; s=4 gives 8; s=8 gives 16; s=16 gives 32. (sizeof(struct S) is then 3s: 2s + 1 rounded up to a multiple of s.)
L4.explanation: offsetof reports where the compiler actually put a member, padding included; it is the tool for checking layout instead of guessing. c sits at 2s because b, not c, forced the padding: c is a char and would have been happy at offset s+1 had b been shorter. Notice that the single char a costs s - 1 bytes of padding, which is the whole case for declaring small members last.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. The program includes stdio.h and stddef.h, declares struct S with exactly three members in this order: char a; {T} b; char c; and its main function executes  printf("%zu %zu %zu", sizeof(struct S), offsetof(struct S, b), offsetof(struct S, c));  Write the exact output: three integers separated by single spaces.
L4.answer: short: 6 2 4. int: 12 4 8. double: 24 8 16. (All three verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux.)
L4.explanation: a is at 0; b is pushed to the first multiple of its alignment (2, 4 or 8) and occupies that many bytes; c follows immediately; then the total is rounded up to the largest alignment so that an array of S keeps every b aligned. For int: a@0, pad 1..3, b@4..7, c@8, pad 9..11, sizeof 12. The struct is three times the size of its largest member every time, and two of those thirds are padding around single chars.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux with gcc, a struct declared with exactly the members int i; char c; in that order has sizeof equal to {n}, not 5. Which statement gives the real reason?
L4.answer: Three trailing padding bytes make the size a multiple of int's alignment, so every element of an array of this struct has its i at a 4-byte boundary
L4.explanation: Trailing padding exists for arrays: element k lives at base + k * sizeof, so sizeof must be a multiple of the strictest member alignment or element 1's int would start at offset 5. The rounding is to the largest member alignment present (4 here), not to a fixed 8; a struct of two shorts has sizeof 4. char stays one byte: offsetof(c) is 4 and the three bytes after it are padding, which no member owns.
options: Three trailing padding bytes make the size a multiple of int's alignment, so every element of an array of this struct has its i at a 4-byte boundary
The compiler rounds every struct up to a multiple of 8 bytes on 64-bit platforms
A char member is stored as a 4-byte int inside a struct so that all members are the same width

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. struct S is declared with four members in this order: char a[{k}]; T b; char c[{k}]; T d;  where T has sizeof == alignof == {s}. Compute sizeof(struct S) as declared, then the smallest sizeof reachable by reordering the same four members. How many bytes does the best reordering save? Answer with the number of bytes saved (0 if none).
L4.answer: As declared each char array is followed by padding up to the next multiple of s, so the layout is a@0, b@s, c@2s, d@3s, total 4s. Largest-first (b, d, a, c) has no internal padding: 2s + 2k bytes, rounded up to a multiple of s. Saving = 4s - ceil((2s + 2k)/s) * s. Worked draws (verified with gcc): s=4, k=1: 16 vs 12, saves 4. s=4, k=2: 16 vs 12, saves 4. s=4, k=3: 16 vs 16, saves 0. s=8, k=1: 32 vs 24, saves 8. s=8, k=3: 32 vs 24, saves 8.
L4.explanation: Reordering removes the padding between members but cannot remove the final rounding to the largest alignment, so the saving is quantised in units of s. With s=4 and two 3-byte arrays the packed payload is 14 bytes, which rounds up to 16 - exactly the declared size - so the reorder saves nothing. Estimate the payload first, round it up, then compare; a reorder that is obviously tidier is not always smaller. The compiler may not do this for you: C17 6.7.2.1p15 fixes member order as declared.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. A protocol header is declared as a struct with two members in this order: uint16_t type; uint32_t len;  The sender fills both members and calls fwrite(&hdr, sizeof hdr, 1, sock) to send it. The receiver, written from the protocol document, reads {n} bytes per header. What actually goes on the wire?
L4.answer: 8 bytes: 2 of type, 2 bytes of padding whose contents are unspecified, then 4 of len - so the receiver's field boundaries are wrong and two bytes of the sender's memory leak per header
L4.explanation: len must sit at a 4-byte offset, so offsetof(len) is 4 and sizeof is 8; fwrite copies all 8 bytes including the padding at 2..3. Nothing in C zeroes those bytes for an automatic object, and C17 6.2.6.1p6 says padding takes unspecified values even after a whole-struct store, so whatever the stack held is sent. This is a real information-leak class (CWE-200 via uninitialised padding). Serialise field by field, or memset the struct to zero before filling it and still document the 8-byte layout.
options: 8 bytes: 2 of type, 2 bytes of padding whose contents are unspecified, then 4 of len - so the receiver's field boundaries are wrong and two bytes of the sender's memory leak per header
6 bytes: the compiler packs structs that are passed to I/O functions so that no padding is written
8 bytes: 2 of type, 2 bytes guaranteed to be zero, then 4 of len - the receiver only needs to skip two bytes

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. struct In has two members: char a; then T b; where T has sizeof == alignof == {s}. struct Out has three members in this order: char x; struct In in; char y;  Derive sizeof(struct Out). Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.answer: struct In is a@0, b@s, sizeof 2s, and its alignment is the largest of its members' alignments, s. In struct Out: x@0, in must start at a multiple of s so it is at s and ends at 3s, y@3s, total 3s + 1 rounded up to a multiple of s = 4s. Worked draws (verified with gcc): s=2 gives 8; s=4 gives 16; s=8 gives 32.
L4.explanation: A nested struct is not flattened: it is one member whose size is its padded sizeof and whose alignment is the strictest alignment inside it, so the outer struct must place it as it would place a T. That is why in lands at offset s, not at 1, and why the outer size inherits the inner rounding. Getting 3s + 1 or 2s + 3 means you either aligned in to 1 or forgot that sizeof(struct In) already includes its own padding.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, no packing attributes. A record type is declared with these members in this order: char flags; double price; int32_t qty; char code[{k}]; uint16_t port;  You may reorder the members freely. What is the smallest sizeof(struct) that any ordering can achieve? Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.answer: The members total 8 + 4 + 2 + k + 1 = 15 + k bytes and the struct must be a multiple of 8 (double's alignment), so no ordering can beat ceil((15 + k)/8) * 8. Largest-first (price, qty, port, code, flags) reaches it with no internal padding. Worked draws (verified with gcc): k=1 gives 16 (as declared: 24); k=3 gives 24 (as declared: 32); k=5 gives 24 (as declared: 32); k=9 gives 24 (as declared: 32); k=13 gives 32 (as declared: 40).
L4.explanation: The lower bound is the payload rounded up to the largest alignment; descending-size order achieves it because every member then starts on a boundary at least as strict as its own. That is the whole design rule for hot structs, and it must be done by hand: C17 6.7.2.1p15 requires members to be laid out in declaration order, so the compiler cannot reorder for you (Rust and Go compilers may; C may not). As declared, the char flags at offset 0 costs seven bytes of padding before price.

L4.prompt_tpl: An array of {n} elements of struct A (char c; int i; char d; sizeof 12 on x86-64) is replaced by an array of struct B (int i; char c; char d; sizeof 8) holding the same values. A loop sums every element's i. Cache lines are 64 bytes and the array starts on a line boundary. How many fewer cache lines does the loop have to bring in from memory after the change? Answer with the number of cache lines saved.
L4.explanation: The loop touches only i, but the hardware fetches whole 64-byte lines, so every byte of padding in the array is paid for in memory traffic. Reordering to struct B cuts the array by a third and the line count with it, which The memory hierarchy in this domain turns into wall-clock time: a sequential scan runs at memory bandwidth, so one third fewer lines is about one third less time. This is why hot structs are declared largest-first and why padding is a performance question, not only a size question.

L4.prompt_tpl: struct S is declared with members char c; {T} v; char d; in that order, on x86-64 Linux with gcc. Explain, in about four sentences: (1) why the C compiler is not allowed to silently reorder the members to the smaller v, c, d layout even though it knows the sizes; (2) what __attribute__((packed)) or #pragma pack(1) changes about sizeof and about the addresses of v; (3) what a load of v from a packed struct costs on x86-64 and what it can do on an ISA that requires aligned access.
L4.answer: (1) C17 6.7.2.1p15 requires members to have increasing addresses in declaration order, so layout is part of the type's public contract: code that casts to the first member's type, computes offsetof, or maps the struct onto a file format or a hardware register block depends on it, and a reordering compiler would break every one of them. (2) Packing sets every member's alignment to 1: sizeof drops from 12 (int) or 24 (double) to 6 or 10, and v now lives at offset 1, an address that is not a multiple of its natural alignment; the compiler must then emit code that never assumes alignment for v. (3) On x86-64 an unaligned integer or scalar double load is legal and usually costs nothing unless it straddles a cache line, where it costs an extra line access; taking the address of v and using it through an ordinary pointer, or with alignment-requiring SIMD instructions, can fault. On an ISA that requires aligned access (classic SPARC, older ARM and MIPS, and ARM device memory) the misaligned load traps with SIGBUS or equivalent, so packed structs are a portability decision, not a free size optimisation.
L4.explanation: Declaration order is normative because C exposes layout: offsetof, first-member casts and memory-mapped structs all rely on it, so the optimisation is the programmer's job (C17 6.7.2.1p15). Packing buys size by giving up the alignment guarantee, which x86-64 mostly tolerates in scalar code and other ISAs do not; Undefined behaviour in this domain covers why a misaligned pointer is undefined even where the hardware happens to cope.

L0.cloze: malloc returns {{c1::NULL}} on failure, and each successful allocation must be released exactly once with {{c2::free}}.

concepts.L1: malloc reserves n bytes on the heap and returns their address, or NULL. free returns a block to the allocator. Ownership - who is responsible for the matching free - is a convention C cannot express or check.
concepts.L2: free(p) does not change p; it only invalidates what p points at. Using p afterwards is use-after-free, and freeing it twice is double-free - both are exploitable, not merely crashy. Write `sizeof *a` rather than `sizeof(int)` so changing the declared type cannot silently halve the allocation.
concepts.L3: Three failure modes, all silent. A leak: overwrite the only pointer to a block, and it is unreachable but still mapped, so RSS grows without bound. Use-after-free: the allocator may hand the block to another caller, so your write corrupts unrelated data and the crash appears far from the bug. Double-free: corrupts the allocator's free list, which modern allocators detect and abort on, but not always. valgrind --leak-check=full and gcc -fsanitize=address find all three, and running them once on your own code teaches more than any explanation.

L4.prompt_tpl: char *s = malloc({n}); strcpy(s, "{w}"); free(s); printf("%s", s);  Name every defect.
L4.answer: (1) Possible overflow if strlen(w)+1 > n - "hello" needs 6 bytes. (2) malloc's return is not checked for NULL. (3) Use-after-free in printf.
L4.explanation: Each is independently undefined behaviour, and each can appear to work. The habit of enumerating all three on sight is what the exercise is training.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. int *a = malloc({n} * sizeof *a); with sizeof(int) equal to 4. How many bytes does this call request from the allocator? Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.answer: n * 4: sizeof *a is sizeof(int) which is 4 here, so the request is n times 4 bytes. Worked draws: n=4 gives 16; n=8 gives 32; n=16 gives 64; n=100 gives 400.
L4.explanation: The idiom sizeof *a asks for the size of what a points at, so the request scales with the element type without naming it. Writing sizeof *a instead of sizeof(int) means that if a's type later changes to long, the allocation grows with it and cannot silently halve. On x86-64 an int is 4 bytes, so n elements need 4n bytes.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. long *a = calloc({n}, sizeof *a); with sizeof(long) equal to 8. How many bytes does calloc allocate and set to zero? Answer with the number of bytes.
L4.answer: n * 8: calloc(count, size) allocates count times size bytes and zeroes every one of them. sizeof(long) is 8 on x86-64, so that is 8n bytes. Worked draws: n=4 gives 32; n=8 gives 64; n=16 gives 128; n=100 gives 800.
L4.explanation: calloc differs from malloc in two ways: it takes the count and the element size separately (and checks their product for overflow), and it guarantees the returned bytes are all zero. malloc leaves its bytes indeterminate, so reading them before writing is undefined behaviour. Here every one of the 8n bytes is a defined zero.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. A program calls void *p = malloc({n}); and the allocator cannot satisfy the request. According to the C standard, what happens?
L4.answer: malloc returns a null pointer and no memory is allocated, so the program must check the result before using it
L4.explanation: On failure malloc returns a null pointer and allocates nothing; it never aborts the program on its own. Dereferencing that null pointer is where the crash comes from, which is why the NULL check after every allocation is not optional. The block is either fully allocated or not allocated at all - there is no half-sized block.
options: malloc returns a null pointer and no memory is allocated, so the program must check the result before using it
malloc returns a pointer to a zero-length block that the program may still write to
malloc terminates the program with an out-of-memory error before it can return

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. int *a = malloc(3 * sizeof *a); a[0] = {v}; a[1] = {v}+1; a[2] = {v}+2; a = realloc(a, {n} * sizeof *a); printf("%d", a[0]+a[1]+a[2]); What single number is printed? Answer with that number.
L4.answer: 3v + 3: realloc grows the block but preserves the existing contents, so a[0..2] still hold v, v+1, v+2 and their sum is 3v+3, whatever the new size n. Worked draws (verified with gcc): v=1 prints 6; v=2 prints 9; v=3 prints 12; v=5 prints 18.
L4.explanation: realloc(p, size) returns a block of the new size whose first min(old, new) bytes equal the old block's; growing therefore keeps every value already written. The returned pointer may differ from p if the block moved, which is why you must assign it back - using the old p after a move is use-after-free. The sum does not depend on n because only the first three ints are read.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. A library exposes char *dup_upper(const char *s); which returns a newly malloc'd upper-cased copy of s. A caller writes: for (int i = 0; i < {n}; i++) puts(dup_upper(words[i])); State (1) who owns the returned pointer and what the caller must do with it, and (2) what this loop does wrong and how many blocks it leaks after {n} iterations.
L4.answer: (1) dup_upper allocates with malloc and returns the address, so ownership transfers to the caller: the caller must free that pointer exactly once when done with it. C cannot express or check this contract - it lives only in the function's documentation. (2) The return value is passed straight into puts and never stored, so the only pointer to each block is discarded the moment the statement ends. The loop leaks one block per iteration: n blocks after n iterations (n=3 leaks 3, n=10 leaks 10, n=100 leaks 100). Fix: char *u = dup_upper(words[i]); puts(u); free(u);
L4.explanation: A function that returns a malloc'd pointer is handing you ownership, and every such function must document who frees. Discarding the pointer (not storing it) makes the block unreachable but still mapped - the textbook leak. The habit is to name the returned pointer, use it, then free it, so that every malloc in the program has a matching free you can point to.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. Review this fragment: char *buf = malloc({n}); read_into(buf, {n}); free(buf); if (had_error) free(buf); log_msg(buf); Identify every memory defect, and for each explain why 'it seemed to work when I tested it' is not evidence that it is safe.
L4.answer: Three defects. (a) The malloc return is never checked for NULL, so on failure read_into writes through a null pointer. (b) Double-free: on the error path free(buf) runs a second time, corrupting the allocator's free list - modern glibc detects this and aborts with 'double free detected', but the standard does not require detection. (c) Use-after-free: log_msg(buf) reads a block that free already returned to the allocator, which may have handed it to another caller, so the bytes are now unrelated data. (b) and (c) are undefined behaviour: the optimiser may assume they never happen, and any crash appears far from the line at fault, so a passing test only means the UB was not triggered on that input - not that the code is correct.
L4.explanation: This is the failure the concept exists to prevent: free(p) does not change p, so nothing stops the later reads and frees. Both the double-free and the use-after-free are undefined behaviour, and the lesson from the Undefined behaviour concept applies - UB that happens to look correct today is a latent bug, not a safe one. Set buf = NULL after free (free(NULL) is a no-op) and stop touching it.

concepts.t: Control flow and its C-specific traps

L0.cloze: A switch case without {{c1::break}} falls through into the next case; = is assignment while {{c2::==}} is comparison.

concepts.L1: C offers if/else, while, do/while, for, switch, break, continue, goto and return. A condition is any scalar - integer, floating-point or pointer - tested against zero: 0 or NULL is false, anything else is true. switch cases fall through to the next case unless broken out of.
concepts.L2: `if (x = 5)` assigns and then tests 5, which is always true, and it compiles cleanly without -Wall. _Bool exists since C99, but no condition is required to be one: any assignment, pointer or arithmetic expression is a legal condition - the reason experienced C programmers write comparisons and enable -Wparentheses.
concepts.L3: A switch is a computed jump: the controlling expression selects a case label, and a label is only a position in the block, not a branch, so execution runs on past the next label until a break. So fall-through is the default; C23's [[fallthrough]] marks it as intended. break leaves only the innermost switch or loop: a break in a switch inside a for stays in the for. Three more legal parses mislead: else binds to the nearest unmatched if (C17 6.8.4.1), so an unbraced nested if hands it to the wrong condition; `for (i = 0; i < n; i++);` runs an empty body n times; and since a comparison yields 0 or 1, `x & 1 == 0` is `x & (1 == 0)`, always 0, and `0 < x < 10` is `(0 < x) < 10`, always true. Loops obey integer rules: `for (unsigned i = n; i >= 0; i--)` never ends (Fixed-width integers wrap), and `i <= n` with n == INT_MAX overflows i, undefined (Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C).

L4.prompt_tpl: int c = '{ch}'; switch (c) {{ case 'a': printf("A"); case 'b': printf("B"); break; default: printf("D"); }}
L4.answer: 'a' -> AB (falls through); 'b' -> B; 'z' -> D
L4.explanation: Case labels are entry points, not independent branches. Execution continues past the next label until a break or the end of the switch.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc with no warning flags. int x = {a}; if (x = {b}) printf("yes %d", x); else printf("no %d", x); What exactly is printed? Answer in the form  yes N  or  no N.
L4.answer: yes {b}
L4.explanation: x = {b} is an assignment, not a comparison. Its value is the value assigned, {b}, which is non-zero, so the condition is true whatever x held before, and x now holds {b}: the output is yes {b}. The program compiles cleanly; only -Wall (via -Wparentheses) reports 'suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value'. Verified with gcc 13 on x86-64: for a=3, b=7 it prints yes 7.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. int i, s = 0; for (i = 0; i < {n}; i++); s += i; printf("%d", s); Note the semicolon straight after the for header. What number is printed?
L4.answer: {n} (n=4: 4; n=7: 7; n=10: 10). The semicolon is the loop body, so the loop only counts i up to {n}; s += i then runs once with i == {n}. Without the stray semicolon the sum would be 0 + 1 + ... + ({n} - 1).
L4.explanation: A lone semicolon is the null statement, and it is the entire body of the for. The loop runs {n} times doing nothing but incrementing i, exits with i == {n}, and then s += i executes exactly once, giving s = {n}. Verified with gcc 13. This is legal C with no diagnostic by default; gcc's -Wempty-body (in -Wextra) catches it for if and while but not for for, which is why bracing every body, even a deliberately empty one, is the accepted style.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C, double d, int *p and struct {st} s are all declared and initialised. Exactly ONE of the following does not compile. Which?
L4.answer: if (s)
L4.explanation: C17 6.8.4.1 requires the controlling expression of if (and of while, do and for, 6.8.5) to have scalar type: any arithmetic type or any pointer type, compared against 0. A double and a pointer both qualify - if (d) tests d != 0, if (p) tests p != NULL - which is why 'conditions are integers' is too narrow. A struct is an aggregate, not a scalar, so if (s) is a constraint violation; gcc says 'used struct type value where scalar is required'. switch is stricter still: its controlling expression must be an integer type (6.8.4.2).
options: if (d)
if (p)
if (s)

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. int count = 0; then a for loop runs i from 0 up to but not including {n}. The whole loop body is one switch on i % {m} with two labels:  case 0: break;  and  default: count = count + 1;  After the loop, printf prints count. A reader expects the break to leave the for loop the first time i % {m} is 0. What number is actually printed?
L4.answer: {n} minus the number of multiples of {m} in 0..{n}-1, i.e. n - ceil(n/m): (6,2): 3; (6,3): 4; (7,2): 3; (7,3): 4; (10,2): 5; (10,3): 6. The break leaves only the switch; the for keeps going.
L4.explanation: break terminates the innermost enclosing switch or loop (C17 6.8.6.3), and here the innermost is the switch. So at every i with i % {m} == 0 the switch is exited and the for continues; at every other i the default label increments count. The loop always runs all {n} iterations, and count is {n} minus the multiples of {m} below {n}. To leave the loop from inside a switch you need a flag, a goto, or a return - there is no 'break 2' in C. Verified with gcc 13 for all six draws.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. int x = {x}; if (x & 1 == 0) printf("even"); else printf("odd"); What is printed? Answer even or odd.
L4.answer: odd
L4.explanation: == binds tighter than &, so the condition is x & (1 == 0). The comparison 1 == 0 yields the int 0, and x & 0 is 0 for every x, so the condition is always false and the else branch prints odd even when x is {x}. Verified with gcc 13: 4, 6, 7 and 10 all print odd. gcc -Wall reports 'suggest parentheses around comparison in operand of &'. In C the bitwise operators & | ^ sit BELOW the comparisons in precedence, a historical accident from before && existed; write (x & 1) == 0.

L4.answer: The else belongs to the inner if (b > 0), whatever the indentation says. a=5, b=3: 1. a=5, b=-3: 2. a=-5, b=3: 0. a=-5, b=-3: 0 - when a is not positive nothing runs at all, so r stays 0.
L4.explanation: C17 6.8.4.1p3: an else is associated with the lexically nearest preceding if that is allowed by the syntax - the inner one here, since it has no else yet. Indentation is not syntax. So r = 2 runs only when a > 0 and b <= 0; when a <= 0 neither branch runs and r remains 0, which is the case the indentation lies about. gcc -Wall warns 'suggest explicit braces to avoid ambiguous else' (-Wdangling-else). Braces on every block make the intended binding the only possible one. Verified with gcc 13 for all four draws.
L4.answer_expr: max(0, min(1, a)) * (2 - max(0, min(1, b)))

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc, where unsigned is 32 bits. for (unsigned i = {n}; i >= 0; i--) printf("%u ", i); What happens when this runs?
L4.answer: Prints {n} down to 0, then 4294967295, and never stops
L4.explanation: An unsigned value is never negative, so i >= 0 is true for every i and the condition can never fail. After printing 0, i-- wraps modulo 2 to the power 32 to 4294967295 and the loop continues forever. It compiles; gcc warns only with -Wextra (-Wtype-limits: 'comparison of unsigned expression in >= 0 is always true'). Verified with gcc 13: the body ran 11 times for n = 3 before a test cut it off. Write the countdown as for (unsigned i = {n} + 1; i-- > 0; ) or loop on a signed index. See Fixed-width integers wrap.
options: Prints {n} down to 0, then stops: {n} + 1 numbers
Prints {n} down to 0, then 4294967295, and never stops
Does not compile: i >= 0 is a type error for unsigned

L4.prompt_tpl: C, gcc. int hit = 0; and for every integer x from {lo} to {hi} inclusive the statement  if (0 < x < 10) hit = hit + 1;  is executed once. Derive from how C evaluates a comparison what hit is at the end. (In Python the same text 0 < x < 10 is a chained conjunction and would count only 1..9.) Answer with the number.
L4.answer: Every x counts: hit = {hi} - {lo} + 1 (lo=-20, hi=30: 51; lo=-20, hi=100: 121; lo=-5, hi=30: 36; lo=-5, hi=100: 106). 0 < x < 10 parses as (0 < x) < 10; the inner comparison yields 0 or 1, and both are less than 10.
L4.explanation: Relational operators are left-associative and produce an int that is 0 or 1 (C17 6.5.8p6). So 0 < x < 10 means (0 < x) < 10: for x <= 0 the inner result is 0 and 0 < 10 is true; for x > 0 it is 1 and 1 < 10 is true. The condition is true for every integer, and hit counts all {hi} - {lo} + 1 values. gcc -Wall says 'comparisons like X<=Y<=Z do not have their mathematical meaning'. Python makes a < b < c mean a < b and b < c (see Conditionals and truthiness); in C you must write 0 < x && x < 10. Verified with gcc 13 on all four draws.

L4.prompt_tpl: C on x86-64 Linux, gcc. A function receives  int {n}  and runs  for (int i = 0; i <= {n}; i++) count = count + 1;  then returns count. It is called with {n} equal to INT_MAX. (a) Explain why the language does not define what this program does. (b) Explain why gcc -O2 and gcc -O0 are entitled to give different results, and state a plausible result for each. (c) Rewrite the loop so that it executes exactly {n} + 1 times for every non-negative {n}, including INT_MAX.
L4.answer: (a) When i == INT_MAX the test i <= {n} is true, the body runs, and then i++ must produce INT_MAX + 1, which does not fit in int: signed overflow, undefined behaviour, so the standard imposes no requirement on the whole run. (b) An optimiser may assume overflow never happens, so it may treat i <= {n} as a loop that runs exactly {n} + 1 times and fold it to count = {n} + 1; gcc 13 -O2 does exactly that, and the 32-bit addition wraps to -2147483648. At -O0 the increment is executed literally: i wraps to INT_MIN, i <= INT_MAX stays true, and the loop never terminates. Both are permitted because UB removes every guarantee. (c) Test before the increment:  for (int i = 0; ; i++) with the body  count = count + 1; if (i == {n}) break;  - or count with a wider type:  for (long long i = 0; i <= {n}; i++)  - or use unsigned i with i <= (unsigned){n}. In each version i never exceeds INT_MAX in int arithmetic.
L4.explanation: The loop looks like a control-flow question and is really an arithmetic one: the loop variable is an int, and the exit test can only become false after an increment that is undefined for INT_MAX. Because the compiler may assume undefined behaviour never occurs, it may derive the trip count in closed form (-O2 returned -2147483648 in this session) or run the wrapping increment forever (-O0 did). The fix is any formulation in which the last comparison happens before the overflowing increment, or in which the counter has more range than the bound. See Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C.

L0.body:
/* point.h */
#ifndef POINT_H
#define POINT_H
struct Point { int x, y; };
int dist2(struct Point a, struct Point b);   /* declaration */
#endif

#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))    /* parenthesise EVERYTHING */
L0.cloze: An include guard uses {{c1::#ifndef}} / #define / {{c2::#endif}} to make a header safe to include twice.

concepts.L1: The preprocessor is a textual pass that runs before compilation: #include splices a file in, #define does token substitution, #ifdef selects text. Headers carry declarations; .c files carry definitions.
concepts.L2: Macros are text, not functions. #define SQUARE(x) x*x makes SQUARE(1+2) expand to 1+2*1+2 = 5. Even fully parenthesised, SQUARE(i++) evaluates i++ twice. Prefer static inline functions, which obey the type system and evaluate arguments once.
concepts.L3: Run gcc -E on a file and you see what the compiler actually sees: thousands of lines from the headers, macros already substituted, no comments. That is why a macro error reports a line in your file with an expansion you never wrote, and why -E is the fastest way to diagnose one. Include guards matter because #include is literal insertion: without them, including point.h twice redefines struct Point and fails to compile. #pragma once does the same job in one line and is universally supported despite not being standard.

L4.prompt_tpl:
#define SQ(x) x*x
printf("%d", SQ({a}+{b}));
L4.answer: expands to a+b*a+b = a + (b*a) + b: 1+2 -> 5; 2+3 -> 11
L4.explanation: Substitution is textual and ignores precedence. With ((x)*(x)) the results would be 9 and 25 instead.

L4.prompt_tpl:
C, x86-64 Linux, gcc.
#define SQ(x) ((x)*(x))
printf("%d", SQ({a}+{b}));
What number is printed? Answer with that number.
L4.answer: $(a+b)^{2}$: the fully parenthesised body expands to ((a+b)*(a+b)). Worked draws (verified with gcc): a=1,b=2 prints 9; a=2,b=3 prints 25; a=3,b=4 prints 49.
L4.explanation: Macro expansion is token substitution: the argument text a+b is dropped into the body wherever x appears. Because the body wraps every use of x and the whole result in parentheses, the substituted text keeps its grouping and the arithmetic is the one you meant. Compare the unparenthesised x*x, which turns the same call into a+b*a+b.

L4.answer: $n \cdot m$: ROWS is replaced by (N*m), then N by n, before the compiler sees the array declaration, so grid has n*m elements and sizeof grid / sizeof grid[0] is that count. Worked draws (verified with gcc): n=3,m=4 prints 12; n=3,m=6 prints 18; n=5,m=4 prints 20; n=5,m=6 prints 30.
L4.explanation: Object-like macros are rescanned after substitution, so a macro body may name another macro and the chain is resolved textually before compilation. The compiler then sees int grid[(3*4)]; a plain constant expression, which is why macros can size arrays where a variable could not (before C99 VLAs). sizeof grid is the whole array in bytes; dividing by one element gives the element count.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file main.c in directory {dir} contains #include "point.h" and #include <stdio.h>. According to the C standard and gcc, how does the quoted form differ from the angle-bracket form in where the header is looked for?
L4.answer: The quoted form is searched first in the directory of the file doing the including, and only if that fails is it searched exactly as the angle-bracket form would be
L4.explanation: C17 6.10.2: the quoted form searches in an implementation-defined way first, and if that search fails the directive is reprocessed as if written with angle brackets. gcc's implementation-defined place is the directory containing the including file (not the shell's working directory), then any -iquote directories, then the -I and system chain shared with angle brackets. So #include "point.h" finds your own header sitting beside main.c, while <stdio.h> goes straight to the system directories.
options: The quoted form is searched first in the directory of the file doing the including, and only if that fails is it searched exactly as the angle-bracket form would be
The angle-bracket form is searched first in the current directory; the quoted form searches only the system include directories
They are interchangeable; the choice between them is a style convention with no effect on the search

L4.answer: $2k^{2}$: the expansion is ((next())*(next())), so next runs twice, returning k and 2k, and the product is $k \cdot 2k = 2k^{2}$. Worked draws (verified with gcc): k=1 prints 2; k=2 prints 8; k=3 prints 18; k=5 prints 50. Afterwards calls is 2k, not k.
L4.explanation: Parentheses fix precedence but not evaluation count: a macro parameter is pasted in as text wherever it appears, so an argument with a side effect runs once per appearance. The two calls return k and 2k whichever order gcc evaluates the operands of * in, so the product is 2k^2 either way. A static inline function int sq(int x) evaluates its argument exactly once and would print k^2.

L4.answer: small
L4.explanation: It compiles. C17 6.10.1p4: after macro expansion, any identifier still remaining in a #if expression (other than true/false in C23) is replaced by the constant 0. So the test is 0 > n, false for every positive n, and the #else branch survives. This is why a misspelt macro name in #if silently selects the wrong code instead of failing; gcc -Wundef turns the silent 0 into a warning.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. point.h has no include guard and contains two lines: struct Point with fields int x, y; and the prototype int dist2(struct Point a, struct Point b); A .c file includes point.h {times} times. What does gcc report?
L4.answer: error: redefinition of struct Point - the struct definition may appear only once per scope; the repeated prototype on its own would have been accepted
L4.explanation: #include is literal insertion with no memory of what it already inserted, so the header's text appears in the translation unit once per directive. C allows a function to be declared repeatedly with compatible types, so the prototype is harmless; a struct tag with a member list may be defined only once in a scope, so the second copy is a redefinition error (verified with gcc 13). That asymmetry is why the guard, or #pragma once, is mandatory the moment a header defines a type.
options: error: redefinition of struct Point - the struct definition may appear only once per scope; the repeated prototype on its own would have been accepted
error on the prototype - a function may be declared only once per translation unit; the repeated struct on its own would have been accepted
No error - the preprocessor detects that the file has already been inserted and skips the later copies

L4.answer: $c+k$: after expansion the line reads if (flag) puts("hit"); count += k; so only the puts is governed by the if, and count += k runs unconditionally even though flag is 0. Worked draws (verified with gcc): c=10,k=4 prints 14; c=10,k=3 prints 13; c=20,k=7 prints 27.
L4.explanation: A macro that expands to two statements is not one statement to the parser: the first semicolon ends the if. gcc -Wall even warns 'macro expands to multiple statements'. The fix is the do-while-zero idiom, wrapping the body in do { ... } while (0), which makes the expansion a single statement that still takes a trailing semicolon; or, better, a static inline function, which needs no idiom at all.

L4.answer: VER
L4.explanation: The stringification operator # is applied to the argument as written, before that argument is macro-expanded (C17 6.10.3.2), so STR(VER) becomes the string literal "VER", never the number. To stringify the value you add a level of indirection: #define XSTR(x) STR(x) - the argument of XSTR is expanded during substitution, and only then does the inner STR see the digits. gcc -E shows both: puts("VER") and puts("7").

L4.prompt_tpl: A header geom.h is included by {n} different .c files that are compiled separately and linked into one program. You want a small function sq(x) that returns x*x. Compare three ways of putting it in the header: (a) #define SQ(x) ((x)*(x)), (b) int sq(int x) with its body, (c) static inline int sq(int x) with its body. For each, say whether the program compiles and links, whether sq(next()) calls next once or twice, and why (c) is the usual choice.
L4.answer: (a) Compiles and links: a macro is text, so nothing is emitted for the linker; but SQ(next()) expands to ((next())*(next())) and calls next twice, and the argument is untyped. (b) Compiles, but each of the n translation units emits its own external definition of sq, so the linker reports multiple definition of sq (n copies where exactly one is allowed). Calls next once. (c) static makes the definition internal to each translation unit, so the n copies do not collide at link time; inline lets the compiler expand it at each call site as a macro would; it is a real function, so the argument is evaluated exactly once and type-checked. That is why headers carry declarations plus static inline definitions, and .c files carry everything else.
L4.explanation: The preprocessor is textual and the linker resolves symbols across translation units; the header sits between them. A non-static function definition in a header is compiled once per includer and the linker sees n definitions of one external name - the 'multiple definition' error from the linking stage described in A C program, compiled and run. static inline sidesteps it by giving each unit a private copy while keeping function semantics: one evaluation per argument, real types.

L0.body:
/* all undefined behaviour, all compile cleanly: */
arr[n];              /* out of bounds        */
*p;                  /* p is NULL or freed   */
int x; return x;     /* uninitialised read   */
INT_MAX + 1;         /* signed overflow      */
i = i++ + 1;         /* unsequenced modify   */
L0.cloze: Undefined behaviour means the standard imposes {{c1::no requirements}} at all - the compiler may assume it never {{c2::happens}}.

concepts.L1: A construct with undefined behaviour places no requirement on the implementation (C17 3.4.3). Not 'implementation-defined', not 'unspecified': any execution that reaches it has no defined meaning, including the code that ran before it. Executions that never reach it stay fully defined.
concepts.L2: UB is not merely a run-time event that yields a bad value. Because the optimiser may assume UB never occurs, a null check placed after a dereference is deleted as dead code - the dereference 'proved' the pointer non-null. So UB deletes your safety checks rather than merely producing a wrong value.
concepts.L3: Definition (C17 3.4.3): behaviour 'for which this document imposes no requirements'. Add the as-if rule (5.1.2.3): a compiler must reproduce only the observable behaviour of executions the standard constrains. Trace `int v = *p; if (!p) return; use(v);`: where p is null, `*p` has already discharged every requirement, so anything after it conforms; where p is non-null the branch is never taken. Deleting it changes no constrained execution, and gcc -O2 does delete it (-fdelete-null-pointer-checks). UB therefore belongs to an execution, not to source text: a null store guarded by argc > 3 is fully defined when argc is 1. And there is no '-O0 semantics' to fall back on: no promise was made. -fsanitize=undefined,address catches overflow, bounds, null and use-after-free, not strict aliasing. 'Why Rust changes the calculus' (sec) shows what a language pays to have no UB at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone argues that signed overflow 'wraps in practice, so the check works'. Give the argument that it does not.
L4.answer: The optimiser assumes overflow never happens and deletes any branch whose truth would require it, so the check compiles to nothing. The wrap may still occur at run time; only the guard disappears.
L4.explanation: Testing on -O0 and shipping -O2 is how this reaches production. Assume UB is exploited by the compiler, not tolerated by it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Complete the C standard's definition (C17 3.4.3). Undefined behaviour is 'behavior, upon use of a nonportable or erroneous program construct or of erroneous data, for which this document imposes ___'. Fill the blank with the two words the standard uses.
L4.answer: no requirements
L4.explanation: The whole concept hangs on those two words. 'Imposes no requirements' is stronger than 'produces a wrong value': once an execution reaches UB, nothing the implementation does, before or after, can be non-conforming. Contrast implementation-defined (a documented choice, e.g. the size of int) and unspecified (a choice from a listed set, e.g. argument evaluation order).

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. In main: int i = {n}; i = i++ + 1; printf("%d", i); What does the C standard guarantee is printed?
L4.answer: Nothing is guaranteed: i is modified twice with no sequencing between the modifications, so the behaviour is undefined
L4.explanation: C17 6.5p2: if a side effect on a scalar object is unsequenced relative to another side effect on the same object, the behaviour is undefined. i++ writes i and the assignment writes i, with no sequence point between them. gcc 13 happens to print {n} plus 1 at every optimisation level and warns with -Wsequence-point, but that is one observed outcome of a program with no defined meaning, not an answer.
options: Nothing is guaranteed: i is modified twice with no sequencing between the modifications, so the behaviour is undefined
{n} plus 2: the postfix increment happens first, then the assignment adds 1 to the incremented value
{n} plus 1: the assignment happens last and overwrites the increment

L4.prompt_tpl: int is 32 bits, so INT_MAX = 2147483647. A function receives int a = {a} and int b, both non-negative, and must reject any b for which a + b would overflow, without ever evaluating an expression that overflows. The check it uses is: reject if b > INT_MAX - a. What is the largest b that passes the check?
L4.explanation: INT_MAX - a never overflows for non-negative a, so comparing b against it is defined for every input; that is the whole trick. Writing if (a + b < a) instead evaluates the overflowing sum first, which is UB, and gcc -O2 rewrites that test as b < 0 (verified in the assembly), so it stops detecting anything. For a = 2000000000 the largest safe b is 147483647.

L4.prompt_tpl: Exactly one of these is undefined behaviour in C. Which?
L4.answer: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
L4.explanation: Signed overflow is UB (C17 6.5p5: the result is not representable). The order in which f() and g() are evaluated is unspecified (6.5p3): either order is allowed, both are defined. The size of int is implementation-defined (6.2.5, 5.2.4.2.1): the implementation must choose and document it. Only UB discharges every requirement on the implementation.
options: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
int r = f() + g(); where f and g each print one line, so the two lines may come out in either order
sizeof(int) is 2 on one compiler and 4 on another

L4.prompt_tpl: A C program contains, in main: if (argc > 3) then a block that does int *p = 0; *p = 1; and nothing else touches p. It is compiled with gcc -O2 and run with no command-line arguments, so argc is 1. What does the standard say about that run?
L4.answer: That execution is fully defined: undefined behaviour is a property of an execution, and this execution never reaches the null store
L4.explanation: C17 3.4.3 defines UB 'upon use of' an erroneous construct or erroneous data: it is triggered by an execution, not by the presence of text. The compiler may assume the guarded block is never entered and may compile it to anything, but it must preserve every execution that avoids it. Verified: gcc 13 -O2 prints 'ok' with no arguments and segfaults with three.
options: That execution is fully defined: undefined behaviour is a property of an execution, and this execution never reaches the null store
The whole program has no defined meaning on any input, because the source contains a null dereference
The run is defined only if the compiler cannot prove the block reachable; at -O2 it may delete main entirely

L4.prompt_tpl: int is 32 bits (INT_MAX = 2147483647). A loop runs int i = 0; i < n; i++ and computes int y = i * {k}; on each iteration. For large enough n the multiplication overflows and the program has undefined behaviour. What is the smallest value of i at which i * {k} exceeds INT_MAX?
L4.explanation: The last safe i is floor(INT_MAX / k); the next one overflows. For k = 65536 that is i = 32768, so a loop that 'only' runs to 40000 is already UB. The trap: the compiler may have transformed the loop on the assumption that i * k never overflows (for instance by strength-reducing it to a 64-bit running sum), so the wrapped value you expected to observe at that iteration may never exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux. The body of int f(int *p) is: int v = *p; if (!p) return -1; use(v); return 0; It passes every test at -O0. Describe what gcc -O2 does to the null check, why the standard permits it, and the one-line fix.
L4.answer: gcc -O2 removes the if entirely: f loads *p, calls use, returns 0. Reading *p is UB when p is null, so the compiler may assume p is non-null after the load, which makes !p always false and the branch dead. Fix: test p before dereferencing it - if (!p) return -1; int v = *p;
L4.explanation: Verified on gcc 13 -O2: the assembly for f contains no comparison of p. This is -fdelete-null-pointer-checks, on by default at -O2. The check was never protecting anything, because a null p had already made the execution undefined one statement earlier; the order of the statements is the bug, not the optimiser.

L4.prompt_tpl: Start from two sentences of the C standard: UB is behaviour for which the standard imposes no requirements (3.4.3), and a conforming implementation need only reproduce the observable behaviour of the abstract machine (5.1.2.3, the as-if rule). Derive, execution by execution, why replacing int v = *p; if (!p) return; use(v); with int v = *p; use(v); is a correct transformation, and then state exactly which executions of the original program the transformed program is allowed to differ on.
L4.answer: Partition executions by p. If p is non-null, the branch is not taken in the original, so both programs perform exactly the same observable steps. If p is null, the original reached *p first, which is UB, so the standard imposes no requirement on that execution at all; whatever the transformed program does there is conforming. Every constrained execution is preserved, so the as-if rule is satisfied. The two programs may differ only on executions in which p is null, and those are exactly the executions the standard has already given up on.
L4.explanation: The derivation is a case split over executions, which is why the per-execution definition matters: legality is checked against constrained executions only. Note what the argument never uses: the optimisation level, the hardware, or whether address 0 is mapped. The compiler is not exploiting a loophole; it is reasoning from the only executions it is obliged to preserve.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux. A file declares static int (*Do)(void); with no initialiser. static int EraseAll(void) has the body: puts("erased"); return 0. void NeverCalled(void) has the body: Do = EraseAll. int main(void) has the body: return Do(); Nothing in the program calls NeverCalled. Compiled with clang 18 -O2 the program prints 'erased' and exits 0; with gcc 13 -O2 it segfaults. Explain, from the standard, how a conforming compiler can produce the first output, and name the UB.
L4.answer: Do is a static function pointer that starts null. Calling a null function pointer is UB, so the compiler may assume main's call never happens through a null Do. The only store to Do anywhere in the translation unit assigns EraseAll, so under that assumption Do can only ever be EraseAll, and the indirect call is devirtualised into a direct call to EraseAll, which prints 'erased'. gcc leaves the indirect call in place and jumps to address 0. Both are conforming: the execution is undefined, so nothing is required of it.
L4.explanation: This is Krister Walfridsson's example, discussed by both the clang and gcc communities. Nothing in the program's text says 'call EraseAll', yet that is what runs: the compiler reasoned about all defined executions and found only one. The function that was never called was executed by an execution with no meaning. Outputs were verified here on clang 18.1 and gcc 13.3 at -O2.

L4.prompt_tpl: Safe Rust claims to have no undefined behaviour. Take the five UB lines from this concept's L0 (out-of-bounds index, null dereference, uninitialised read, signed overflow, unsequenced double modification) and for each say what Rust does instead and whether the cost is paid at compile time or at run time.
L4.answer: Out-of-bounds index: a run-time bounds check that panics. Null dereference: references cannot be null, Option<T> makes absence explicit; compile time. Uninitialised read: definite-initialisation analysis rejects the program; compile time. Signed overflow: defined either way - debug builds panic, release builds wrap two's complement, and wrapping_add etc. are explicit; run time (a check or a defined wrap). Unsequenced modification: the language has no ++ and fixes evaluation order, and the borrow rules forbid two live mutable paths to one value; compile time.
L4.explanation: Each C UB is a place where the C standard chose to require nothing so that the compiler need not check; Rust chooses between a static proof and a run-time check at each of those places. Bounds checks and overflow checks are the run-time costs; the rest is paid in the type system. 'Why Rust changes the calculus' in the security domain takes this up from the attacker's side.

prereqs: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C
Arrays and the decay to pointers
