concepts.t: Error handling by return code and errno

L0.cloze: C reports failure by {{c1::return value}}; the detailed reason is left in the global {{c2::errno}}.

concepts.L1: C has no exceptions. A function signals failure in its return value - NULL, -1, EOF or a nonzero code - and most library functions and every system-call wrapper also set errno to a code saying why. Nothing forces the caller to look: checking every return is the programmer's job, and the compiler does not enforce it.
concepts.L2: errno is meaningful only right after a call whose return value said it failed. No library function ever zeroes it, and a successful call may set it nonzero, so read without a failure indicator it is stale. Where the sentinel is itself a legal result - strtol returns LONG_MAX on overflow - set errno = 0 first, then test ERANGE.
concepts.L3: errno is not a variable but a macro naming a per-thread int lvalue (C11 7.5; glibc expands it to (*__errno_location())), so two threads' failures never overwrite each other. On Linux the value comes from the kernel: a failed system call returns -errno in rax, and the libc wrapper, seeing a value between -4095 and -1, negates it into errno and returns -1. The return value is the signal; errno is only the reason. No function ever zeroes errno and any may set it, so: test the documented indicator, read errno at once, and save it (int saved = errno;) before cleanup calls such as close, which can fail and replace it. perror prints the prefix, a colon, then strerror(errno). Without destructors, one goto-cleanup label per function releases every resource on every error path once; exceptions exist to make an ignored error loud. See os:The syscall ABI: registers, errno and the libc wrapper.

L4.prompt_tpl: FILE *f = fopen("{p}", "r"); char buf[64]; fgets(buf, 64, f);  What is missing and what happens?
L4.answer: fopen's NULL return is unchecked; if the file is missing, fgets dereferences NULL and the program crashes with SIGSEGV rather than reporting the real problem.
L4.explanation: The crash location is fgets, but the fault is the unchecked fopen. Passing NULL to fgets is undefined behaviour; glibc on Linux dereferences it and the process dies with SIGSEGV (verified with gcc on x86-64). Reading errors backwards from the crash site to the unchecked call is the core C debugging skill. The fix is if (f == NULL) then perror("fopen") and return.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux (LP64, gcc, glibc) a program runs: errno = 0; long v = strtol("{s}", &end, 10); What are v and errno afterwards?
L4.answer: v is LONG_MAX, 9223372036854775807, and errno is ERANGE
L4.explanation: strtol never wraps: on overflow it returns LONG_MAX (or LONG_MIN for a negative overflow) and sets errno to ERANGE (C17 7.22.1.4). Every draw here exceeds $2^{63} - 1$, the largest 64-bit long. Because LONG_MAX is also a legal result, only errno can tell the two apart, which is exactly why the idiom clears errno before the call. Verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux: all three strings give 9223372036854775807 with errno 34 (ERANGE).
options: v is LONG_MAX, 9223372036854775807, and errno is ERANGE
v is 0 and errno is EINVAL
v silently wraps to a negative number and errno is unchanged

L4.prompt_tpl: On Linux with glibc, FILE *f = fopen("{p}", "r"); returns NULL because no such file exists. The next statement is perror("fopen"); What exact line appears on stderr?
L4.answer: fopen: No such file or directory
L4.explanation: perror(s) writes s, then a colon and a space, then strerror(errno), then a newline, to stderr. fopen on a missing path fails with errno ENOENT, whose glibc text is 'No such file or directory'. The path itself is not printed unless you put it in the prefix, which is why real code usually builds the message with fprintf(stderr, "%s: %s", path, strerror(errno)). Verified on x86-64 Linux with gcc.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C program (x86-64 Linux, gcc) includes stdio.h, stdlib.h and errno.h. Its main declares char *end; and then runs, in order: errno = 0; long v = strtol("{n}kg", &end, 10); printf("%ld %d\n", v, errno); Two numbers are printed. Answer with the first one, the value of v.
L4.answer: v is the leading number: 42kg prints 42 0, -15kg prints -15 0, 7kg prints 7 0, 1000kg prints 1000 0, 0kg prints 0 0 (verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux).
L4.explanation: strtol converts the longest valid prefix and stops at the first character that cannot belong to the number, leaving end pointing at the 'kg'. Trailing garbage is not a failure: errno stays 0 and no ERANGE occurs. If you need to reject '42kg' you must test *end != 0 yourself; the library only reports what it converted, and its error channel is reserved for overflow.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C program (x86-64 Linux, gcc, glibc) includes stdio.h, stdlib.h and errno.h. main declares char *end; then runs, in order: errno = 0; strtol("{s}", &end, 10); long v = strtol("42", &end, 10); printf("%ld %d\n", v, errno == ERANGE); What exact line is printed?
L4.explanation: The first strtol overflows and sets errno to ERANGE. The second converts 42 perfectly, but a successful call never clears errno, so errno == ERANGE is still true and the program prints 42 1. Read errno only immediately after a call whose return value signalled failure, and reset it to 0 before each call whose sentinel is a legal value. Verified by running the program with gcc on x86-64 Linux for all three draws.

L4.prompt_tpl: int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY); If fd is negative the code then runs, in order: {cleanup}; perror("open"); return -1; The log sometimes reports open failing with a reason that makes no sense for open. What is the bug and what is the fix?
L4.answer: The cleanup call sits between the failure and perror. close, fclose and unlink are themselves calls that can fail and overwrite errno (for example a bad descriptor gives EBADF), so perror reports the cleanup's error instead of open's. Fix: int saved = errno; immediately after the failed call, then do the cleanup, then errno = saved; before perror, or print strerror(saved) directly.
L4.explanation: errno is one global (per-thread) slot, and every function that can fail is entitled to write it. Anything you run between the failing call and the report can clobber the reason; this includes cleanup, logging and even a successful call, which the standard allows to set errno nonzero. Verified on Linux: open on a missing file followed by close(999) makes perror print 'open: Bad file descriptor'. Save errno first.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux the open system call fails and the kernel places the raw value {raw} in rax. Derive what the glibc wrapper does with it: what value ends up in errno, and what does open() return to the C caller? Answer with the errno value.
L4.answer: errno = -raw and open returns -1: -2 gives errno 2 (ENOENT), -13 gives 13 (EACCES), -12 gives 12 (ENOMEM), -17 gives 17 (EEXIST), -21 gives 21 (EISDIR).
L4.explanation: The kernel has no errno; it returns a single integer in rax, and encodes failure as the negated error number. The wrapper tests whether rax lies between -4095 and -1; if so it stores the negation in the thread's errno slot and returns -1, otherwise it returns rax unchanged. That is why a real result can never be confused with an error: kernel results are never in that range. Verified with a raw syscall instruction on x86-64 Linux (open of a missing path leaves -2 in rax). See os:The syscall ABI: registers, errno and the libc wrapper.

L4.prompt_tpl: A production log from a Linux/glibc service contains the line '{fn}: Success'. The service treats this as a fatal error and exits. Explain what value errno held, what that proves about the call that preceded perror, name the specific misreading of {fn}'s return value that produces it, and give the fix.
L4.answer: errno was 0, so no call had failed: perror was run on a path where the return value did not indicate an error. read and recv return 0 at end-of-file or orderly connection shutdown, and fgets returns NULL at end-of-file, none of which sets errno; the code treated end-of-data as failure (or tested errno instead of the return value). Fix: read/recv fail only when they return -1 (0 is EOF; a short count is not an error); for fgets, on NULL call ferror(f) to separate an error from feof(f), and only then consult errno.
L4.explanation: 'Success' is strerror(0). It cannot arise from a failed call, because a failure always leaves a nonzero code, and no library function ever zeroes errno. So the message proves the program reached its error path by misreading a legitimate return: 0 from read or recv means end of data, NULL from fgets means EOF unless ferror says otherwise. Verified: read at EOF then perror prints 'read: Success'; fgets on /dev/null then perror prints 'fgets: Success'.

prereqs: A C program, compiled and run

sections.note: You have not learned one until you have written it and broken it.

L0.body:
ADT  'stack':  push(x), pop() -> x, is_empty()
implementations: Python list | C array + top index | linked list
Same contract. Different memory behaviour, same big-O.
L0.cloze: An {{c1::ADT}} specifies operations and their contract; the {{c2::implementation}} decides the memory layout and constants.

concepts.L1: An abstract data type is a set of operations and their guarantees. A data structure is one concrete realisation of it. A stack is an ADT; an array-backed stack and a linked stack are two data structures satisfying it.
concepts.L2: Interview and textbook answers collapse the two, which is why people believe 'a queue is a linked list'. Python's list is an ADT-agnostic dynamic array, so using it as a queue gives O(n) pops from the front - correct behaviour, wrong complexity. collections.deque is the right structure for the same ADT.
concepts.L3: An ADT is a specification: which operations exist and what each must return, silent on memory. For a stack: pop after push(x) yields x; is_empty holds when every push has been popped. Whatever satisfies them is a correct stack - an array with a top index, or a chain of nodes. It holds only if the layout is hidden: a C header declaring just typedef struct Stack Stack and functions on pointers to it, a Python class used only via its methods. Callers cannot compile against the representation, so a swap is invisible: that is where real performance work happens - same interface, same asymptotics, ten times the throughput because one layout is contiguous and the other chases pointers ('Array versus linked list: the real trade'). It also says what a bound describes: 'O(1) push' is about an implementation; a stack whose push does insert(0, x) is still a stack. The ADT promises LIFO order only.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need a FIFO queue in Python with {n} enqueue and dequeue operations. Compare list.pop(0) against collections.deque.popleft() in big-O and total work.
L4.answer: list.pop(0) is O(n) per call because every remaining element shifts left, so n operations cost O(n**2) (about 5e7 or 5e11 element moves). deque.popleft() is O(1), total O(n).
L4.explanation: Identical ADT, identical output, quadratically different cost. Recognising 'pop from the front' as the tell is the practical skill.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these names an abstract data type - a set of operations and their guarantees - rather than a data structure, a concrete layout in memory?
L4.answer: Priority queue
L4.explanation: A priority queue is a contract: insert(x) and extract_min() with the promise that extract_min returns the smallest element inserted and not yet removed. Nothing in that says how it is stored. A binary heap is one layout that satisfies it (an array with the completeness invariant, O(log n) per operation); a sorted linked list is another (O(n) insert, O(1) extract). An open-addressing hash table is a layout too, one realisation of the map ADT. The tell is whether the name describes what you can do or how the bytes are arranged.
options: Priority queue
Binary heap
Open-addressing hash table

L4.answer: Both implementations yield the last two pushed values in reverse order, so out is [last, second-last, last, second-last]. [1, 2, 3, 4] -> [4, 3, 4, 3]; [7, 8, 9] -> [9, 8, 9, 8]; [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] -> [9, 8, 9, 8].
L4.explanation: One stores a contiguous Python list and pops from its end; the other stores a chain of tuples and unlinks the head. The caller loop cannot tell them apart, because it uses only push and pop - that is what 'same contract' means. LIFO order is the ADT's whole promise, so both print the most recent push first, then the one before it. Output verified by running the code on CPython 3.

L4.prompt_tpl: A teammate replaces every list in a codebase with collections.deque 'because deque is O(1) at both ends and list is not'. A hot loop reads xs[i] for i near the middle of a million-element sequence. What happens to that loop?
L4.answer: It gets far slower: deque indexing away from the ends is O(n), because CPython's deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks that must be walked to reach the middle
L4.explanation: deque does support xs[i], but the docs say it plainly: indexed access is O(1) at both ends and slows to O(n) in the middle. Measured here on CPython 3: d[500000] on a million-element deque took about 34 microseconds against 0.04 for a list, roughly 800 times slower. Same sequence ADT, two structures, and each is O(1) for a different operation set. The right structure is decided by which operations dominate, never by one bound in isolation.
options: It gets far slower: deque indexing away from the ends is O(n), because CPython's deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks that must be walked to reach the middle
Nothing changes: deque supports the same indexing as list and both are O(1) by index
It raises TypeError: deque does not support indexing at all

L4.prompt_tpl: 'A stack has O(1) push.' Is that a claim about the stack ADT or about an implementation of it? Give a concrete stack implementation that is correct - every pop returns the right element - yet for which the claim is false, and state what the ADT itself actually guarantees.
L4.answer: About an implementation. Counterexample: a stack stored in a Python list whose push does xs.insert(0, x) and whose pop does xs.pop(0). Every pop returns the most recently pushed element still present, so it is a correct LIFO stack, but both operations shift the whole list and cost O(n). The ADT guarantees only ordering - pop returns the most recent push not yet popped, is_empty is true exactly when nothing remains - and says nothing about cost.
L4.explanation: Complexity is a property of a data structure, never of an ADT: the specification fixes what the operations return, and any layout that honours that is correct, however slow. The array-with-top-index and linked implementations happen to give O(1) push, which is why the claim is usually stated as if it were about stacks in general. The habit to build is asking, for every stated bound, which implementation it describes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Estimate, then verify if you can. A Python program enqueues {n} items with list.append and then dequeues all of them with list.pop(0). Each pop shifts every remaining element left by one slot; assume one shifted element costs about {t} ns of memmove time. Roughly how many seconds do the dequeues take in total? Answer in seconds.
L4.explanation: The first pop shifts n - 1 elements, the next n - 2, down to 0: an arithmetic series summing to n(n-1)/2, about $n^{2}/2$. Multiplying by the per-element cost gives seconds for a task that deque.popleft() finishes in milliseconds. Measured here on CPython 3: 100000 pops from the front took 12.5 s (about 2.5 ns per shifted element on this machine) while 100000 popleft calls took 5 ms. Same queue ADT, quadratically different structure.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, gcc, x86-64 Linux. stack.h declares: typedef struct Stack Stack; Stack *stack_new(void); void stack_push(Stack *s, int x); int stack_pop(Stack *s); int stack_empty(const Stack *s); The struct body (int *data; int top; int cap;) now lives only in stack.c. Yesterday the header defined struct Stack in full and everything compiled. main.c includes stack.h and contains the loop: while (s->top != 0) printf("%d\n", stack_pop(s)); Today gcc reports: main.c:6: error: invalid use of incomplete typedef 'Stack'. Where is the bug, what is the one-line fix, and why is this compile error the correct outcome rather than a regression?
L4.answer: The bug is in main.c: it reaches through the ADT boundary to the representation (s->top) instead of using the operations. Fix: while (!stack_empty(s)). The header is the contract; with only an incomplete type visible, callers cannot name any member, so stack.c is free to switch to a linked list or rename fields without touching a single caller. The error is that boundary being enforced by the compiler - it caught the one caller that had silently depended on the array layout.
L4.explanation: An opaque pointer is how C spells 'abstract data type': the header exposes the operations and an incomplete struct, the .c file owns the layout. Yesterday's full definition let main.c compile against the layout, which is exactly the coupling that makes swapping implementations impossible. Reproduced here with gcc 13.3: the s->top loop fails with 'invalid use of incomplete typedef', and the stack_empty version compiles and prints 2 then 1. The compile error is cheaper than the runtime bug it would have become after a linked-list rewrite.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design a FIFO queue using only two stacks (push, pop, is_empty). State enqueue and dequeue, then prove that any sequence of n enqueues and n dequeues performs at most 4n stack operations in total, so dequeue is amortised O(1) even though one dequeue can cost O(n). Which Whetstone concept does that kind of bound belong to?
L4.answer: enqueue(x): push x onto stack IN. dequeue(): if OUT is empty, pop every element of IN and push it onto OUT (reversing the order, so the oldest is on top); then pop OUT. Each element is pushed onto IN once, moved IN to OUT once (it moves only when OUT is empty, and never moves back), and popped from OUT once: 4 stack operations per element, at most 4n in total. So the average over the sequence is at most 4 per operation - amortised O(1) - while a single dequeue that triggers a transfer costs O(k) for the k elements in IN. This is the bound described in 'Worst, average and amortised'.
L4.explanation: The queue ADT is implemented on top of the stack ADT, never touching how the stacks store their elements - abstraction stacks. The proof is accounting per element, not per operation: charge four operations to each element when it is enqueued, and every transfer is paid for in advance. Checked here by simulating 2000 random interleavings of n enqueues and n dequeues: the count never exceeded 4n. The worst single dequeue is still O(n); amortised analysis promises nothing about latency spikes, as 'The dynamic array and amortised append' warns.

concepts.t: The dynamic array and amortised append

L0.cloze: Growth must be {{c1::multiplicative}} (double the capacity), not additive, to make append O(1) {{c2::amortised}}.

concepts.L1: A dynamic array stores elements contiguously in an oversized buffer with a separate length. Append writes into the spare capacity in O(1); when full it allocates a larger buffer and copies. Doubling makes the copies rare enough that append is O(1) amortised.
concepts.L2: Amortised O(1) is not average-case O(1) over random inputs - it is a worst-case guarantee over any sequence of n operations. Individual appends still cost O(n). That matters for latency: a real-time system sees the spike even though throughput is fine.
concepts.L3: Doubling from capacity 1, copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., so after n appends the total copied is $1 + 2 + \cdots + 2^{k-1} = 2^{k} - 1$, with $2^{k}$ the first power of two at or above n: under 2n. With the n writes, n appends cost under 3n moves, a constant per append. That is the amortised bound: a guarantee over the sequence, not an expectation over inputs. Additive growth by k breaks it: copies at sizes k, 2k, ..., n-k sum to $n(n-k)/(2k)$, quadratic. Any ratio above 1 restores linearity; the ratio trades copy frequency against slack (up to half the buffer idle) and allocator reuse: with factor 2 each new block exceeds all freed blocks combined, so none is recycled; folly's fbvector and Java's ArrayList use 1.5. CPython's list_resize allocates new size + new size/8 + 6, rounded down to a multiple of 4: about 1.125x. 'Worst, average and amortised' makes the guarantee precise.

L4.prompt_tpl: Starting from capacity 1 and doubling, how many elements are copied in total while appending {n} items?
L4.answer: Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ... up to the last power of two below n, so the total is $2^{\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil} - 1$, which is n-1 when n is a power of two: 8 -> 7, 16 -> 15, 1000 -> 1023, 1024 -> 1023.
L4.explanation: A geometric series with ratio 2 sums to one less than its next term, so the copies total just under the final capacity, which is under 2n. Total work per append averages under 3 element moves (2 copies plus the write), a constant: that is the whole amortised argument. For n = 1000 the last copy moves 512 elements, so the total is 1023, not 999; n-1 is only right for powers of two.

L4.prompt_tpl: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles its capacity whenever an append finds it full. After {n} appends, what is the capacity of the buffer?
L4.answer: The first power of two at or above n, $2^{\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil}$: 5 -> 8, 33 -> 64, 100 -> 128, 1000 -> 1024.
L4.explanation: Capacity only ever takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., and it doubles exactly when the size catches up with it, so after n appends the capacity is the smallest power of two that is at least n. Just after a doubling almost half the buffer is empty; just before one it is full. That slack, at most a factor of 2, is the price paid for rare copies.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3. The Vec class from L0 is modified so that the DOUBLE branch also does grows += 1 on a global counter that starts at 0. Then:

v = Vec()
for i in range({n}):
    v.append(i)
print(grows)

What number is printed?
L4.answer: $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$ doublings: 8 -> 3, 100 -> 7, 1000 -> 10, 33 -> 6. Verified by running the code on Python 3.11.
L4.explanation: The buffer starts at capacity 1 and doubles when the size reaches 1, 2, 4, ..., so the branch runs once per power of two below n: for n = 100 at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, seven times. Logarithmically many resizes is what makes their total cost linear: the last one dominates and the earlier ones halve away.

L4.prompt_tpl: A dynamic array doubles when full. Which statement about the cost of append is correct?
L4.answer: Every append is O(1) amortised, but a single append can cost O(n) when it triggers a copy
L4.explanation: The doubling copy moves every element, so that one append costs O(n). But it happens only when the size hits a power of two, so across any n appends the copies total under 2n and the average per append is a constant. Amortised O(1) describes that average over the sequence, never a bound on one operation; the log n count of doublings is the number of expensive appends, not the cost of each.
options: Every append is O(1) amortised, but a single append can cost O(n) when it triggers a copy
Every append is O(1) in the worst case, because the spare capacity is always there
Append is O(log n), because the number of doublings grows with the logarithm of n

L4.prompt_tpl: What breaks if growth is additive? A dynamic array starts with capacity {k} and, whenever an append finds it full, allocates a buffer exactly {k} slots larger and copies everything across. How many elements are copied in total during {n} appends?
L4.explanation: With additive growth the copies form an arithmetic series, not a geometric one: k + 2k + ... + (n-k) has n/k - 1 terms averaging n/2, so the total is about $n^{2}/(2k)$ - quadratic, and roughly n/(2k) copies per append instead of a constant. Raising k only shrinks the constant. Doubling makes each copy pay for the doublings before it; adding k never does.

L4.prompt_tpl: Estimate, then verify. A doubling dynamic array holds {n} elements of {w} bytes each and its buffer is exactly full. The next append allocates the new buffer and copies before freeing the old one. At the moment of the copy, how many bytes do the two buffers occupy together?
L4.explanation: The copy needs both buffers alive at once: the full old one and the newly allocated one twice its size, so peak memory is three times the data, not two. This is the L2 latency point in space rather than time: throughput is fine but a real-time or memory-tight system sees the spike at the instant of the resize. Pre-sizing the buffer removes both spikes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A trading system appends events to a doubling dynamic array and must answer every event within a fixed deadline. A profiler shows one append per few million taking thousands of times longer than the rest. Which diagnosis is right?
L4.answer: Expected: amortised O(1) bounds the total over the sequence, not the single append that copies the whole buffer
L4.explanation: The slow appends are the doublings, each copying every element. The amortised bound only says their cost, spread over all appends, is constant per append; it says nothing about the worst single one. Additive growth makes copies more frequent and the total quadratic, so it is worse, not better. Fixes are reserving capacity up front or an incremental scheme that copies a few elements per append.
options: Expected: amortised O(1) bounds the total over the sequence, not the single append that copies the whole buffer
A bug: amortised O(1) guarantees that no single append exceeds a constant, so the copy must be implemented wrongly
Switching to additive growth by a fixed constant would remove the spikes without changing the total cost

L4.prompt_tpl: An unfamiliar growth rule. CPython 3.11's list_resize computes the new capacity as (newsize + (newsize >> 3) + 6) & ~3, where newsize is the length after the append, >> 3 is integer division by 8, and & ~3 rounds down to a multiple of 4. A list whose capacity is exactly {c} elements receives one more append. What is its new capacity?
L4.answer: newsize = c+1, then add newsize/8 (rounded down) and 6, then round down to a multiple of 4: 8 -> 16, 16 -> 24, 32 -> 40, 52 -> 64, 64 -> 76. Matches the sequence sys.getsizeof shows on Python 3.11.
L4.explanation: For c = 32: newsize 33, plus 33 >> 3 = 4, plus 6, gives 43; clearing the low two bits gives 40. The ratio is roughly 9/8 at large sizes, with the +6 mattering only for tiny lists, so CPython copies about eight times more often than doubling would but wastes at most about an eighth of the buffer. Any constant ratio above 1 keeps append amortised O(1); only the constant changes.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3. A programmer builds a list of n items with

result = []
for x in source:
    result = result + [x]

and finds it far slower than result.append(x). In terms of the dynamic-array model, what is the total work for n items and why?
L4.answer: Theta of n squared: result + [x] builds a fresh list of length i+1 every time, copying all i existing elements, so the copies form 1 + 2 + ... + n
L4.explanation: The + operator returns a new list; nothing is amortised because no spare capacity ever survives to the next step. Every step copies every existing reference, an arithmetic series summing to about n squared over 2. append (and += on a list, which calls extend in place) writes into the over-allocated buffer and copies only at resizes, so its total is linear. Same bug, same fix, for strings built with s = s + ch.
options: Theta of n squared: result + [x] builds a fresh list of length i+1 every time, copying all i existing elements, so the copies form 1 + 2 + ... + n
Theta of n: the interpreter recognises the pattern and grows the existing buffer in place, so it is just the same amortised append with more overhead
Theta of n log n: each concatenation doubles the buffer, so there are log n copies of n elements each

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove the amortised bound by the accounting method. Each append on a doubling dynamic array (capacity 1 at the start) is charged a fixed number of credits; the actual cost is 1 per element written or copied. Find the smallest whole number of credits per append that is never overdrawn, and show how the credits are spent so that every doubling copy is already paid for when it happens.
L4.answer: Three credits per append. One pays for writing the new element. One is saved on the new element to pay for copying it at the next doubling. One is saved to pay for copying an old element - one that has already been copied once and so has no credit left. Just after a doubling to capacity 2m the buffer holds m elements, all with zero credit. The next m appends fill it and each deposits 2 credits: one on itself and one on an old element, so by the time the buffer holds 2m elements every element carries exactly one credit and the copy of 2m elements at the next doubling is paid in full. Two credits fail: the old half would have nothing to pay for its copy.
L4.explanation: The accounting method assigns each operation an amortised charge; as long as the bank never goes negative, the sum of charges bounds the sum of real costs. Here the charge is 3, so n appends cost at most 3n element moves - the same constant as the closed-form sum 2^k - 1 copies plus n writes. The method matters because it works when the sequence is not known in advance, which is what makes the bound a guarantee rather than an average; see 'Worst, average and amortised'.

L0.cloze: Inserting at the head of a linked list is O({{c1::1}}); reaching element k is O({{c2::k}}).

concepts.L1: A chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next. Inserting after a held node, or unlinking the node after it, is an O(1) pointer write; reaching index k is O(k) because there is no arithmetic from index to address, and a node cannot find its own predecessor.
concepts.L2: 'O(1) insertion' is only true once you already hold the node. Inserting at index k costs O(k) to walk there, so inserting into the middle of a linked list is not faster than into an array - the array's O(n) memmove is contiguous and often wins outright.
concepts.L3: Deleting a node means rewriting the pointer that leads to it, and that pointer lives in the predecessor, which a singly linked node cannot reach. So a correct deletion either carries a prev variable, with a special case when the target is the head, or starts from a sentinel node whose next is the real head, so the head is no longer special; Python has no address-of, hence the sentinel. Each node is its own heap object: a 16-byte C node sits in a 32-byte glibc chunk, four times an array's 8 bytes per value, and a CPython __slots__ node is 48 bytes before the int it holds. Reaching index k is k dependent loads - node k+1's address is unknown until node k arrives, so the prefetcher cannot help and each step is a likely cache miss (see 'The memory hierarchy'). The list earns its keep only where you hold nodes by reference: O(1) splice at a held position, and stable node addresses.

L4.prompt_tpl: To delete the node with value {v} from a singly linked list, someone writes: n = head; while n.val != {v}: n = n.nxt; n = n.nxt. Why does the list not change?
L4.answer: It rebinds the local variable n, not the previous node's nxt field. You must track prev and set prev.nxt = n.nxt (and handle deleting the head).
L4.explanation: The list is defined by the links, not by your traversal variable. This is the same names-versus-objects rule from Python, now with structural consequences.

L4.prompt_tpl: A singly linked list has {n} nodes. Starting with n = head, how many times must the statement n = n.nxt execute before n refers to the node at 0-based index {k}? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: Exactly $k$ link-follows: k=0 -> 0, k=7 -> 7, k=250 -> 250, k=999 -> 999. The length n of the list is irrelevant as long as k < n.
L4.explanation: There is no arithmetic from index to address: the only way to reach node $k$ is to follow $k$ pointers from the head, one dependent load each. An array computes base + $k \cdot$ size in one instruction. This is the whole reason indexing a linked list is $O(k)$ and why 'insert at index k' is not the $O(1)$ operation people remember it as.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python 3. With the Node class from L0 (fields val and nxt, constructor Node(val, nxt=None)), this runs: head = None, then for v in [{a}, {b}, {c}]: head = Node(v, head). Then it traverses from head, collecting str(n.val) for each node, and prints them joined by single spaces. What is printed?
L4.explanation: Each iteration makes the new node the head and points it at the old head, so the last value pushed is the first one reached: push-front reverses insertion order. Verified with CPython 3.11: [1, 2, 3] prints '3 2 1'. A push-front loop is $O(1)$ per element and builds the list backwards; to keep insertion order you need either a tail pointer or a final reversal.

L4.prompt_tpl: You hold a reference x to one node in the middle of a singly linked list, and nothing else: no head, no predecessor. Which operation is O(1)?
L4.answer: Insert a new node immediately after x
L4.explanation: Inserting after x is two pointer writes: new.nxt = x.nxt; x.nxt = new. Unlinking x requires changing the predecessor's nxt, and the predecessor is reachable only by walking from the head, $O(k)$. The 'copy the next node's value into x and unlink the next node' trick fakes it, but fails when x is the last node and silently invalidates any other reference to x.nxt. The links only run one way, so only 'after' is cheap.
options: Insert a new node immediately after x
Unlink x itself, so a traversal from the head no longer visits it
Find the node immediately before x

L4.prompt_tpl: In C on x86-64 Linux a node is a struct holding a long value (8 bytes) and a pointer to the next node (8 bytes). Ignoring allocator overhead, how many bytes do the nodes of a {n}-element list occupy, compared with the 8 bytes per element an array of longs would use? Answer with the total node bytes.
L4.answer: $16n$ bytes: n=1000 -> 16000; n=100000 -> 1600000; n=1000000 -> 16000000. Twice the $8n$ bytes of the array, before allocator overhead.
L4.explanation: Every node carries the 8-byte next pointer in addition to its 8-byte payload, so the list spends at least twice the memory of the array for the same values. That is the floor: the allocator adds its own overhead per node (see the tier-2 item), and CPython objects are larger still. Memory per element is one of the two real costs of a linked list; the other is the dependent load per step.

L4.prompt_tpl: x86-64 Linux, glibc malloc. Each node is malloc'd separately and holds {p} bytes of payload plus an 8-byte next pointer. glibc adds an 8-byte size word to every request, rounds the chunk up to a multiple of 16, and never hands out a chunk smaller than 32 bytes. How many bytes of heap do the {n} nodes of the list occupy, allocator overhead included? Answer with the total bytes.
L4.answer: chunk = $\max(32, 16\lceil (p+8+8)/16 \rceil)$, total = chunk $\cdot n$. p=8: 32-byte chunks -> 32000 (n=1000), 3200000 (n=100000); p=16: 32 -> 32000 / 3200000; p=24: 48 -> 48000 / 4800000; p=40: 64 -> 64000 / 6400000. Measured with glibc 2.39: consecutive mallocs of 16, 24, 32 and 48 bytes were 32, 32, 48 and 64 bytes apart.
L4.explanation: A 16-byte node (8 payload + 8 pointer) costs a 32-byte chunk: the request plus the 8-byte size word is 24, rounded up to 32. So the list spends four times what an array of 8-byte values spends, not the two times the struct size suggests, and the p=8 and p=16 cases cost exactly the same. This is implementation-defined (jemalloc and tcmalloc use size classes with out-of-band metadata), but 'a small allocation costs more than its payload' holds for every allocator.

L4.prompt_tpl: Holding only a reference x to a node (no head, no predecessor), someone 'deletes' it in Python with: x.val = x.nxt.val; x.nxt = x.nxt.nxt. It passes the test for value {v} in the middle of a list. Name two distinct situations in which this code is wrong, and say what actually happens in each.
L4.answer: (1) x is the last node: x.nxt is None, so x.nxt.val raises AttributeError - and there is no way at all to unlink the last node without its predecessor. (2) Any other reference to the successor node (x.nxt before the trick) now points at a node that has been silently unlinked, and any other reference to x now sees a different value; the trick swaps identities rather than removing the node, breaking the 'stable node address' property that is the reason to use a linked list. (Also: with a tail pointer, the tail becomes wrong when x.nxt was the tail.)
L4.explanation: The trick works by overwriting x with its successor and dropping the successor, so the object that disappears from the chain is not the one asked for. It fails outright at the tail and quietly corrupts every outside reference elsewhere. Real deletion needs the predecessor's link - a prev variable, a sentinel, or a doubly linked list.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python 3, Node class from L0. The list is head = Node({a}, Node({b}, Node({c}, Node({d})))). Someone reverses it in place with: prev = None; cur = head; then while cur is not None: cur.nxt = prev; prev = cur; cur = cur.nxt (three statements in that order, one per line); then head = prev. Afterwards the program traverses from head and prints the values joined by spaces. What is printed?
L4.explanation: The loop overwrites cur.nxt with prev before reading it, so on the first iteration cur.nxt becomes None, prev becomes the first node, and cur = cur.nxt is None: the loop ends after one iteration with head pointing at a one-node list. The rest of the original chain is unreachable and, in CPython, garbage-collected. Verified with CPython 3.11: for 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 the output is '1'. The correct loop saves the successor first: nxt = cur.nxt; cur.nxt = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt, which prints '4 3 2 1'. Every in-place link rewrite must read the old link before destroying it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design a singly linked list that supports push_front, push_back and pop_front all in O(1) worst case for a list that will hold about {n} items. State what extra state you keep beyond head, which of the four operations push_front, push_back, pop_front, pop_back still costs O(n) and exactly why, and what change to the node makes it O(1).
L4.answer: Keep a tail pointer alongside head. push_back: tail.nxt = new; tail = new (and head = tail = new when empty). push_front and pop_front touch only head (pop_front must also clear tail when the list becomes empty). pop_back stays O(n): it must set the predecessor of tail's nxt to None, and the predecessor is reachable only by walking from head, because links run one way. Adding a prev pointer to each node (a doubly linked list) makes pop_back O(1) at the cost of an extra pointer per node and two more writes per insertion. This is why collections.deque is a doubly linked structure and why a stack only ever needs head.
L4.explanation: A tail pointer buys O(1) append but not O(1) removal at the tail, because removal always needs the predecessor of the removed node. Compare 'The dynamic array and amortised append': the array gives O(1) append only amortised, but O(1) pop at the back trivially. The invariants matter more than the pointers: every operation must keep head, tail and the empty case consistent, and forgetting tail on the last pop_front is the classic bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: C, x86-64 Linux, gcc. struct node has fields long val and struct node *next; the list head is a variable head. Deletion of the first node holding value {v} is written without a prev variable: struct node **pp = &head; while (*pp != NULL && (*pp)->val != {v}) pp = &(*pp)->next; if (*pp != NULL) *pp = (*pp)->next; (ignore freeing). Explain what pp points at on each iteration, why this needs no special case for deleting the head node, and why the same trick cannot be written in Python with the L0 Node class.
L4.answer: pp always points at a pointer variable that leads to the current node: first at the variable head itself, then at the next field inside each successive node. Deleting is one assignment through pp: *pp = (*pp)->next overwrites whichever link led to the victim. Since head is just another pointer-sized variable, deleting the first node is the same write as deleting any other, so there is no special case and no prev. Python cannot do this because it has no address-of: a name or attribute cannot be referred to, only the object it is bound to. n = n.nxt rebinds a local name; nothing you hold can stand for 'the slot in the previous node'. Hence Python uses a sentinel node whose nxt is the real head, or a prev variable.
L4.explanation: This is 'Pointers: address-of and dereference' applied to structure: a pointer-to-pointer names the link rather than the node, and links are what deletion changes. The idiom is Torvalds' 'good taste' example. Python's model ('Names are bound to objects') offers only references to objects, never to variables or fields, so the head special case reappears and is usually removed with a sentinel.

concepts.t: Array versus linked list: the real trade

L0.body:
array      linked list
index k          O(1)        O(k)
insert front     O(n)        O(1)
insert at held   O(n)        O(1)
memory/elem      4-8 B       24-32 B (Python: far more)
cache            excellent   terrible
L0.cloze: An array gives O(1) {{c1::indexing}} because address = base + i * size; a linked list cannot, because its nodes are not {{c2::contiguous}}.

concepts.L1: Arrays give constant-time indexing and perfect locality but pay O(n) for insertion away from the end. Linked lists give O(1) splicing at a held position and stable node addresses, but no indexing and one cache miss per step.
concepts.L2: The big-O table understates the array by an order of magnitude. Walking 1M linked nodes costs about 1M cache misses; 1M contiguous ints cost 62.5k line fetches, prefetched. Arrays often win even at middle insertion into thousands of elements, since memmove runs at bandwidth.
concepts.L3: Insert into the middle of a 10,000-element int32 sequence. The array shifts 5,000 elements: 20 KB of memmove, streamed at 10-20 GB/s as independent, prefetched loads - about 1-2 microseconds. The list first walks 5,000 nodes; each load needs the address the previous one returned, so nothing overlaps or prefetches. With nodes scattered across a cold heap each hop is a DRAM miss at ~80 ns: roughly 400 microseconds, 200-400x slower. If the list is warm (10,000 nodes at 32 B is 312 KiB, L2-resident) a hop is ~4 ns and the gap shrinks to ~20x; it never closes. Big-O agrees once you count the walk: insertion at index k is O(n) moves for the array and O(k) hops for the list, both linear. The O(1) row is for a held node: compare 'held position' with 'index'. Where you hold the node the list wins: 'LRU and its failure mode' puts a hash map over a doubly linked list for O(1) move-to-front.

L4.prompt_tpl: Choose a structure and justify: you must maintain {n} items, appending at the end and reading by index constantly, never inserting in the middle.
L4.answer: Dynamic array. Indexing is O(1) versus O(k); append is O(1) amortised for the array and O(1) for the list only if it keeps a tail pointer (O(n) walk otherwise); and the array is contiguous, so scans run near memory bandwidth. A linked list has no advantage in this access pattern.
L4.explanation: Pick the structure from the operation mix. The linked list only earns its keep when you hold node references and splice without traversing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A contiguous array holds {n} elements. Inserting a new element at index {k} (0-based) must shift every element from index {k} onward up by one slot. How many existing elements are moved?
L4.explanation: The elements at indices k .. n-1 move, which is n - k of them: inserting at the front moves all n, appending moves none. That is why append is the array's cheap operation and insert at 0 its expensive one. The moves are one contiguous memmove, so the constant per element is a fraction of a nanosecond, against a dependent load per node when a list walks to the same index.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CPython list of {n} elements keeps one 8-byte pointer per element in a contiguous buffer. lst.insert(0, x) shifts every existing pointer up by one slot. How many bytes of pointers are moved?
L4.explanation: A Python list is a dynamic array of object pointers, not a linked list: inserting at the front is O(n), moving 8 bytes per element. At roughly 10 GB/s, 8 MB takes under a millisecond, which is why the cost hides until it sits inside a loop. The objects themselves never move, only the pointers to them. collections.deque exists for O(1) insertion at the front.

L4.prompt_tpl: For which operation is a linked list genuinely O(1) while an array is O(n)?
L4.answer: Inserting a new node right after a node you already hold a reference to
L4.explanation: The O(1) row of the table is for a held position: you hold the node, so the splice is two pointer writes. Given only a number k, the list must walk k hops first, O(k), while the array moves n - k elements: both linear. Reading index k is O(1) for the array (base + k * size) and O(k) for the list. The honest comparison is always 'held position' versus 'index'.
options: Inserting a new node right after a node you already hold a reference to
Inserting at index k, where k is given as a number
Reading the element at index k

L4.prompt_tpl: A doubly linked list node holds a {w}-byte value plus two 8-byte pointers (prev and next); an array holds only the {w}-byte value per element. Ignoring allocator overhead, how many times the array's per-element memory does the list use? Answer with the ratio.
L4.explanation: Every node pays 16 bytes of links whatever the payload, so small payloads are dominated by overhead: a list of int32 uses 5x the array's memory before the allocator adds its own header and rounds up (glibc turns a 24-byte request into a 32-byte chunk). This is the 'memory/elem' row of the table and one reason a list walk touches far more cache lines than the array scan.

L4.prompt_tpl: Estimate, then check: you insert at the middle of a sequence of {n} elements of {w} bytes each. The array memmoves half the elements at {B} GB/s (1 GB/s = 1 byte per ns). The linked list walks half the nodes at {t} ns per dependent load, then splices in negligible time. Roughly how many times slower is the list than the array? Answer with the ratio.
L4.answer: $tB/w$, independent of n. Array time $(n/2) w / B$ ns, list time $(n/2) t$ ns, and $n/2$ cancels: (w=4, B=10, t=80) -> 200; (w=4, B=20, t=80) -> 400; (w=8, B=10, t=80) -> 100; (w=8, B=20, t=100) -> 250.
L4.explanation: Both costs are linear in n, so n cancels: the ratio is one dependent load divided by the time to stream one element, $t / (w/B)$. That is why 'switch to a list for middle insertion' never becomes right by making n larger; it becomes right only when the walk disappears, that is when you already hold the node. The estimate assumes cold, scattered nodes; a cache-resident list cuts t to 4-15 ns and the ratio to 10-50x, still not 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C you keep a pointer p to element 5 of a dynamic array, then append until the array has to grow (realloc). Separately you keep a pointer q to a node in a linked list and push {m} new nodes at its head. After both, which statement is true?
L4.answer: p may dangle - the buffer was moved and the old block freed - while q is still valid, because list nodes never move
L4.explanation: realloc may return a different block and frees the old one, so p now points into freed memory (a use-after-free) and element 5 lives at newbase + 5 * size. A list node is its own heap allocation and stays put however many nodes are added. This is the 'stable node addresses' half of the trade, and the reason kernel-style intrusive lists and iterators that must survive insertion use linked nodes.
options: p may dangle - the buffer was moved and the old block freed - while q is still valid, because list nodes never move
Both p and q remain valid: neither structure moves existing elements
q may dangle because pushing at the head reallocates the list, while p is safe

L4.prompt_tpl: The L3 estimate charges about 80 ns per hop, the cost of a DRAM miss. A linked list of {n} nodes of {s} bytes each occupies how many KiB in total? Compare with an L2 cache of about 1024 KiB to judge whether the 80 ns assumption holds. Answer in KiB.
L4.explanation: A 10,000-node list at 32 B is 312.5 KiB: it fits in L2, so a warm walk pays about 4 ns per hop, not 80, and the 400x becomes roughly 20x. Only from about 100,000 nodes does the list overflow L2 (and L3 on smaller chips) so that the DRAM figure applies. Always check an estimate's assumption; but note the array wins in every regime, because its loads are independent and prefetched.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program empties a CPython list of {n} elements with a loop that calls lst.pop(0) until the list is empty. Each pop(0) shifts every remaining pointer down by one slot. Derive the total number of pointer moves over the whole loop and give it as a number.
L4.explanation: The first pop moves n - 1 pointers, the next n - 2, down to 0: an arithmetic series summing to $n(n-1)/2$, so an innocent-looking loop is quadratic - five billion moves for 100,000 elements, seconds instead of microseconds. pop() from the end is O(1) per call, and collections.deque, a linked list of fixed-size blocks, makes popleft O(1) while keeping most of the array's locality; that hybrid is the shape most real 'linked' structures take. See 'Worst, average and amortised'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design the storage for an LRU cache of capacity {c}: get(key) must be O(1), and every get must move that key's entry to the most-recent end in O(1). Explain why a plain array fails, why a plain linked list fails, and what combination works, in terms of 'index' versus 'held position'.
L4.answer: A hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency. An array gives O(1) access by index but not by key, and moving an entry to the end shifts O(n) neighbours. A linked list gives O(1) unlink-and-append at the tail once you hold the node, but finding the node by key is an O(n) walk. The map turns the key into a held node in O(1); the doubly linked list (the prev pointer is needed to unlink without walking) then does the O(1) splice. Stable node addresses are what let the map keep pointers to nodes across insertions and evictions. Eviction pops the least-recent end, also O(1). This is what CPython's OrderedDict.move_to_end does underneath.
L4.explanation: This is the case where the linked list earns its keep: an external index (the hash map) supplies the held position, so the walk that dominated the L3 estimate never happens, and node addresses stay valid across inserts so the map's pointers cannot dangle. 'LRU and its failure mode' in the Caching domain builds exactly this structure and shows its cost: the read path writes to a shared list.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague repeats Stroustrup's experiment: insert {n} random integers into a sorted sequence, each at its sorted position found by a linear search from the front, then delete them at random positions found the same way. The linked list loses to the contiguous array at every n, and they object: 'but insertion is O(1) for the list'. Explain what dominates in each structure, in terms of dependent loads and cache lines, and name the one change to the access pattern that would let the list win.
L4.answer: Both structures do an O(n) linear search per operation, and the search dominates; the O(1) splice is negligible next to it. The array's search streams: independent loads, hardware prefetch, 16 int32 per 64-byte cache line, and its O(n) memmove after the search is streamed too. The list's search is n dependent loads - each address comes from the previous node - so nothing can be overlapped or prefetched, and every node costs a whole cache line of which a few bytes are used. The list would win only if the search disappeared: if positions arrived as held node references from an external index, making each operation a pure splice, which is exactly the LRU-cache design.
L4.explanation: The experiment isolates the walk from the splice. The list's advertised O(1) is for the splice; the walk is O(n) in dependent, unprefetchable loads and swamps it. The array's O(n) is in streamed, independent memory traffic that the hardware makes cheap. Stroustrup's point is not that lists are evil but that the comparison must be made on the whole operation, at the machine, not on the one row of the table that flatters the list.

L0.body:
def h(key, nbuckets):
    return hash(key) % nbuckets      # Python's hash(), then fold

# the two required properties:
#   a == b  =>  h(a) == h(b)        (consistency)
#   spreads unequal keys uniformly  (dispersion)
L0.cloze: If a == b then h(a) must equal h(b); the converse need not hold, and two unequal keys sharing a hash is a {{c1::collision}}.

concepts.L1: A hash function maps a key to a fixed-size integer. It must be deterministic and consistent with equality; it should distribute distinct keys as if uniformly at random. It is not a cryptographic requirement unless adversaries pick your keys.
concepts.L2: Equal hashes do not mean equal keys, so a hash table must still compare keys with == after locating a bucket. A structure that skips that comparison is a Bloom filter, and its false positives are exactly this confusion made deliberate.
concepts.L3: With $b$ buckets and $n$ uniformly hashed keys a bucket holds $n/b$ keys on average (the load factor) and a chained lookup does about $1 + n/b$ work: O(1) only because uniformity holds. Hashing a string to its first letter sends every English word into 26 buckets: 26 linked lists. A real string hash mixes every byte in (h = h*31 + c, or SipHash's rounds); the fold $h \bmod b$ keeps only the low bits when $b$ is a power of two, so those must be well mixed. CPython keeps hash(i) == i for small ints on purpose: dense integer keys fill buckets perfectly. Since 3.3 str and bytes hashes are keyed per process (PYTHONHASHSEED, PEP 456): an attacker who can predict hashes sends $n$ keys into one bucket and each insert scans the chain, $n^{2}/2$ comparisons - hash flooding. So never persist Python string hashes across runs. 'Hash table: collisions and probing' handles what collides anyway.

L4.prompt_tpl: A table has {b} buckets and holds {n} keys hashed uniformly. What is the expected chain length, and the expected number of key comparisons for a successful lookup? Answer with the expected chain length.
L4.answer: Expected chain length = $n/b$ (the load factor); expected comparisons for a successful lookup = $1 + (n-1)/(2b)$. b=16, n=8 -> 0.5 and 1.219; b=1000, n=1500 -> 1.5 and 1.75; b=16, n=1500 -> 93.75 and 47.84; b=1000, n=8 -> 0.008 and 1.0035.
L4.explanation: Chain length is the load factor $n/b$: each of the $n$ keys lands in a given bucket with probability $1/b$, so by linearity of expectation a bucket holds $n/b$ keys. A successful search stops at the match, so on average it examines the matched key plus half of the other $n-1$ keys that share its bucket, $1 + (n-1)/(2b)$ (CLRS Theorem 11.2). Both are $O(1)$ exactly when the load factor is bounded.

L4.prompt_tpl: A polynomial string hash starts with h = 0 and, for each character with code point c, does h = h*31 + c. A two-character key has code points {c1} then {c2}. Fold the result into a table of {m} buckets with h mod {m}. Which bucket index results?
L4.explanation: Two steps of h = h*31 + c give $(0 \cdot 31 + c_{1}) \cdot 31 + c_{2} = 31 c_{1} + c_{2}$; the multiplier spreads earlier characters into higher bits so that 'ab' and 'ba' differ. The fold is a plain remainder: 3105 = 194*16 + 1, so bucket 1. The trap is folding before mixing; the hash is computed over the whole key first, then reduced once.

L4.prompt_tpl:
CPython 3. What does this print?

d = dict()
d[1] = 'int'
d[1.0] = 'float'
d[True] = 'bool'
print(len(d), d)
L4.explanation: 1 == 1.0 == True, and Python's hash contract says equal objects must hash equal, so hash(1) == hash(1.0) == hash(True) == 1. All three assignments therefore find the same bucket and the same key: the dict keeps the first key object inserted (the int 1) and overwrites the value each time, ending as {1: 'bool'} with length 1. Verified on CPython 3.12.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hash table uses h to pick a bucket and then compares keys with ==. Which property of h is required for the table to be correct, as opposed to merely fast?
L4.answer: If a == b then h(a) == h(b): equal keys must land in the same bucket, or a lookup can search the wrong bucket and miss a present key
L4.explanation: Correctness needs only consistency with equality: the lookup goes to h(key)'s bucket, so an equal key hashed elsewhere is invisible. The converse is impossible in general (infinitely many keys, finitely many hashes) and is not needed, because the bucket's keys are compared with == before a match is reported. Uniformity affects speed only: a constant hash function is correct and O(n).
options: If a == b then h(a) == h(b): equal keys must land in the same bucket, or a lookup can search the wrong bucket and miss a present key
If h(a) == h(b) then a == b: distinct keys must never share a hash, otherwise the table returns the wrong value
h must spread keys uniformly over the buckets, otherwise lookups return wrong results

L4.answer: C's % truncates toward zero, so the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: -7 % 16 = -7, -7 % 10 = -7, -37 % 16 = -5, -37 % 10 = -7, -32 % 16 = 0, -32 % 10 = -2, -1 % 16 = -1, -1 % 10 = -1. Python would give 9, 3, 11, 3, 0, 8, 15, 9 respectively.
L4.explanation: Since C99, a/b truncates toward zero and a % b is defined so that (a/b)*b + a % b == a, hence a negative dividend gives a negative or zero remainder: -37/16 = -2 and -37 - (-2)*16 = -5. bucket[-5] is an out-of-bounds read - undefined behaviour and a classic hash-table bug. Python's % floors instead and always returns a value in [0, n). Fix in C: use an unsigned hash, or add n when the result is negative.

L4.answer: TypeError: unhashable type: 'K' at the assignment, because a class that overrides __eq__ without defining __hash__ gets __hash__ set to None
L4.explanation: The data model enforces the consistency rule mechanically: overriding __eq__ changes which objects are equal, so the inherited identity hash would break a == b => hash(a) == hash(b). Rather than let that happen silently, Python sets __hash__ = None and the object cannot be a dict key at all. The fix is to define __hash__ from the same fields __eq__ uses, e.g. return hash(self.v). Verified on CPython 3.12: K.__hash__ is None.
options: TypeError: unhashable type: 'K' at the assignment, because a class that overrides __eq__ without defining __hash__ gets __hash__ set to None
It prints False: the default hash is based on identity, and the second K(1) is a different object with a different hash
It prints True: dict finds keys with __eq__, and the two K(1) objects compare equal

L4.prompt_tpl: A chained hash table has b buckets and n keys, hashed under the simple uniform hashing assumption. Derive the expected number of keys examined by a successful search for a key chosen uniformly among the n, as a formula in n and b. State the assumption you use about which key is searched for and where the other keys sit.
L4.answer: Let the searched key be $x$, equally likely to be any of the $n$ keys. Insertion appends to the chain (or the search scans in insertion order), so the keys examined are $x$ itself plus every key inserted after $x$ that landed in $x$'s bucket. For a fixed pair, the probability the other key shares $x$'s bucket is $1/b$ by simple uniform hashing. If $x$ was the $i$-th key inserted, $n - i$ keys came after it, so the expected examined count is $1 + (n-i)/b$. Averaging over $i = 1 \dots n$: $1 + \frac{1}{nb}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(n-i) = 1 + \frac{n(n-1)}{2nb} = 1 + \frac{n-1}{2b}$, which is $1 + \alpha/2 - \alpha/(2n)$ with $\alpha = n/b$, i.e. $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$.
L4.explanation: This is CLRS Theorem 11.2. The two ingredients are linearity of expectation over indicator variables (does key $j$ share $x$'s bucket?) and the fact that a search stops at the match, so only keys ahead of $x$ in its chain count. The unsuccessful case has no early stop and costs $1 + \alpha$. Both are $O(1)$ precisely when $\alpha$ is held constant by resizing, which is the content of 'Load factor and resizing'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A web framework parses request parameters into a chained hash table whose string hash is fixed and public. An attacker sends one request with {k} distinct parameter names precomputed to hash to the same bucket. Inserting each name first scans the whole chain for an equal key. How many key comparisons does inserting all {k} names cost in total? Answer with that number, then say what a framework must change so this attack stops working.
L4.answer: $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} i = k(k-1)/2$. k=1000 -> 499500; k=10000 -> 49995000; k=65536 -> 2147450880. Fix: key the hash with a per-process random secret (SipHash, as CPython does since PEP 456) so the attacker cannot precompute collisions, and cap the number of parameters.
L4.explanation: The $i$-th insert compares against the $i$ keys already in the chain, so the total is quadratic: 65536 names cost about $2 \times 10^{9}$ comparisons, seconds of CPU from one request. That was the 2011 hash-flooding attack on PHP, Java, Ruby and Python. Uniformity alone is no defence, because the attacker chooses the keys; the hash must be unpredictable to them, which is exactly why CPython randomises str and bytes hashes per process and why PYTHONHASHSEED exists. A parameter-count limit bounds the damage independently.

L0.body:
chaining:        bucket[i] -> [ (k1,v1) -> (k2,v2) ]
open addressing: on collision, try i+1, i+2, ... (linear probing)

def get(k):
    i = h(k)
    while slot[i] is not EMPTY:
        if slot[i].key == k: return slot[i].val
        i = (i + 1) % len(slot)
    raise KeyError
L0.cloze: {{c1::Chaining}} stores colliding entries in a per-bucket list; {{c2::open addressing}} stores them in other slots of the same array.

concepts.L1: Two collision strategies. Chaining hangs a list off each bucket, so load factor may exceed 1. Open addressing keeps one entry per slot and probes forward on collision, requiring load factor below 1 and a tombstone scheme for deletion.
concepts.L2: Deletion in open addressing cannot simply blank the slot: that breaks the probe chain, and every key that probed past it becomes unreachable. You must write a tombstone that lookups traverse but insertions may reuse - a detail beginners' implementations always omit and cannot easily observe.
concepts.L3: Insert A and B that both hash to slot 3; B lands in slot 4. Delete A by clearing slot 3, then look up B: the probe reads slot 3, finds EMPTY, and reports 'not found' even though B is one slot away. With a tombstone in slot 3 the probe continues and finds B. Open addressing wins on cache behaviour, since a probe sequence is contiguous while a chain is a pointer walk - which is why CPython's dict and Go's map are open-addressed, and why chaining survives mainly where entries are large or deletion-heavy.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table with {b} slots inserts keys A and B that both hash to slot {i}. The code deletes A by setting slot[{i}] = EMPTY. What breaks?
L4.answer: B is now unreachable: its lookup probes slot i, sees EMPTY, and stops before reaching slot i+1. The fix is a TOMBSTONE marker that lookup skips over and insertion may overwrite.
L4.explanation: The probe sequence is the index; blanking a slot truncates it. This is the standard interview follow-up on open addressing.

L4.prompt_tpl: An open-addressed table has {m} slots and uses h(k) = k mod {m} with linear probing: try h(k), then h(k)+1, then h(k)+2, and so on. Slots h(k) through h(k)+{r}-1 are already occupied by other keys, and slot h(k)+{r} is EMPTY. No wraparound past the end of the table occurs for this key. Into which slot index does the key k = {k} land? Answer with the slot index.
L4.answer: The key lands at (k mod m) + r. m=16, k=37, r=3: 37 mod 16 = 5, so slot 8. m=32, k=213, r=3: 213 mod 32 = 21, so slot 24. m=16, k=100, r=1: 100 mod 16 = 4, so slot 5.
L4.explanation: Open addressing stores the entry in the array itself, so the home slot h(k) is only a starting point. The probe walks forward one slot at a time until it meets EMPTY, which is r slots later here. This is why a lookup for the same key must repeat exactly the same walk: the position carries no record of which key hashed where.

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3, run as a script. What exactly does it print?

SIZE = 8
slots = [None] * SIZE

def insert(k):
    i = k % SIZE
    while slots[i] is not None:
        i = (i + 1) % SIZE
    slots[i] = k

for k in (3, 11, 19, {last}):
    insert(k)
print(slots)
L4.answer: [None, None, None, 3, 11, 19, {last}, None]
L4.explanation: 3, 11 and 19 all hash to slot 3, so they occupy 3, 4 and 5 in insertion order. The last key hashes to slot 4, finds 4 and 5 taken, and lands in 6 even though it never collided with anything at its own home slot. That knock-on effect is primary clustering: one busy slot lengthens the probes of its neighbours.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hash table must hold {n} distinct keys in an array of {m} slots. The hash function may be anything you like. Which collision strategy makes this impossible?
L4.answer: Open addressing with linear probing
L4.explanation: Open addressing stores at most one entry per slot, so the load factor cannot exceed 1 and n keys need at least n slots (in practice far more, since probes lengthen sharply near a full table). Chaining stores collided entries in a list hanging off the bucket, so its load factor is unbounded: 24 keys fit in 8 buckets as chains averaging 3.
options: Chaining
Open addressing with linear probing
Neither: both can hold more keys than the array has slots

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table with {m} slots starts empty. A broken hash function sends all {n} keys to the same home slot. The keys are inserted one after another. Counting every slot the code examines, including the EMPTY slot each key finally lands in, how many slot examinations happen in total across all {n} insertions? Answer with the total.
L4.answer: The i-th insertion (1-indexed) examines i slots, so the total is n(n+1)/2. n=4: 1+2+3+4 = 10. n=8: 36. n=10: 55.
L4.explanation: Inserting into a cluster of length $i-1$ costs $i$ examinations, so the total is $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = n(n+1)/2$, which is $O(n^{2})$ for n insertions and $O(n)$ per operation. The expected-$O(1)$ promise of a hash table is a claim about the hash function, not about the table: a bad hash turns open addressing into an unsorted array scan.

L4.prompt_tpl: An open-addressed table with {m} slots probes h(k), then h(k)+{s}, then h(k)+2*{s}, and so on, all taken modulo {m}. Inserts start failing with 'table full' while a count of the entries shows the table is nowhere near full. Explain why, and give a rule for the step that fixes it.
L4.answer: A step of s reaches only slots congruent to h(k) modulo $g = \gcd(s, m)$, so the probe sequence visits $m/g$ of the m slots and then repeats forever. With m = 16 and s = 2 that is 8 slots; with m = 16 and s = 4, only 4. Insertion gives up although the other residue classes are empty. Fix: make the step coprime to m. For a power-of-two m that means any odd step, which is why double-hashing schemes force h2 odd; step 1 (linear probing) is the special case that always works.
L4.explanation: A probe sequence is only useful if it eventually visits every slot. Stepping by s from h generates the subgroup of multiples of $\gcd(s, m)$ in the integers modulo m, so unless $\gcd(s, m) = 1$ most of the table is unreachable from a given home slot. This is a property of the step and the table size together, not of the hash function.

L4.prompt_tpl: A table has {m} slots, a power of two. Quadratic probing uses the offsets 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, ... , that is offset i(i+1)/2 for probe number i = 0, 1, 2, .... Prove that the first {m} probes visit all {m} slots exactly once, so an insert can never fail while a slot is free.
L4.answer: Let $T_i = i(i+1)/2$ and suppose $T_i \equiv T_j$ modulo m with $0 \leq i < j < m$ and $m = 2^{p}$. Then $T_j - T_i = (j-i)(j+i+1)/2$ is a multiple of m, so $(j-i)(j+i+1)$ is a multiple of $2m = 2^{p+1}$. The two factors sum to $2j+1$, which is odd, so exactly one of them is odd and contributes no factor of 2; the other must therefore be divisible by $2^{p+1} = 2m$ on its own. But $0 < j-i < m$ and $0 < j+i+1 < 2m$, so neither can be. Contradiction, so the m offsets are pairwise distinct modulo m and, being m of them, they are a permutation of the slots.
L4.explanation: The proof only works because m is a power of two: all the factors of 2 sit in one term. For a general m the triangular offsets do not cover the table, which is why implementations that use this scheme also insist on power-of-two sizing. Connect this to Load factor and resizing: doubling keeps m a power of two, so the guarantee survives every rehash.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table with {m} slots deletes correctly, writing a TOMBSTONE that lookups walk past and inserts may overwrite. It grows only when the number of live entries exceeds two thirds of the slots. A long-running program inserts and deletes so that only {k} keys are live at any moment, though millions of distinct keys have passed through it. Lookups get slower and slower, and eventually one insert never returns. Diagnose it and give the fix.
L4.answer: Tombstones are never counted, so the resize test sees k live entries out of m and never fires, while the tombstones accumulate until nearly every slot is live-or-tombstone. An unsuccessful lookup then walks almost the whole table instead of stopping at an EMPTY slot, and once no EMPTY slot remains the insert loop scans forever: with no EMPTY sentinel, its termination condition never holds. Fix: charge tombstones against the occupancy threshold (live + tombstones), so the table rehashes and purges them; CPython does this by never returning capacity for a DKIX_DUMMY slot. A rehash into a table of the same size is enough - this is one of the rare cases where a table shrinks or restays the same size on 'growth'.
L4.explanation: A tombstone costs a slot for probing purposes even though it holds no entry, so the quantity that governs probe length is live entries plus tombstones, not live entries. This is exactly the invariant that Load factor and resizing assumes, and the reason deletion-heavy workloads are the case where chaining still wins.

L0.body:
load_factor = n / nbuckets

if n > 2 * len(slots) // 3:    # CPython 3.11's dict threshold
    rehash into a bigger table  # CPython: next power of 2 >= 3*n
    # every entry is reinserted; new index = h(k) % new_size
L0.cloze: When the load factor exceeds its threshold the table {{c1::grows}} and every key must be {{c2::rehashed}} into the new table.

concepts.L1: Load factor is entries divided by slots. Expected probe length grows with it - sharply as it approaches 1 for open addressing - so tables grow when it crosses a threshold, reallocating and reinserting every entry.
concepts.L2: O(1) for hash tables is expected-and-amortised, and it hides a full O(n) rehash. A dict insert can therefore take milliseconds instead of nanoseconds, which is why latency-sensitive code preallocates. Worst case per operation is O(n) even without adversaries, because all keys can legitimately collide.
concepts.L3: Knuth's estimate for linear probing puts the expected probes of an unsuccessful search at about $(1 + 1/(1-a)^{2})/2$: $a = 0.5$ costs 2.5 probes, $a = 0.75$ costs 8.5, $a = 0.9$ costs 50.5. That blow-up near 1 is why thresholds sit at 0.66-0.75, not 0.95. Growth is multiplicative, so reinsertions telescope as in The dynamic array and amortised append: $n$ inserts move fewer than $2n$ entries in total, O(1) amortised. CPython 3.11 grows when the entries would exceed $2/3$ of the index table - 5 fit in 8 slots, 10 in 16, 21 in 32 - and sizes the new table as the next power of two at least $3n$, reinserting each entry with its cached hash, so hash() is not called again. Insertion order survives the resize; what a resize endangers is a live iterator, and CPython only catches the size-changing case: delete one key and add another mid-iteration and it silently skips entries.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table doubles when the load factor exceeds {a}. Starting at 8 slots, how many slots after inserting {n} distinct keys?
L4.explanation: Divide n by 0.75 and round up to the next power of two, floored at 8. Doing this by hand once explains why a dict of 100 items occupies far more than 100 slots.

L4.prompt_tpl: A linear-probing table is at load factor a = {a}. Knuth's estimate for the expected number of probes in an UNSUCCESSFUL search is (1 + 1/(1-a)^2)/2. Compute it. Answer with the number of probes.
L4.explanation: The $1/(1-a)^{2}$ term explodes as $a$ approaches 1: halving the free space quadruples the probe count. Going from a load factor of 0.5 to 0.9 costs 20 times more work per miss, which is exactly why tables grow at 0.66-0.75 instead of running nearly full.

L4.prompt_tpl: CPython 3.11 lets a dict hold at most floor(2*s/3) entries in an index table of s = {s} slots, and grows the table when the next insert would exceed that. How many keys does this dict hold before it resizes?
L4.answer: s=8 -> 5, s=16 -> 10, s=32 -> 21, s=64 -> 42, s=128 -> 85. Measured on CPython 3.11 with sys.getsizeof: the dict grows on the 6th, 11th, 22nd, 43rd and 86th key.
L4.explanation: CPython's index table is a power of two and only two thirds of it is usable, so a 100-key dict sits in a 256-slot table. This is why a dict costs several times the memory of a list of the same length, and why preallocating with a known size avoids repeated rehashing.

L4.prompt_tpl:
CPython 3.11. The dict grows several times during this loop. Predict the exact printed line.

d = dict(a=1, b=2, c=3)
del d["b"]
for i in range({n}):
    d[i] = i
print(list(d)[:3])
L4.explanation: A resize copies the compact entries array in order and rebuilds only the index table, so insertion order survives every growth; the deleted key 'b' is squeezed out by the first resize and never comes back. Since Python 3.7 this ordering is a language guarantee, not a CPython accident.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hash table grows by a fixed {k} slots each time it fills - not by doubling - rehashing every entry present at that moment. Starting from {k} slots, how many entry reinsertions happen in total while inserting {n} keys? Answer with the number of reinsertions.
L4.answer: Resizes occur at k, 2k, ..., n-k entries, so the total is $k(1 + 2 + \cdots + (n/k - 1)) = n(n-k)/(2k)$. k=8, n=64 -> 224; k=8, n=1024 -> 65024; k=16, n=1024 -> 32256. Doubling from 8 slots moves only 1016 entries for n=1024.
L4.explanation: Additive growth makes the total rehash work quadratic, $O(n^{2}/k)$, so each insert costs $O(n/k)$ amortised instead of $O(1)$. Multiplicative growth is the whole reason the amortised bound exists; the same argument appears in The dynamic array and amortised append.

L4.prompt_tpl: You will tolerate at most {p} expected probes on an unsuccessful linear-probing lookup. Starting from Knuth's estimate (1 + 1/(1-a)^2)/2, derive the largest load factor a that still meets the budget. Answer with a.
L4.explanation: Inverting the cost formula turns a latency budget into a resize threshold. A budget of 5 probes lands on $a = 2/3$ and 10 probes on $a = 0.77$, which is where real thresholds actually sit: the designers picked a probe budget first, and the load factor fell out of it.

L4.prompt_tpl: An order-matching service must keep every dict insert under {u} microseconds, but rehashing its {n}-entry table takes about {ms} milliseconds and blows the budget whenever it fires. Name two designs that bound the tail latency, and state what each one costs.
L4.answer: (1) Preallocate: size the table for the known maximum up front so no resize ever fires. Cost: memory held from the start, and it fails if the estimate is exceeded. (2) Incremental rehash: allocate the new table but move only a few entries per operation, keeping both tables live until the old one empties (Redis does exactly this). Cost: every lookup must check two tables, code is harder, and peak memory holds both. A third answer worth credit: keep a fixed-capacity structure and reject or shard beyond it.
L4.explanation: Amortised O(1) is a bound on totals, not on any single operation - see Worst, average and amortised. Latency-sensitive systems either pay the cost early (preallocation) or spread it (incremental rehash); no scheme makes the work disappear, they only decide when it is paid.
