L0.body:
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin

$ which python3            # which one actually runs
$ export FOO=bar           # exported: inherited by child processes
$ FOO=bar ./prog           # set for this one command only
L0.cloze: PATH is a {{c1::colon}}-separated list of directories searched {{c2::left to right}} for a command name.

concepts.L1: Environment variables are a string-to-string map each process inherits from its parent. PATH lists the directories searched, in order, for a bare command name. export marks a shell variable for inheritance.
concepts.L2: Environment is inherited at process creation and never shared afterwards, so a child cannot change its parent's environment. That is why a script cannot set a variable in your shell - and why activating a virtualenv must be sourced (`source venv/bin/activate`) rather than executed.
concepts.L3: PATH resolution is userspace policy, not kernel behaviour: execve(2) takes a pathname, so execve("ls", argv, environ) fails with ENOENT though ls runs in that same shell. The search lives in the shell and in the execvp/execlp wrappers of libc - split PATH on colons, join each prefix to the name with a slash, take the first executable match, left to right. Prepending a directory therefore shadows a system tool, which is all a virtualenv does (see Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments) and why a writable directory early in PATH is a privilege-escalation bug. A zero-length entry - a leading, trailing or doubled colon - means the current directory, so one stray colon lets a file named ls in the directory you are standing in run instead of /bin/ls. And bash caches each resolved path in a hash table, searching PATH only on a miss, so a moved binary keeps failing until hash -r.

L4.prompt_tpl: PATH=/a:/b and both /a/tool and /b/tool exist. Which runs for `tool`, and what does `which -a tool` print?
L4.answer: /a/tool runs. which -a prints /a/tool then /b/tool, in PATH order.
L4.explanation: Search is first-match, left to right. This is the whole mechanism behind every 'wrong version of the tool' problem.

L4.prompt_tpl:
bash on x86-64 Linux. You run these four lines, in order:

FOO={v}
bash -c 'echo "[$FOO]"'
export FOO
bash -c 'echo "[$FOO]"'

Each child shell prints exactly one line. Answer with the two output lines, in order, and nothing else.
L4.explanation: A plain assignment creates a shell variable; only export marks it for the environment that the shell hands to a child at exec. The first child therefore has no FOO at all, so `"$FOO"` expands to the empty string and the brackets close on nothing. After export, the child inherits FOO={v}. Verified on bash 5.2.21, x86-64 Linux.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your PATH lists {n} directories and the program you want is installed in the last of them. You then prepend {m} more directories to the front of PATH. In a fresh shell, with nothing in the command hash, how many PATH directories are examined before the program is found, counting the one that matches? Answer with the number of directories examined.
L4.answer: Directories examined = n + m: every prepended directory misses, then every original directory up to and including the last. Worked draws: n=3, m=1 gives 4; n=5, m=2 gives 7; n=8, m=4 gives 12.
L4.explanation: The search is left to right and stops at the first executable match, so a program in the last original directory costs one lookup per directory ahead of it, and {m} prepended directories add {m} more misses: {n} + {m}. This is why a long PATH of near-misses makes a shell feel sluggish, and why bash caches the answer instead of repeating the walk.

L4.prompt_tpl: bash 5.2 on x86-64 Linux. PATH begins with dira, then dirb, and both hold an executable named tool. Running tool prints A. You then delete dira/tool, changing nothing else, and run tool again. Bash prints 'bash: /home/you/dira/tool: No such file or directory' and exits 127, although dirb/tool still exists and is executable. Explain why the shell did not fall back to dirb/tool, and name the one builtin that repairs it.
L4.answer: Bash remembers the full pathname of each command it has resolved in a hash table and does a full PATH search only on a miss, so it re-executed the remembered /home/you/dira/tool and reported the exec failure rather than searching again. hash -r (or hash -d tool) drops the cache; the next run searches PATH, finds dirb/tool and prints B. Assigning to PATH also flushes the table, which is why this only bites when the binary moves and PATH does not. Reproduced on bash 5.2.21.
L4.explanation: 'command not found' and 'No such file or directory' are different failures: the second means the shell already had a pathname and the exec failed. A stale hash entry is the usual cause after a reinstall, a venv rebuild or a pull that moves a script. hash shows what the shell remembers; type -a tool shows what PATH holds now.

L4.prompt_tpl: A login script builds PATH by string concatenation, and one day the extra directory is empty, leaving PATH={pathval}. A user then runs ls while standing in a world-writable upload directory that happens to contain an executable file named ls. Which statement is true in bash or any POSIX shell?
L4.answer: The empty entry is a zero-length prefix, which POSIX defines as the current directory, so the upload directory is searched at that position and its ls runs instead of /bin/ls.
L4.explanation: POSIX keeps a zero-length PATH prefix as a legacy spelling of the current working directory: a leading colon, a trailing colon, or two adjacent colons all count, and the shell searches it in that position. Verified on bash 5.2.21 with both PATH=:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin and PATH=/usr/local/bin::/usr/bin:/bin, where a local file named ls ran instead of /bin/ls. Write . explicitly if you really mean it, and never for a privileged user.
options: The empty entry is a zero-length prefix, which POSIX defines as the current directory, so the upload directory is searched at that position and its ls runs instead of /bin/ls.
Empty entries are skipped by POSIX shells, so /bin/ls runs exactly as usual.
A PATH containing an empty entry is rejected by the shell, so PATH keeps its previous value and /bin/ls runs.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux with gcc and glibc, a C program builds an argv array holding "ls" and NULL and calls execve("ls", argv, environ). It fails with errno ENOENT, although typing ls in the same shell and the same directory works. Explain what PATH resolution actually is and where it lives, name the libc call that would have succeeded unchanged, and say what the third argument has to do with inheritance.
L4.answer: execve(2) takes a pathname, not a command name: the kernel never reads PATH, so it looked for a file called ls in the current directory and returned ENOENT. PATH search is a userspace convention implemented by the shell and by the p-suffixed libc wrappers execvp, execlp and execvpe; execvp("ls", argv) does the search and succeeds. The third argument is the child's environment, an array of NAME=value strings; passing environ is what makes the child inherit yours, and it is a copy taken at exec, not a link (see What a process is). Verified with gcc on x86-64 Linux: the execve form printed ENOENT, the execvp form printed 'ls (GNU coreutils) 9.4'.
L4.explanation: The kernel loads a program image from a path; naming, searching and shadowing are shell and libc policy sitting above it. That split is why every version manager works by editing PATH rather than asking the kernel for anything, and why a program that needs one specific interpreter should exec an absolute path instead of a bare name.

L4.prompt_tpl: You install a tool at /opt/bin/deploy and add /opt/bin to PATH in your ~/.bashrc. Running deploy works. Running sudo deploy says 'sudo: deploy: command not found', and sudo env prints a PATH you never set, with no /opt/bin in it. Name the mechanism, say why it exists, and give two ways to run the tool under sudo.
L4.answer: The sudoers option secure_path: when set, sudo replaces the invoking user's PATH with that fixed value for the command it runs. Most distributions ship it enabled, and sudo itself has enabled it by default since 1.9.16, precisely so that a user cannot put a fake deploy - or a fake ls - early in PATH and have root execute it. Two ways round it: invoke the absolute path, sudo /opt/bin/deploy; or have an administrator add /opt/bin to secure_path with visudo.
L4.explanation: Environment inheritance is a default, not a law: a privileged program may discard what it was handed, and sudo does exactly that for PATH. The general rule is that anything running with more privilege than you must not resolve command names through your PATH, which is also why systemd units and setuid programs set PATH explicitly.

L0.body:
$ ls -l script.sh
-rwxr-xr--  1 me staff  120 Sep 2 10:00 script.sh
 type|owner|group|other

r=4 w=2 x=1
chmod 755 f   -> rwxr-xr-x
chmod +x f    -> add execute, except bits set in umask

# directory x = permission to ENTER, not to list
L0.cloze: In numeric mode, r={{c1::4}}, w={{c2::2}}, x={{c3::1}}, so 755 means rwx for owner and {{c4::r-x}} for group and other.

concepts.L1: Every file carries an owner, a group and three permission triples for owner, group and others. Read, write and execute are 4, 2 and 1, summed per triple to give the familiar three-digit octal.
concepts.L2: On a directory the bits differ: r lists names, x enters and resolves paths through it, w creates and deletes entries. A directory with r but not x shows filenames and opens nothing. And deleting a file needs write on its DIRECTORY, not the file - so you can delete what you cannot read.
concepts.L3: Read the mode as three octal digits, one per class: 755 is 7=rwx owner, 5=r-x group, 5=r-x others. The kernel matches exactly one class and stops - you are the owner, or you are in the file's group, or you are other - so a file with mode 077 that you own is unreadable by you and readable by everyone else in its group. Execute on a regular file lets the kernel run it: execve needs a format it recognises, so a script with no shebang fails with ENOEXEC and runs only because your shell then retries it under /bin/sh. The usual failure is a readable but non-executable script - bash prints 'Permission denied' and exits 126, and the fix is chmod +x, not editing the file. New files are created 0666 and directories 0777 with the umask bits cleared, which is why umask 022 gives 644 and 755 - the same x bit a #!/usr/bin/env python3 script needs in Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does chmod {mode} produce in symbolic form, and can a user in the group execute the file?
L4.explanation: Convert each octal digit to its rwx bits: 7=4+2+1, 6=4+2, 5=4+1, 4=4. Group execute is the x bit of the middle digit.

L4.prompt_tpl: One permission triple grants read={r}, write={w} and execute={x}, where 1 means granted and 0 means not granted. What single octal digit encodes that triple? Answer with the digit.
L4.answer: The digit is 4r + 2w + x. r=1, w=1, x=1 gives 7; r=1, w=0, x=1 gives 5; r=1, w=0, x=0 gives 4; r=0, w=1, x=0 gives 2; r=0, w=0, x=0 gives 0.
L4.explanation: A triple is three bits with fixed weights: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1, so any subset sums to a digit from 0 to 7. That is why 755 reads as rwx for the owner and r-x for group and others, why 6 always means rw- and never r-x, and why an odd digit is exactly the case where the execute bit is set.

L4.prompt_tpl:
On x86-64 Linux with bash and GNU coreutils, in an empty directory you run:

    umask {mask}
    touch f.txt
    mkdir d
    ls -l

What mode string does ls -l print for f.txt, and what mode string for d?
L4.answer: umask 022: -rw-r--r-- for f.txt and drwxr-xr-x for d. umask 002: -rw-rw-r-- and drwxrwxr-x. umask 077: -rw------- and drwx------.
L4.explanation: touch asks for mode 0666 and mkdir for 0777; the kernel clears every bit set in the umask, so 0666 with 022 cleared is 644 and 0777 with 022 cleared is 755. Creation never sets an execute bit on a regular file, which is why a script you have just written is not runnable until chmod +x. Output verified by running the commands.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Linux, report.txt is owned by user {user} and its group is {grp}, which is also {user}'s own group. Its mode is ----rwxrwx, that is octal 077. Working as {user}, what happens on: cat report.txt
L4.answer: It fails with Permission denied: the kernel matches the owner class first and stops there, and the owner triple grants nothing.
L4.explanation: The check walks one branch only: if your effective uid is the file's owner, the owner triple decides and the group and other triples are never consulted. Verified on Linux: a file with mode 077 owned by uid 65534 is unreadable by 65534 and readable by any other member of its group. chmod 077 is a self-lockout, not a way to share.
options: It fails with Permission denied: the kernel matches the owner class first and stops there, and the owner triple grants nothing.
It prints the file: the owner is also in the group, so the group's rwx applies.
It prints the file: access is the union of every class the user belongs to.

L4.prompt_tpl:
deploy.sh currently has mode 644. On Linux with GNU coreutils you run, in a shell whose umask is {mask}: chmod +x deploy.sh

What mode does ls -l show afterwards, and why does the umask matter here at all?
L4.answer: umask 022: -rwxr-xr-x (755). umask 077: -rwxr--r-- (744), owner execute only. umask 027: -rwxr-xr-- (754). Verified with GNU coreutils 9.4.
L4.explanation: With no u, g, o or a letter in front of it, POSIX and GNU chmod treat +x as a+x but leave alone any bit set in the umask. umask 022 masks only write bits, so all three execute bits are set; umask 077 masks group and other entirely, so only the owner gains x. Write chmod a+x when you mean all three regardless of the umask.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are creating a shared drop directory {dir} on a multi-user Linux box: any user may create files in it and read what is there, but no user may delete or rename a file owned by someone else. Answer with the four-digit octal mode you would set on {dir}.
L4.explanation: Deleting a file is a write to its directory, so a plain 0777 drop box lets anyone unlink anyone's file. The leading 1 is the sticky bit, S_ISVTX: inside that directory only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root may unlink or rename. ls prints it as t in the last position, drwxrwxrwt, which is exactly how /tmp is set.

L4.prompt_tpl: A web server running as user {svc} on Linux returns 403 for /home/{owner}/public/index.html. The file is mode 644, the directory /home/{owner}/public is mode 755, and /home/{owner} is mode 700 owned by {owner}. Name the check that fails, and give the one chmod command that fixes it without letting {svc} list the rest of {owner}'s home.
L4.answer: Path resolution needs search (x) permission on every directory in the path. /home/alice (or /home/priya) at 700 denies x to www-data (or nginx), so the walk stops there and the 755 directory and 644 file are never reached. Fix: chmod o+x /home/alice - mode 711, x without r, allows traversal to a known path but not listing.
L4.explanation: The permission on the file is only the last check. The kernel resolves a path one component at a time and needs the x bit on each directory to step through it, so a mode-700 home blocks every other user no matter how open the leaves are. Granting o+x alone gives traversal, not listing, which is why 711 home directories are the standard fix.

L0.body:
$ ./long_job &        run in the background
$ jobs                this shell's jobs, running and stopped
$ fg %1               bring job 1 to the foreground
$ bg %1               resume stopped job 1 in the background (SIGCONT)
Ctrl-C                send SIGINT (polite interrupt)
Ctrl-Z                SIGTSTP (suspend)
$ ps aux | grep name  find a pid
$ kill -9 <pid>       SIGKILL: cannot be caught
L0.cloze: Ctrl-C sends {{c1::SIGINT}}, which a program may catch; kill -9 sends {{c2::SIGKILL}}, which it cannot.

concepts.L1: The shell runs commands as child processes and can suspend, background and foreground them. Signals are the mechanism for asking a process to stop, and most of them can be handled by the program.
concepts.L2: kill -9 is not 'kill harder', it is 'kill without letting the program clean up' - no flushed buffers, no removed temp files, no released locks. Try SIGTERM (plain kill) first and reserve SIGKILL for a process that ignored it, because a database killed with -9 must replay its log on restart.
concepts.L3: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the entire foreground process group, which is why it stops a whole pipeline and not just the last stage. A program that catches SIGINT can finish writing a file and exit cleanly; Python turns it into KeyboardInterrupt, which is precisely why a bare `except:` breaks Ctrl-C. Background jobs still share the terminal's stdout, so their output interleaves with yours - hence `./job > log 2>&1 &`, and nohup or a terminal multiplexer for anything that must survive a disconnect.

L4.prompt_tpl: A process ignores Ctrl-C. List, in order, what you try and why.
L4.answer: 1) kill <pid> (SIGTERM) - catchable, lets it clean up. 2) Wait a few seconds. 3) kill -9 <pid> (SIGKILL) - uncatchable, no cleanup, risks corrupt state. Ctrl-Z then kill also works if you need it stopped immediately first.
L4.explanation: Escalate from catchable to uncatchable. Reaching for -9 first is how people corrupt files and then blame the tool.

L4.prompt_tpl: In bash on Linux, a foreground command is terminated by signal number {sig}, which the program does not catch. What number does bash then report as that command's exit status? Answer with the number.
L4.answer: 128 + sig. sig=1 (SIGHUP): 129. sig=2 (SIGINT): 130. sig=9 (SIGKILL): 137. sig=13 (SIGPIPE): 141. sig=15 (SIGTERM): 143.
L4.explanation: Bash encodes death-by-signal as 128 + the signal number, so any status above 128 means the process did not choose its own exit code - something killed it. 130 is Ctrl-C (SIGINT, 2), 137 is kill -9 (SIGKILL, 9), 143 is plain kill (SIGTERM, 15). A process that exits normally reports the value it passed to exit(), 0 to 255.

L4.prompt_tpl:
On x86-64 Linux with CPython 3, this script is run from a terminal. What single line does it print?

import os, signal
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
    signal.pause()
else:
    os.kill(pid, {sig})
    _, status = os.waitpid(pid, 0)
    print(os.WIFSIGNALED(status), os.WTERMSIG(status))
L4.answer: True {sig}
L4.explanation: The child blocks in signal.pause() and is killed by the signal before it can return, so it never exits on its own. waitpid gives the parent a wait status that encodes 'terminated by a signal': WIFSIGNALED is True and WTERMSIG is the signal number, {sig}. A shell would show the same fact as exit status 128 + {sig}.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are running ./{prog} in the foreground of a bash shell. You press Ctrl-Z, the shell prints Stopped, and you then type bg. What happens to the command?
L4.answer: It is sent SIGCONT and carries on from where it stopped, now running in the background, still writing to the same terminal.
L4.explanation: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, which stops the process without killing it: its memory, its open files and its pid all survive. bg sends SIGCONT to that job, so it resumes at the instruction where it stopped. Its stdout is still the terminal, so its output now interleaves with your prompt unless you redirected it when you started it.
options: It is sent SIGCONT and carries on from where it stopped, now running in the background, still writing to the same terminal.
It restarts from the beginning as a new process with a new pid, because a stopped process cannot be resumed.
Nothing happens until you type fg; bg only moves the entry in the jobs table.

L4.prompt_tpl: You start a script in the background with ./{script} & . It prints nothing, and bash reports: [1]+  Stopped (tty input). The script's first statement is a read of a value from standard input. Name the signal that stopped it, say who sent it and why, and give two ways to make the script work.
L4.answer: SIGTTIN, sent by the terminal driver because a process in a background process group tried to read from the controlling terminal. Fixes: bring it to the foreground with fg %1 so its process group owns the terminal; or feed the input from a file or a heredoc (./{script} < answers.txt &) so it never touches the tty; or take the value as a command-line argument or an environment variable instead of reading it.
L4.explanation: Only the foreground process group may read the terminal; a background read is stopped with SIGTTIN so that two programs cannot fight over your keystrokes. Writing is allowed by default, which is why background output still interleaves with your prompt - with stty tostop set, a background write raises SIGTTOU as well. The job is stopped, not dead: fg %1 resumes it and the read then succeeds.

L4.prompt_tpl: ps shows a process listed as [{name}] <defunct> with pid {pid}. You run kill -9 on that pid and it is still there a minute later. Choose what to do next and justify it: (a) keep sending SIGKILL, (b) kill the parent process, (c) do nothing and watch.
L4.answer: (b) or (c), never (a). A <defunct> process is a zombie: it has already exited and all that remains is a process-table entry holding its exit status until the parent calls wait(). A dead process cannot receive a signal, so (a) can never work. If the parent is alive and simply not reaping, killing or fixing the parent makes pid 1 adopt the zombie and reap it at once; if the parent is about to call wait() anyway, (c) is right and the entry disappears by itself. A pile of zombies is a bug in the parent, not in the child.
L4.explanation: A zombie holds no CPU, no memory and no open files - only its slot in the process table and its exit status, kept so the parent can read it with wait() or waitpid(). That is why signals do nothing to it. Zombies disappear when the parent reaps them, or when the parent dies and the orphan is reparented to init/systemd, which reaps continuously.

L4.answer: Ctrl-C makes the terminal driver send SIGINT to the foreground process group; CPython's handler raises KeyboardInterrupt in the main thread. KeyboardInterrupt inherits from BaseException, not from Exception, and a bare except: catches BaseException, so the interrupt is swallowed, retrying is printed, and the loop goes round again. Fix: write except Exception: so KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit propagate - or catch KeyboardInterrupt explicitly, clean up, and re-raise.
L4.explanation: Python puts KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit and GeneratorExit directly under BaseException precisely so that except Exception: does not eat them; a bare except: re-opens that hole. This is the concrete cost of the rule taught in Exceptions - name the exceptions you can actually handle. Note that the signal is only delivered to the main thread, so a worker thread cannot be interrupted this way either.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux, bash runs the pipeline: yes | head -n {n} > /dev/null . head exits after line {n} while yes is still writing. Work out what stops yes, and what exit status bash records for the first stage of the pipeline (element zero of its PIPESTATUS array). Answer with that status number.
L4.answer: 141, for every n. head closes the read end of the pipe and exits 0; the next write by yes goes to a pipe with no reader, so the kernel sends SIGPIPE (signal 13), whose default action is to terminate. Bash records 128 + 13 = 141 for the first stage.
L4.explanation: A write to a pipe whose read end is closed raises SIGPIPE, and its default disposition terminates the writer. That is the mechanism by which a finite consumer stops an infinite producer, which is what the Pipes concept quietly relies on when you write a long command ending in head. The status is 141 whatever n is. A program that ignores SIGPIPE gets EPIPE back from write() instead and must handle it itself.

L0.body:
$ python3 script.py arg1
$ python3 -m pytest             run a module as a script
$ python3 -c 'print(1+1)'

$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate     prepends .venv/bin to PATH
(.venv) $ pip install requests
(.venv) $ pip freeze > requirements.txt
L0.cloze: A virtual environment works by putting its own {{c1::bin}} directory at the front of {{c2::PATH}}, so `python` and `pip` resolve inside it.

concepts.L1: Python runs a file (python3 script.py), a module found on sys.path (python3 -m pkg.mod), or a command string of one or more statements (-c). A virtual environment is a directory with its own interpreter link and site-packages; activating it prepends its bin directory to PATH.
concepts.L2: `pip install` with no active environment writes into the system Python and eventually breaks it - hence the 'externally-managed-environment' refusal on modern distributions. `python -m pip` is safer than `pip`: it uses that interpreter's pip, not whatever PATH finds first.
concepts.L3: Activation is a shell edit, not a mode. source .venv/bin/activate saves the old PATH in _OLD_VIRTUAL_PATH, prepends .venv/bin, exports VIRTUAL_ENV and runs hash -r so the shell drops any cached path to python. These are exported variables, so every child inherits them - a subshell, bash -c, a make recipe; what does not inherit is anything started from a fresh environment, which is why cron and systemd get the system Python. Nothing needs activation: .venv/bin/python already reports sys.prefix inside the venv, not the system install, so an absolute interpreter path is the robust invocation. The other half is sys.path[0]: python3 pkg/mod.py puts the script's own directory there, python3 -m pkg.mod puts the current directory. That is why an import can work one way and fail the other, and why python -m pytest sees your package when the bare command does not (pytest in practice).

L4.prompt_tpl: A script works in your terminal but fails with ModuleNotFoundError under cron. Name the most likely cause and the fix.
L4.answer: cron runs with a minimal environment and does not source your shell profile, so PATH lacks the virtualenv and the system Python runs instead. Fix: invoke the venv's interpreter by absolute path, /path/.venv/bin/python script.py.
L4.explanation: Activation is a PATH change and PATH is inherited, not global. Absolute interpreter paths remove the dependency entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: CPython 3.11 on Linux. The directory /home/{user}/proj contains a directory pkg holding __init__.py and mod.py, and mod.py is exactly two lines: import sys, then print(sys.path[0]). From /home/{user}/proj you run the command python3 -m pkg.mod and it prints one line. What is that line?
L4.answer: /home/ana/proj - the current directory, written as an absolute path (for raj, /home/raj/proj; for mei, /home/mei/proj). Running python3 pkg/mod.py from the same place would print /home/ana/proj/pkg instead.
L4.explanation: -m locates the module by name, so the current directory is what goes on the front of sys.path; a script puts its own directory there. On CPython 3.11 that entry is an absolute path. This one difference is the usual reason an import works under -m and fails when the same file is run as a script.

L4.prompt_tpl: You ran python3 -m venv .venv but have NOT sourced the activate script; the prompt has no (.venv) on it. You now run: .venv/bin/python -c 'import sys; print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)'. What is printed, and what does that tell you?
L4.answer: True. sys.prefix points at the .venv directory while sys.base_prefix still points at the system installation, so this interpreter is already using the venv and its site-packages even though nothing was activated.
L4.explanation: A venv is selected by which interpreter binary you start, not by a shell mode. sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is the documented test for being inside one. Activation only edits PATH so that the bare names python and pip resolve there; naming the interpreter by path skips that step entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two Pythons are installed and an old pip is also on PATH. You want requests installed into exactly the interpreter that /srv/app/.venv/bin/python will run. Which command is guaranteed to do that?
L4.answer: /srv/app/.venv/bin/python -m pip install requests
L4.explanation: python -m pip runs the pip belonging to that interpreter, so the install lands in that interpreter's site-packages. Bare pip is whatever PATH finds first, which may belong to another Python; sudo pip3 targets the system Python and is the command that earns the externally-managed-environment refusal.
options: /srv/app/.venv/bin/python -m pip install requests
pip install requests
sudo pip3 install requests

L4.prompt_tpl: CPython 3.11 on Linux. From /home/{user}/proj you run: python3 -c 'import sys; print(repr(sys.path[0]))'. What is printed? Say how it differs from what python3 -m pkg.mod prints from the same directory.
L4.answer: It prints '' (two quote characters, the repr of the empty string) for every user. With -m the same slot holds the absolute current directory, /home/ana/proj. Both mean 'look in the current directory first'; only the spelling differs.
L4.explanation: -c and -m both put the current directory at the front of sys.path, but -c leaves it as the empty string, which the import machinery resolves against the process's cwd at import time. So a -c snippet that chdirs before importing searches the new directory, while the absolute entry -m inserts does not move.

L4.prompt_tpl: You source .venv/bin/activate in a terminal. Then (a) you type bash to start a child shell and run which python, and (b) at the same moment a cron job you own runs which python. Which of (a) and (b) sees the venv, and what single rule decides it?
L4.answer: (a) sees it, (b) does not. Activation exports PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV, and exported variables are copied into every child process, so the child bash inherits the modified PATH. The cron job is not a descendant of your terminal: cron starts it from its own minimal environment, so PATH there never contained .venv/bin.
L4.explanation: The rule is inheritance, not scope: an exported variable reaches children, never siblings or unrelated processes. Anything launched outside your session - cron, systemd, a CI runner, an editor started from a desktop menu - begins from a different environment, which is why absolute interpreter paths are the fix there.

L4.prompt_tpl: Argue from the mechanism: (a) why activate must be sourced rather than executed as ./activate, and (b) how deactivate can put your old PATH back when activation only assigned to a variable.
L4.answer: (a) An executed script runs in a child process. Its assignment to PATH changes that child's copy of the environment and dies with it, leaving the parent shell untouched; sourcing runs the same lines in the current shell, which is the only process whose PATH you care about. (b) Before overwriting PATH, activate stores the old value in _OLD_VIRTUAL_PATH and defines deactivate as a shell function in that same shell. deactivate copies the saved value back, unsets VIRTUAL_ENV, restores PS1 and runs hash -r.
L4.explanation: Both halves follow from one fact: a process can change only its own environment, and children get a copy. That is also why deactivate cannot be a separate program on disk - it has to be a function living in the shell that was modified.

L4.prompt_tpl: A project has mypkg/ and tests/ side by side and was never installed into the venv. With that venv active, python3 -m pytest passes, but running the bare command pytest fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named mypkg. Both come from the same venv. Explain the difference and give two fixes, saying which you would ship.
L4.answer: python3 -m pytest puts the current directory at the front of sys.path, so import mypkg finds the source tree; the pytest console script is an ordinary program and adds nothing, so only installed packages are importable. Fixes: run python3 -m pytest, or install the project into the venv with python3 -m pip install -e . - the editable install is what to ship, because it makes the import work from any directory and under any runner.
L4.explanation: The pytest documentation states that the two invocations are equivalent except that python -m pytest adds the current directory to sys.path. Setting PYTHONPATH=. also works and is the fragile answer: it hides the fact that the package is not installed and breaks the moment the test runner changes directory.

concepts.t: git: commits and the staging area

L0.body:
working tree  --git add-->  index (staging)  --git commit-->  repository

$ git status
$ git add file.c            stage this file's current content
$ git commit -m "message"
$ git diff                  working tree vs index
$ git diff --staged         index vs last commit
$ git log --oneline
L0.cloze: git add moves changes into the {{c1::index}}; git commit records the index as a new {{c2::commit}}.

concepts.L1: Git has three places content lives: the working tree, the index, and the repository. A commit is an immutable snapshot of the whole tree plus a parent pointer, identified by the hash of its content.
concepts.L2: A commit stores a full snapshot, not a diff - diffs are computed on demand between snapshots. And git add stages content, not a file: editing a file after staging it means the commit records the older version, which is why `git diff` and `git diff --staged` can both be non-empty.
concepts.L3: The index is a real file, .git/index: a sorted list of paths, each carrying a file mode, the SHA of a blob object, and stat data for cheap change checks. git add hashes the file's current bytes, writes that blob into .git/objects at once, and records the path-to-blob mapping; a later edit touches only the working tree, so the commit gets the bytes that were staged. git commit turns the index into tree objects and writes a commit object naming that tree, the parent commit(s), author, committer and message, and its SHA covers all of that. Changing any historical commit therefore changes every descendant's hash - the reason rewritten history diverges from a pushed branch and requires a force push (git: remotes, clone, push and pull). A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit and HEAD points at the current branch, which is why creating a branch is instant however large the repository.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run: git add f.c ; then edit f.c again ; then git commit -m 'x'. What is in the commit, and what does git status show afterwards?
L4.answer: The commit contains the version staged by git add, not the later edit. git status afterwards shows f.c as modified but unstaged.
L4.explanation: add snapshots content into the index at the moment it runs. This is exactly why `git add -p` then `git diff --staged` before committing is the reviewable workflow.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run git init in an empty directory, create {n} files at the top level, each with different content, then run git add . followed by one git commit. How many objects does git write into the object database in total (blobs plus trees plus commits)? Answer with the number of objects.
L4.answer: n blobs, one tree for the top-level directory, one commit object: n + 2. n=1 gives 3, n=3 gives 5, n=5 gives 7, n=8 gives 10.
L4.explanation: git add hashes each file's content into its own blob as soon as it runs; git commit converts the index into one tree object per directory and one commit object naming that tree. Distinct content means distinct blobs, so the total is n + 2. Counted with git cat-file --batch-all-objects on git 2.43 for n = 1, 3, 5 and 8.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux with git 2.43: {f} is already committed. You edit it, run git add {f}, then edit it a second time and do not stage that edit. git status --short now prints a two-letter code before the path. What are those two letters? Answer with the two letters only.
L4.answer: MM
L4.explanation: The left column is index versus HEAD, the right column is working tree versus index. The first edit is staged, so the left column is M; the second edit is not staged, so the right column is M too. Verified by running the sequence on git 2.43: git status --short prints MM before the path.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a repository where you have staged some changes and then made further edits, what does git diff with no arguments compare?
L4.answer: The working tree against the index: only the edits you have not staged
L4.explanation: git diff is working tree versus index, git diff --staged (or --cached) is index versus HEAD, and git diff HEAD is working tree versus HEAD. Both of the first two can be non-empty at once, which is exactly the situation this concept's L2 describes.
options: The working tree against the index: only the edits you have not staged
The working tree against the last commit: every change since HEAD
The index against the last commit: only what is staged

L4.prompt_tpl: You create a brand-new file {f} and never run git add on it, you also edit a file git already tracks, and then you run git commit -am 'save'. Which of the two changes ends up in the commit, and what does git status show afterwards?
L4.answer: Only the edit to the already-tracked file. The -a flag stages modifications and deletions of files git already tracks; it never stages an untracked file. Afterwards git status still lists the new file as untracked (?? in git status --short), and it is in no commit at all.
L4.explanation: commit -a is a shortcut for staging tracked files, not for staging everything. This is why a new source file silently misses a commit and the build breaks for everyone else while it still works for you. Verified on git 2.43: after commit -am, git ls-tree HEAD does not list the new file and git status --short shows ?? for it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A branch has {n} commits sitting on top of an older commit whose message you dislike. You run git rebase -i and change nothing but that old commit's message. Derive how many commit hashes change, and why changing only a message is enough to change them. Answer with the number of commit hashes that change.
L4.answer: n + 1: the reworded commit itself plus all n descendants. n=3 gives 4, n=7 gives 8, n=12 gives 13.
L4.explanation: A commit's SHA is the hash of the whole commit object, message included, so a new message means a new commit id. Each child names its parent by id, so the child's own object changes too, and the change cascades to the tip. That is why a rewritten branch cannot fast-forward the remote and the push is rejected (git: remotes, clone, push and pull).

L4.prompt_tpl: You committed {f} containing a live API key, noticed one commit later, deleted the file, committed again, and pushed both commits. Review what someone who clones the repository can still obtain, and say what actually fixes it.
L4.answer: The key is still there. The first commit's tree still names the blob holding it, a clone copies the whole object database, and git show on that commit prints the secret; deleting the file only changes later snapshots. The fix, in order: rotate the credential, because it must be treated as leaked; then rewrite history (git filter-repo or BFG) and force-push; then have every collaborator re-clone, and add the path to .gitignore.
L4.explanation: Commits are snapshots reachable by hash, not diffs applied in sequence, so a later deletion removes nothing from history. Rewriting history changes the hash of every descendant commit and still leaves copies in forks, clones, CI caches and the host's UI, which is why rotation comes first and rewriting second.

L0.body:
$ git switch -c feature       create and switch
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature

<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
their version
>>>>>>> feature

$ git merge --abort           back out of a bad merge
L0.cloze: A branch is a movable {{c1::pointer}} to a commit; a conflict occurs when two branches change the {{c2::same lines}} of a file.

concepts.L1: A branch is a named pointer to a commit that advances as you commit. Merging finds the common ancestor and combines both sides; where the two sides changed the same region, git stops and asks you to resolve.
concepts.L2: Git merges by line, not by meaning, so a clean merge is not a correct merge: two branches can each edit different lines of one function and produce code that compiles and is wrong. A merge with no conflicts still needs the tests run.
concepts.L3: A three-way merge compares both branch tips against their merge base, the commit git merge-base prints. A region changed on only one side is taken from that side; a region changed on both sides is a conflict, unless the two sides made textually identical changes, in which case git takes the agreed text silently. If the merge base is already your own tip, git fast-forwards: the branch pointer moves and no commit is created. Otherwise the result is a commit with two parents, and the resolution you typed lives only in that commit's tree. The markers delimit yours (HEAD), theirs, and the boundary; resolving means editing the file into what you want, deleting all three markers, then git add and git commit. Rebasing often keeps the base near the other tip, so each reconciliation is smaller - and a small divergence is what keeps a push fast-forwardable in git: remotes, clone, push and pull.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two branches both edited different lines of the same function and merged with no conflict. Is the result correct? Justify.
L4.answer: Not necessarily: git merges by line region, not by meaning, so a clean merge can still change behaviour
L4.explanation: 'No conflict' means git found no textual overlap. It is not a statement about program behaviour, which is why CI runs on merge commits.
options: Not necessarily: git merges by line region, not by meaning, so a clean merge can still change behaviour
Yes: git replays both sides and refuses to write a merge commit that does not build
Yes, provided the two sides touched different lines - a three-way merge is clean only when the result is semantically equivalent to both parents

L4.prompt_tpl: `git merge feature` stops with a conflict in {f}. Give the commands that finish the merge, and the one that abandons it.
L4.answer: Edit the file to remove the conflict markers and keep the intended result, then `git add` that file, then `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`). `git merge --abort` throws the whole attempt away and restores the pre-merge tree.
L4.explanation: Staging the file is what tells git the conflict is resolved - there is no separate resolve command. Until every conflicted path is staged, the commit is refused.

L4.prompt_tpl: Branch main has {b} commits in its history and has not moved since you created feature from its tip. feature has {n} new commits on top. From main you run git merge feature and git reports Fast-forward. How many commits are reachable from main afterwards? Answer with the number of commits.
L4.answer: {b} + {n} commits. A fast-forward creates no commit at all: main's tip was already an ancestor of feature's tip, so the branch pointer is moved to feature's tip and the two histories are identical afterwards. Worked draws: b=3, n=2 gives 5; b=12, n=5 gives 17; b=40, n=1 gives 41.
L4.explanation: A merge only makes a commit when the two sides have actually diverged. Here main contributed nothing since the branch point, so there is nothing to reconcile and nothing to record: git moves the pointer and prints Fast-forward. Use git merge --no-ff when you want the branch recorded as a merge commit anyway.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 Linux with git 2.43, main and feature have each changed the same line of {f} since they diverged. From main you run git merge feature. Give the three lines git prints, and the two-letter code git status --short then shows for {f}.
L4.explanation: Git works file by file (Auto-merging), names every path it could not reconcile (CONFLICT (content)), then stops without committing. UU means both sides modified this path and it is still unmerged; the merge finishes only when every unmerged path has been staged with git add, which is what marks it resolved.

L4.prompt_tpl: Both main and feature changed line {n} of app.py from the same original text to exactly the same new text, in separate commits. From main you run git merge feature. Does git stop with a conflict? State what git prints and what the merge commit contains.
L4.answer: No conflict. Each side is compared against the merge base, and the two sides made the identical change, so the region has one agreed result. Git prints Merge made by the 'ort' strategy. and writes a merge commit with two parents; line {n} of app.py holds the new text, and the merge commit's tree differs from neither side there.
L4.explanation: A conflict is not 'both sides touched this region', it is 'both sides touched this region and disagree'. Identical edits agree, so git resolves them without asking. Verified with git 2.43.0, whose default merge strategy has been ort since git 2.34.

L4.prompt_tpl: On main you removed {f} with git rm. On feature someone edited {f}. From main you run git merge feature and git reports CONFLICT (modify/delete). Which version of the file is in your working tree now, and what are the two commands that each resolve it?
L4.answer: Git leaves feature's version of {f} in the working tree and says so: '{f} deleted in HEAD and modified in feature. Version feature of {f} left in tree.' git status --short shows DU. Resolve with git rm {f} to keep the deletion, or git add {f} to keep the edited file, then git commit.
L4.explanation: There are no conflict markers here, because the disagreement is about whether the file exists at all rather than about its lines. So the working tree looks deceptively clean and the wrong outcome is easy to commit. You state the outcome you want by staging it: git rm for gone, git add for kept.

L4.prompt_tpl: You created a repo locally, committed, then added a remote that already had commits, ran git fetch, then git merge origin/{b}. Git answers: fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories. Explain the mechanism that produces this message, and give the two ways forward.
L4.answer: The two lines of history share no commit, so there is no merge base and a three-way merge has nothing to compare either side against. Since git 2.9 git refuses this by default rather than merging against an empty base. Either force it with git merge --allow-unrelated-histories origin/{b}, or - usually the right move - clone the remote and move your files into that clone, because a repo created locally and one created on the host each have their own root commit.
L4.explanation: Every mechanism in this concept starts from the merge base, so with no common ancestor there is nothing for git to reason about and it declines to guess. The message is about the commit graph, not about the files. That same graph reasoning decides whether a push fast-forwards in git: remotes, clone, push and pull.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your branch has {n} commits, and every one of them edits the same line that main has since changed. Work out how many separate conflict resolutions git can ask you for when you run git rebase main, how many when you run git merge main instead, and why the counts differ. Answer with the maximum number of resolutions the rebase can require.
L4.answer: Up to {n} for the rebase, 1 for the merge. Rebase replays your commits one at a time onto the new base, so each replay is its own three-way merge against a base that already absorbed the previous replay, and each can stop on that same line. A merge does one three-way merge of the two tips and stops once. Worked draws: n=3 gives 3, n=5 gives 5, n=8 gives 8. git rerere records a resolution and replays it, which is what makes a repeated rebase bearable.
L4.explanation: This is the honest cost of the linear history a rebase buys: the same disagreement is re-asked once per replayed commit. A merge asks once and stores the answer in the merge commit's tree, where it cannot be lost. Neither is wrong; the trade is a readable history against re-resolving conflicts.

concepts.t: git: remotes, clone, push and pull

L0.body:
$ git clone <url>            copy the repo + set 'origin'
$ git fetch origin           download; moves origin/main, not your branch
$ git pull                   = fetch + merge (or rebase)
$ git push origin main
$ git remote -v

origin/main   a read-only pointer to what the remote had at last fetch
L0.cloze: git {{c1::fetch}} downloads without changing your branches; git {{c2::pull}} is fetch followed by a merge.

concepts.L1: A remote is a named URL for another copy of the repository. fetch updates your remote-tracking pointers; pull additionally merges into your current branch; push uploads your commits if the remote's branch is an ancestor of yours.
concepts.L2: origin/main is a cached pointer to what the remote looked like at your last fetch, not a live view - so a stale origin/main makes `git log main..origin/main` misleading. And a rejected push almost always means the remote has commits you do not, which is fixed by pulling, never by force-pushing over a shared branch.
concepts.L3: Because every commit hashes its parents, a push is only accepted when your branch tip has the remote tip as an ancestor - a fast-forward. If someone else pushed first, your history diverged and git refuses rather than silently discarding their work. Pull with merge creates a merge commit joining both lines; pull with --rebase replays your commits on top of theirs for a linear history at the cost of new commit hashes. Both are correct; teams pick one and stay consistent.

L4.prompt_tpl: git push is rejected with 'non-fast-forward'. What happened, and why is --force the wrong first response?
L4.answer: The remote branch has commits your branch does not, so your tip is not a descendant of theirs. --force overwrites those commits and destroys someone else's work. Fix: git pull (merge or rebase), resolve, then push.
L4.explanation: The rejection is git protecting commits that are not in your history. git says '(non-fast-forward)' once you have fetched and '(fetch first)' when your origin/main is still stale, but both mean the same thing. Force-pushing a shared branch is the one git operation that loses other people's commits; if you must rewrite a branch that is only yours, --force-with-lease refuses when the remote moved since your last fetch.

L4.prompt_tpl: git status says: Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have {n} and {m} different commits each, respectively. You run git pull with pull.rebase=false and it merges with no conflicts. By how many commits does the number printed by git rev-list --count HEAD grow? Answer with a single number.
L4.answer: m + 1: their m commits, plus the one merge commit. n=1, m=1 gives 2; n=2, m=2 gives 3; n=3, m=4 gives 5. Your own n commits were already reachable from HEAD, so n does not enter the count.
L4.explanation: In that status line the first number is your commits, the second is theirs. A merge pull downloads their m commits and builds one merge commit with two parents, so HEAD newly reaches m+1 commits. Your n commits were already counted. With --rebase the growth is only m, because your n commits are replayed rather than added. Re-run here on git 2.43.0 with n=2, m=2: the count went from 9 to 12.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your clone's main is at exactly the commit origin/main names. A colleague then pushes {k} commits to the remote's main. On git 2.43 you run, in order: git fetch origin ; git status -sb ; git log --oneline main..origin/main | wc -l. Give the output of the last two commands, and say whether HEAD or the working tree moved.
L4.answer: git status -sb prints: ## main...origin/main [behind K], where K is the number of commits the colleague pushed. wc -l prints that same K. HEAD and the working tree do not move: fetch only advanced the remote-tracking ref origin/main. Run before the fetch, the same log command prints 0.
L4.explanation: fetch is a download plus a ref update: objects land in .git and origin/main advances, but no branch of yours moves. That is also why the count is 0 before the fetch even though the commits already exist on the server - main..origin/main is measured against your cached copy of the remote, not against the remote. Verified on git 2.43.0 with K=3.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague tells you git fetch changes nothing locally. Which statement is exactly right?
L4.answer: It downloads the objects and advances remote-tracking refs such as origin/main; your branches, index and working tree are untouched.
L4.explanation: fetch is a download plus a ref update. The .git directory grows and origin/main moves; nothing you are editing moves. Option 2 is the misconception that makes a stale origin/main so confusing - it is exactly backwards, since the commits are already local after a fetch. Option 3 describes pull, which is fetch followed by a merge or a rebase.
options: It downloads the objects and advances remote-tracking refs such as origin/main; your branches, index and working tree are untouched.
It changes nothing at all - the new commits stay on the server until git pull downloads them.
It downloads the objects and fast-forwards your current branch, but leaves the working tree alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: On git 2.43 you run git pull on a branch that has diverged from origin/{b} and get: fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches. Nothing was merged. What state is the repository in, why did git refuse instead of merging, and give three different ways to answer the question git is asking.
L4.answer: Both sides gained commits since the merge base, so the pull cannot fast-forward. Current git will not choose merge or rebase for you when neither pull.rebase nor pull.ff is set. Answer per invocation with git pull --no-rebase, git pull --rebase, or git pull --ff-only; or set it once with git config pull.rebase false, git config pull.rebase true, or git config pull.ff only. The fetch half already ran, so origin has moved and nothing needs repairing.
L4.explanation: The refusal is specific to divergence: a pull that is a pure fast-forward still succeeds with no configuration at all. Reproduced on git 2.43.0 - origin/main advanced from bde61ce to e19148e and the branch was left untouched, with git status then reporting ahead 1, behind 2. Reading which half of the command failed is the whole skill here.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the fast-forward rule. Given that a commit's id is a hash over its tree, its message and its parent ids, explain why your commits cannot simply be appended to the remote's newer history, and why refusing a non-fast-forward branch update is what keeps commits from being lost. Then state what git push --force-with-lease checks that --force does not.
L4.answer: Your commits were built with the old remote tip as parent, and that parent id is inside their hashes, so re-parenting them onto the new tip yields different ids: a rewrite, not an append. A branch update whose new tip does not have the old tip as an ancestor would leave every commit reachable only from the old tip unreferenced on the server, so git refuses it unless forced. --force-with-lease additionally refuses unless the remote ref is still at the value you last fetched, so it can only overwrite history you have actually seen; --force overwrites whatever is there, including a commit pushed one second ago.
L4.explanation: This is the same immutability that makes editing any historical commit change every descendant hash - see 'git: commits and the staging area' - and it rests on the collision resistance covered in 'Hash functions'. The fast-forward test itself is pure reachability: is the old remote tip an ancestor of the proposed new tip. Nothing about content or correctness enters into it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A teammate rebased the shared branch {b}, which you had both already pushed, and force-pushed the result. Your local {b} still points at the old commits. Say what your next git pull does, why the resulting history looks duplicated, and give the safe recovery sequence.
L4.answer: Fetch moves the remote-tracking ref onto the rewritten commits. Those commits carry the same changes under new ids, so git sees two diverged lines, and the pull either merges them - replaying every rewritten change a second time and inventing conflicts - or stops with the divergent-branches fatal. Recovery: git fetch origin; inspect both directions with git log --oneline HEAD..origin/BRANCH and git log --oneline origin/BRANCH..HEAD; keep a safety pointer with git branch backup; git reset --hard origin/BRANCH; then cherry-pick back only the commits that were genuinely yours and never got rewritten.
L4.explanation: Rebase gives every replayed commit a new id, so identical content looks like unrelated work to git and a merge duplicates it. The fix is to adopt the remote's version of the shared branch and re-apply your own commits on top. This is why L2 says a rejected push is fixed by pulling, never by force-pushing a shared branch: the cost lands on everyone downstream, not on the person who forced.

L0.body:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "a.py", line 10, in <module>
    main()
  File "a.py", line 6, in main
    return parse(s)
  File "a.py", line 3, in parse
    return int(s)
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'

# read the LAST line first, then the frame above it
L0.cloze: In a Python traceback the {{c1::last}} line names the exception, and the frame just above it is where it was {{c2::raised}}.

concepts.L1: An error message names what went wrong, where, and how the program got there. Python prints the call chain oldest first and the exception last; C compilers print errors in source order with the first being the most trustworthy.
concepts.L2: For compiler errors, fix the first one and recompile - later errors are usually cascade damage from the first, and a missing semicolon or unbalanced brace can produce fifty messages about unrelated lines. For tracebacks the opposite holds: read from the bottom.
concepts.L3: A traceback's deepest frame is where the exception was raised, but the bug is usually a frame or two up, in the last frame that produced a value it should not have: int('x') behaved correctly, the code that handed it 'x' did not. Read bottom-up and stop at the first file you wrote. With two blocks, the older exception prints first, so the bottom block is the newer failure and the one above it the cause. The C cascade has a mechanism too: after a syntax error the parser discards tokens until it can resynchronise, so later messages describe a state the first error created, and the line gcc names is the line after the omission. A segfault carries no diagnostic: the shell reports 'Segmentation fault' with no location, so rebuild with gcc -g -fsanitize=address, which turns the crash into a file, a line and an access description. Debugging with a debugger takes over where the message stops.

L4.prompt_tpl:
You compile a C file with gcc on x86-64 Linux and get 40 errors. The first is:

file.c:{n}:5: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'return'

What do you do?
L4.answer: Fix the first error only, then recompile: after a syntax error the parser has lost sync and the rest is cascade noise
L4.explanation: After a syntax error the parser's state is wrong, so every later message is suspect: one fix and one rebuild beat reading all forty. Note where gcc points - line {n}, column 5, at the token it could not accept - while the semicolon belongs at the end of the statement above.
options: Fix the first error only, then recompile: after a syntax error the parser has lost sync and the rest is cascade noise
Fix the last error first: the compiler emits errors in reverse dependency order, so the final one is the root cause
Scan all forty and fix whichever message repeats most: repetition marks the real defect

L4.prompt_tpl: A Python traceback ends with `{exc}`. Which line names the code that raised, and which names the code you probably need to change?

exc: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'

L4.answer: The bottom frame, immediately above the exception line, is where the raise happened. The code to change is usually higher up: the lowest frame that is your own code and that produced the bad value. Python prints the call chain oldest first, so read the last line for what and walk upward for why.
L4.explanation: C compilers print in source order and the FIRST message is the trustworthy one; Python prints in call order and the LAST line is. Getting the direction right is most of the skill.

L4.answer: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '{bad}'
L4.explanation: The last line is always the exception type, a colon, then the message; the File lines above it are the route the program took to get there. int() raises ValueError, not TypeError: a str is an acceptable argument type, this particular text is not a base-10 numeral. The message quotes the offending value, which is how you know which element of values failed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Python script defines {n} functions. Module level calls the first, each function calls the next, and the last one raises ValueError with nothing catching it. How many lines beginning with the word File does the traceback print? Answer with the count.
L4.answer: n + 1: one File line for the module-level call plus one per function still on the stack. n=2 gives 3, n=3 gives 4, n=5 gives 6, n=7 gives 8.
L4.explanation: Python prints one frame per active call, oldest first, beginning with the module frame that ran the script; the chain of {n} calls adds {n} more. Verified by running such a script on CPython 3.11. Counting frames tells you how deep the failure is, and the frame worth reading is rarely the deepest one.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C file compiled with gcc on x86-64 Linux has one statement per line and no blank lines or comments. gcc's first message is file.c:{n}:5: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'return'. On which line must the missing semicolon actually be typed? Answer with the line number.
L4.answer: Line n - 1, the statement above the one gcc names. n=6 gives 5, n=12 gives 11, n=41 gives 40, n=58 gives 57.
L4.explanation: The parser only discovers the missing semicolon when it reads a token that cannot follow the previous statement, so it reports that token's position, not the omission's. Verified on gcc 13.3.0: a statement missing its semicolon on line 5 is reported as file.c:6:5: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'return'. When a syntax error looks impossible, look one line up.

L4.answer: RuntimeError
L4.explanation: Python prints the older exception first, then the sentence During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred, then the newer one. The bottom block is the most recent failure, RuntimeError, and the KeyError block above it is what actually went wrong. Read the last line for what, then read upward - past the separator - for why.

L4.prompt_tpl:
On x86-64 Linux you run gcc main.c -o app and get:

/usr/bin/ld: main.o: in function 'main':
main.c:(.text+0xe): undefined reference to '{sym}'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

Which stage failed, and what does that tell you about the fix?
L4.answer: The link stage: every call to {sym} type-checked against a declaration, but no object file or library on the command line defines it, so add the missing .c file or the -l library
L4.explanation: gcc drives three tools, and the message names which one spoke: /usr/bin/ld and collect2, not cc1. The compiler accepted main.c because a declaration was in scope; ld failed because no definition of {sym} exists in any input. Missing declaration is a compile error, missing definition is a link error, missing shared library is a run-time error - three stages, three fixes.
options: The link stage: every call to {sym} type-checked against a declaration, but no object file or library on the command line defines it, so add the missing .c file or the -l library
The compile stage: the header that declares {sym} was not included, so add the include directive and recompile
The run stage: {sym} was resolved at start-up and the dynamic loader could not find it, so set LD_LIBRARY_PATH and rerun

L4.prompt_tpl:
Python 3.11 prints this traceback for a script you wrote, load.py:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/me/load.py", line 10, in <module>
    load(["2026-01-05,3", "{bad},4"])
  File "/home/me/load.py", line 8, in load
    return [parse_row(l) for l in lines]
  File "/home/me/load.py", line 8, in <listcomp>
    return [parse_row(l) for l in lines]
  File "/home/me/load.py", line 5, in parse_row
    return datetime.strptime(stamp, "%Y-%m-%d"), int(value)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.11/_strptime.py", line 567, in _strptime_datetime
    tt, fraction, gmtoff_fraction = _strptime(data_string, format)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.11/_strptime.py", line 349, in _strptime
    raise ValueError
ValueError: time data '{bad}' does not match format '%Y-%m-%d'

Which frame do you change, why is the deepest frame not the bug, and what do you print first?
L4.answer: The two deepest frames are in _strptime.py, library code doing exactly what it was asked: it reports which value it rejected. Reading bottom-up, the first frame in a file you wrote is line 5 of load.py, in parse_row, so that is where the fix or the check goes. Print stamp (and the whole line) at the top of parse_row, then ask the real question: which caller put a row shaped like {bad} into lines. The listcomp frame is not noise - Python gives a comprehension its own frame.
L4.explanation: Read bottom-up and stop at the first frame in a file you wrote: that is the boundary between the library behaving correctly and your data being wrong. Library frames tell you which API rejected the value; your frame tells you which value, and the frame above that tells you where it came from. Next step: Debugging by print and bisection.

L0.body:
print(f'{i=} {x=}', file=sys.stderr)     # 3.8+: prints 'i=3 x=7'
fprintf(stderr, "i=%d x=%d\n", i, x);

bisection: does the bug exist at the halfway point?
  yes -> search the first half     no -> search the second
  ~log2(n) checks to localise it
$ git bisect start / bad / good     # same idea over commit history
L0.cloze: Bisection localises a fault in about log2({{c1::n}}) checks by halving the {{c2::search space}} each time.

concepts.L1: Print debugging inserts observations at chosen points; bisection halves the region under suspicion each time. Together they localise most bugs without any tooling, and bisection is what makes print debugging efficient rather than random.
concepts.L2: Print to stderr, not stdout: redirected stdout is block-buffered, so a crash discards the buffer and your last prints never appear. But stderr is not simply unbuffered: C guarantees only that it is not fully buffered, and CPython line-buffers it, so a stderr write with no newline is lost too. flush=True closes that gap.
concepts.L3: Bisection is binary search over program state or over history. Between a point where the invariant holds and a point where it does not, check the midpoint: 20 checks localise a fault among a million lines executed. git bisect automates it over commits, finding the breaking commit in log2(n) builds - about 10 for a thousand commits. The discipline that makes it work is choosing a single yes/no predicate before you start; without one you are just adding prints and hoping.

L4.prompt_tpl: A regression appeared somewhere in the last {n} commits. How many builds does git bisect need in the worst case?
L4.explanation: Each test halves the candidate range. That is why bisecting a year of history is a coffee break rather than a project.

L4.answer: It prints {bad}, the first index where the predicate holds. Worked draw n=100, bad=41: the probes are 50, 25, 38, 44, 41, 40 and the loop ends after 6 steps with lo = hi = 41. Draw n=256, bad=7: 8 probes, prints 7.
L4.explanation: Bisection is binary search over an index range. The loop keeps one invariant - the first true index always lies in [lo, hi] - so halving is safe, and when lo == hi that single surviving value is the answer. Six or seven probes cover a hundred candidates. This is exactly the loop in Binary search, run over program state or over commits instead of over an array.

L4.prompt_tpl: You run git bisect start, then git bisect bad on HEAD, then git bisect good on tag {tag}. git checks out a commit in the middle of that range; you build it and test, and the bug is present. Which command do you type next?
L4.answer: git bisect bad
L4.explanation: Each step you label the commit you just tested, not the state you are hoping for. The bug is present, so this commit is bad; bisect throws away everything newer and checks out the midpoint of the older half. git bisect good would send the search the wrong way and hand you a wrong first-bad commit; git bisect reset abandons the session and returns you to the branch you started on.
options: git bisect bad
git bisect good
git bisect reset

L4.prompt_tpl:
x86-64 Linux, CPython 3.11, PYTHONUNBUFFERED unset. The script is run as: python3 t.py > out.txt 2> err.txt, so both streams are files on disk, not a terminal.

import sys, os, signal
print('{a}')
sys.stdout.write('{b}')
print('{c}', file=sys.stderr)
sys.stderr.write('{d}')
os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGKILL)

SIGKILL cannot be caught, so no exit handler runs and nothing is flushed on the way out. How many of the four writes actually appear in the two files? Answer with the count.
L4.answer: Exactly 1. out.txt is empty: redirected stdout is block-buffered, so both stdout writes die inside the buffer. err.txt holds only the newline-terminated stderr line, because CPython line-buffers stderr; the fragment written without a newline is lost with the process. Run and checked on this machine: out.txt 0 bytes, err.txt 6 bytes.
L4.explanation: Two lessons in one trace. First, never debug through redirected stdout: a block buffer is discarded when the process dies. Second, stderr is not magic - CPython line-buffers it, so a complete line lands immediately but a fragment does not. In C on glibc stderr really is unbuffered and even the fragment survives. End every debug print with a newline, or pass flush=True.

L4.prompt_tpl: Halfway through bisecting a range of {n} commits, the commit git checked out does not compile at all, so your test can call it neither good nor bad. Which single git command tells bisect to set that commit aside and offer a neighbour instead? Answer with the command only.
L4.answer: git bisect skip
L4.explanation: Guessing a label to keep the bisect moving poisons the search: bisection is only valid while the predicate is monotone (all good, then all bad), and one invented answer discards the half that held the real first-bad commit. git bisect skip drops the untestable commit; if a whole region is unbuildable, bisect ends by naming a set of candidates rather than one commit, which is an honest answer rather than a wrong one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the reach of bisection from first principles: every test returns one bit, yes or no, and you choose the next test after seeing the previous answer. At most how many distinct candidate positions can {k} tests tell apart? Answer with that count.
L4.answer: Two to the power of the number of tests: k=5 distinguishes 32 candidates, k=10 distinguishes 1024, k=16 distinguishes 65536. Read the other way, pinning one candidate out of $n$ needs at least $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$ tests, which is the count the git bisect item on this concept asks for.
L4.explanation: A run of $t$ yes/no tests produces one of $2^{t}$ possible answer sequences, and two candidates that produce the same sequence can never be told apart. So $2^{t}$ is a hard ceiling, and bisection reaches it exactly because each test splits the surviving set in half. That is the same counting argument that gives the $\log$ in Binary search and the growth class $O(\log n)$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your reproducer is flaky: on a commit that is genuinely good it still fails with probability {p}, independently on each run. You run the test once per bisect step, and all {k} steps happen to land on good commits. What is the probability that not one step lies to you? Answer as a decimal between 0 and 1.
L4.answer: The probability that every step is honest is one minus the flake rate, raised to the number of steps. p=0.05, k=10: 0.5987. p=0.05, k=20: 0.3585. p=0.1, k=10: 0.3487. p=0.1, k=20: 0.1216.
L4.explanation: Each step is an independent Bernoulli trial, so honest runs multiply. A 5 percent flake rate over ten steps already gives a 40 percent chance that one spurious failure marks a good commit bad, and bisection then discards the half containing the real culprit - silently, with a confident answer at the end. Fix the reproducer first: see Determinism, and why tests go flaky.
