concepts.t: Regression tests: reproduce before you fix

L0.body:
1. reproduce the bug reliably
2. write a FAILING test that captures it
3. fix the code
4. watch the test go green
5. keep the test forever

# if you cannot make it fail on demand, you cannot know you fixed it
L0.cloze: Write the {{c1::failing}} test before the fix, so that seeing it go {{c2::green}} proves the fix addressed the actual bug.

concepts.L1: A regression test encodes a bug that actually occurred, so it can never recur silently. Writing it before the fix proves both that you reproduced the bug and that your change is what resolved it.
concepts.L2: Fixing first and testing after produces tests that pass for the wrong reason - a test written against fixed code often exercises a different path than the bug did. If the test does not fail before the fix, you have not demonstrated it tests the bug at all.
concepts.L3: The order matters most for bugs that are hard to reproduce. A concurrency bug reproducible one time in a thousand needs the reproduction made reliable first - forcing a delay, pinning a seed, shrinking the input - and that work is what turns 'seems fixed' into 'is fixed'. A suite built this way is a record of every mistake the system has actually made, which is far better targeted than tests written from imagination, and it is why bug-driven suites tend to catch more than coverage-driven ones.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague fixes a bug and says the test suite passes, so no new test is needed. Give the argument against.
L4.answer: The suite passing before and after proves the bug was untested. Without a test that fails on the old code, nothing prevents the bug from returning in the next refactor, and there is no evidence this change is what fixed it.
L4.explanation: Every bug that reached production is by definition a gap in the suite. The fix is incomplete until the gap is closed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team fixes {bugkind} and then adds a test for it to the suite. Which statement best describes what makes that test a regression test rather than just one more unit test?

bugkind: a lost update in a queue

L4.answer: It is derived from a defect that actually occurred, and it fails on the unfixed code.
L4.explanation: A regression test is defined by its origin and its evidence: it comes from a real defect, and it was seen to fail on the code that had the defect. Speed and authorship are irrelevant. Without the observed failure you have a test of unknown power sitting next to a fix of unproven effect.
options: It is derived from a defect that actually occurred, and it fails on the unfixed code.
It runs faster than the rest of the suite because it exercises only one function.
It is written by the person who reported the bug rather than by the author of the fix.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have reproduced {symptom} and written a test that captures it. You now run that test against the code exactly as it stands today, with no fix applied. For the reproduce-before-you-fix workflow to have done its job, what single result must you see? Answer with one word: pass, fail, or skip.

symptom: an off-by-one in a page index

L4.answer: fail
L4.explanation: The red run is the whole point. It is the only evidence that the test actually touches the buggy behaviour, and it is the baseline against which the later green run means anything. A test that passes on the unfixed code is testing something else; a skipped test is testing nothing at all.

L4.prompt_tpl:
A bug report says this function returns the wrong value for even-length inputs. On CPython 3.12, what does the last line print? Answer with the number.

def median(xs):
    xs = sorted(xs)
    return xs[len(xs) // 2]

print(median([{a}, {b}, {c}, {d}]))
L4.answer: The third smallest element, c. Draw a=1, b=3, c=6, d=9 prints 6; draw a=2, b=4, c=7, d=9 prints 7; draw a=1, b=4, c=6, d=9 prints 6. The true median of four values is the mean of the middle two.
L4.explanation: The list has four elements, so len(xs) // 2 is 2 and the function returns xs[2] - the upper of the two middle values, not their mean. Reproduce the report exactly before touching the code: a test written with three inputs would pass on this buggy version and prove nothing.

L4.prompt_tpl:
The bug report says tail returns the whole list when asked for zero elements. On CPython 3.12, how many elements does the printed list contain? Answer with the count.

def tail(xs, n):
    return xs[-n:]

xs = list(range(1, {k} + 1))
print(tail(xs, 0))
L4.answer: All k elements. k=5 prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; k=7 prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]; k=9 prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The intended answer was the empty list.
L4.explanation: There is no negative zero in Python ints, so -0 is 0 and xs[-0:] is xs[0:] - the whole list. This is exactly the case a test written after the fix would omit: any test using n=2 passes on the broken code. Reproduce with n=0 first, watch it fail, then fix.

L4.prompt_tpl:
This test was added to close bug 412 and was never run against the unfixed code. It passes, and it went green on the very first run. Say why it would pass against any implementation of {fn} whatsoever, and rewrite it so that it could have failed.

def test_issue_412():
    expected = {fn}("  A b ")
    assert {fn}("  A b ") == expected
L4.answer: Both sides of the assertion call the same function on the same input, so the test asserts only that the function is deterministic - it holds for a function that returns the empty string, or the input unchanged, or anything else. The expected value must be a literal written by hand from the bug report, for example: assert normalise("  A b ") == "a b". Run that against the unfixed code first and confirm it goes red.
L4.explanation: A test that compares an implementation to itself is a tautology. The green-on-first-run smell is the tell: a regression test that has never been red carries no information. The fix is a hand-written literal expectation taken from the report, checked against the buggy build before the patch lands.

L4.prompt_tpl: You turned your reproduction into a script that exits 0 when the bug is absent and non-zero when it is present, so git bisect run can drive it. There are {n} candidate commits between the last known-good commit and the known-bad one, exactly one of which introduced the bug. In the worst case, how many of those commits does the bisect have to test? Answer with the number of test runs.
L4.answer: $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$ runs. n=8 gives 3, n=16 gives 4, n=32 gives 5, n=64 gives 6, n=1024 gives 10.
L4.explanation: Each run halves the surviving candidates, so $k$ runs can separate at most $2^{k}$ of them and you need $k = \lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$. This is why the reproduction has to be automated and reliable before it is useful: bisection over a flaky predicate reports a random commit. See Debugging by print and bisection.

concepts.t: Determinism, and why tests go flaky

L0.body:
sources of nondeterminism:
  unseeded random          -> random.seed(0) / np.random.default_rng(0)
  wall-clock time          -> inject a clock, do not call time.time()
  set iteration order      -> hash-randomised per process; sort before comparing
  concurrency & timing     -> sleeps are not synchronisation
  filesystem & network     -> tmp_path, and stub the network
  floating point           -> compare with a tolerance
  (a Python dict iterates in insertion order; a Go map deliberately does not)
L0.cloze: A {{c1::flaky}} test passes and fails on the same code, and the usual cure is removing a source of {{c2::nondeterminism}}.

concepts.L1: A test is deterministic when the same code always yields the same verdict. Flaky tests fail intermittently for reasons unrelated to correctness, and they destroy the suite's value because failures stop being believed.
concepts.L2: The damage from a flaky test exceeds its usefulness: once a suite has a few, every red build is assumed to be noise and real regressions get merged. A flaky test should be fixed or deleted, and 'rerun until green' is a policy for shipping bugs.
concepts.L3: Determinism is achieved by injecting the varying thing rather than calling it. Pass a clock or a random generator in as a parameter and the test supplies a fixed one - the same dependency-injection move that makes network and filesystem access testable. Sleeps deserve special mention: `time.sleep(0.1)` to wait for a thread is timing-dependent by construction, so it passes on your laptop and fails on a loaded CI machine. Wait on an event or a condition variable instead. Float comparisons need math.isclose for exactly the reasons in the numbers section - the same test can pass on one CPU and fail on another with different vectorisation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A test does: start_worker(); time.sleep({t}); assert queue.empty(). Why is it flaky, and what replaces the sleep?
L4.answer: It assumes the worker finishes within t seconds, which depends on machine load - so it passes locally and fails under a loaded CI. Replace the sleep with a synchronisation primitive: wait on an Event the worker sets, or join the thread with a generous timeout and assert it completed.
L4.explanation: A sleep encodes a guess about timing, so the test passes on a fast machine and fails on a loaded CI runner. Waiting on an explicit signal - a queue join, a condition variable, a future - is both faster and correct, because it waits exactly as long as necessary and no longer.

L4.prompt_tpl: CPython 3.11 on Linux. A script runs, in this order: import random; random.seed({s}); a = [random.random() for i in range(3)]; random.seed({s}); b = [random.random() for i in range(3)]; print(a == b). What single word does it print?
L4.answer: True. Verified by running it here: with seed 7 the first draw is 0.32383276483316237 and with seed 12345 it is 0.41661987254534116, and in both cases a == b prints True.
L4.explanation: seed() sets the generator's whole internal state, so the second seeding rewinds it and the same three draws come out again. That is what makes a seeded test reproducible: the numbers are still arbitrary, but they are the same arbitrary numbers on your laptop and on CI. An unseeded generator is seeded from the OS entropy source instead, and then every run is a different test.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CI suite has {n} tests. Each one fails spuriously with probability {p} on any given run, independently of the others. What percentage of runs are red for a reason that has nothing to do with the code? Answer with the percentage.
L4.answer: $100(1-(1-p)^{n})$ percent. Worked draws: $n=200$, $p=0.001$ gives 18.14 percent; $n=200$, $p=0.002$ gives 32.99 percent; $n=500$, $p=0.001$ gives 39.36 percent; $n=500$, $p=0.002$ gives 63.25 percent.
L4.explanation: The run is green only if every test is green, so the green probability is $(1-p)^{n}$ and the red-for-nothing probability is its complement. This is why a per-test flake rate that sounds negligible is not: at one failure in a thousand, a 500-test suite is red for no reason on about two runs in five, and the team learns to ignore red.

L4.prompt_tpl: A test writes its output to the fixed path {path} and then asserts on the contents. Two pytest processes running the suite at the same time overwrite each other's file, so each sometimes fails. Which built-in pytest fixture should supply the directory instead, so that every test gets its own? Answer with the fixture name only.
L4.answer: tmp_path
L4.explanation: tmp_path is a pathlib.Path to a directory pytest creates fresh for that one test, so no two tests and no two processes can collide, and the contents survive afterwards for inspection. tmp_path_factory is the session-scoped sibling for fixtures that need a shared directory. A hard-coded path in a test is shared mutable state on the filesystem.

L4.prompt_tpl: CPython 3.11 on Linux, default settings. A test does: got = list(set([{words}])) and asserts that got equals a hard-coded list in that order. It passes every time you run it locally that afternoon, then fails on CI. Say what varies and what does not, and give the one-line fix.
L4.answer: Set iteration order follows the hash table layout, and CPython randomises the hash of str and bytes per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the order is stable within one process - which is why repeated local runs agreed - and varies between processes. Fix: assert on sorted(got), or compare sets rather than lists. Setting PYTHONHASHSEED=0 pins it but hides the bug rather than fixing it.
L4.explanation: Confirmed by running it: four separate processes printed four different orders, two prints inside one process agreed, and PYTHONHASHSEED=0 pinned the order. A dict would not have shown this - Python dicts iterate in insertion order since 3.7 - so the culprit here is the set, not dicts in general. The rule is to compare on an order-independent view: sorted, or set to set.

L4.prompt_tpl: A function stamps every record with the current UTC time, and a reader treats a record as expired once it is more than {mins} minutes old. Design a test that checks both sides of that boundary without sleeping and without depending on the machine clock. State the change to the production signature and what the test passes in.
L4.answer: Make the clock a parameter: def stamp(record, now=time.time) and def is_expired(record, now=time.time), keeping the real clock as the default so callers are unchanged. The test passes a fake: now = lambda: 1_000_000.0 to stamp, then a reader clock returning 1_000_000.0 + mins*60 - 1 (not expired) and + 1 (expired). Two assertions, no sleep, no wall clock. Where the call is buried in a third-party library, monkeypatch the module attribute instead, but injection is the version that survives refactoring.
L4.explanation: This is dependency injection used as a testing tool: the varying thing becomes an argument, and the test supplies a constant. The boundary values come straight from 'Test the boundaries' - one second either side of the cutoff distinguishes a strict comparison from a non-strict one, which no sleep-based test can do, and the test now runs in microseconds instead of minutes.

L4.prompt_tpl: pytest 9 on x86-64 Linux. test_order.py is exactly: {state} = [] , then def test_first(): {state}.append('a'); assert {state} == ['a'] , then def test_second(): {state}.append('b'); assert {state} == ['b'] . Running pytest on the file reports 1 failed, 1 passed, with test_second failing on assert ['a', 'b'] == ['b']; running pytest test_order.py::test_second on its own passes. Name the defect class, say which test is genuinely at fault, and give the fix.
L4.answer: An order-dependent test: the module-level list is shared mutable state that survives between tests, so test_second sees what test_first left behind. Neither test arranges its own state, but test_second is the one asserting on state it did not create. Fix: build the list inside each test, or hand it over by an autouse fixture that constructs a fresh one per test - never a module global. Then run the suite in a shuffled order (pytest-randomly, or pytest-xdist across processes) so that any remaining order dependence fails immediately rather than on the day someone adds a test in the middle.
L4.explanation: Verified by running it here: the whole file gives 1 failed, 1 passed, and test_second alone passes. This is nondeterminism without any clock or random number in sight - the varying input is the set and order of the other tests. It is also the reason 'arrange' is the first A in arrange-act-assert: a test that does not build its own state is reading someone else's.
